DIGNITY OF LOWLY WORK. Nls not this the carpenter, the son of Mary P"—ST. A lesson, Lord, those eighteen years to me; Not elsewhere I could so divinely learn That humble tasks are best, howe'er I yearn For higher sphere where I may work more free. Blest were those patient toiling years to Thee, Their secret kept within Thy lonely heart, While Thou wait trained by daily skill of att To build new world for human destiny. Thy Future was the Now. 'Twas from its height Thine eye read meanings in the passing day. 14 cross of Death cast shadows on Thy way, What sun was that so darkened in his light? 0 Nazarene out of these toils there came That which prize most dear—a Brother's name. —Harper's Monthly Magazine. A TYPOGRAPHICAL TALL Net three years ago the Rotten Globe started on his trawls an Arab donkey-driver, who has since met with a series of surprising adventures, some of which have been typograpically descriSed by she GlebeT contemporaries in various parte of the count-y. As will be seen by the following, the Arab has just stopped travel Enc.- An Arab came to the river side With a donkey bearing an obelisk ; Tut he would not try to ford the tide, For he had too good an *.
—Boston Glo;se,1881. So he camped all night by the river side, And remained till the tide had ceased ta swell, For he knew, should the donkey from life subside, He should never find its j.

—Salem Sunbeam. When morning dawned and the tide was out, The pair crossed over 'ncath Allah's protection, For the Arab was happy, we have no doubt, For he had the best donkey in all that §. —Somerville Journal. That donkey was seen by some Yen Lee man, Who raised his voice and loud did ballot, "Bow much you'll take for that era beast In gold or silver er paper S ?" —Detroit Free Press.

The Arab knew, when the man said "etc," He belonged to the dickering 'Yankee nation, And believing Yankees never swapped fair, He paid no heed to the?. —Glok. But soon was spied a Texas chap, Who wore long hair and had a swagger: " Look here, pard, I want that beast," And in the Arab he stuck his t. , —New Bedford Nom
As fortune would have it, the t glanced, Or it might have made the &rat) croak, And. seizing the obelisk, the latter chanced To make on tho Taxan a fatal —Brooklyn Chronicle.

So the ass was saved, and the obelisk too, And homeward the Arab made his way. To Allah his thanks he gave anew, That a . had come to the hapless fray. —Detroit Free Press, Jane, 18E2. Soon they reached their courney's end, The male was frisky under the lash, And while the girls looked brightly on The male and master cut a —. —Philadelphia Est/sing Ni-zrs. And when the man got off the mule, He looked so charming and so grand, Each girl a leap year privilege took, And begged him to accept her Sir. —Monthly Union.
He thought he'd like to marry them all, And smiled on them with an artless grace, They made a rush for the haughty man, And he caught them all in an —Boston Star.
The Caliph said he loved too well, And embraced so much he deserved the rod, So before the shades of evening fell. The Arab and ass were safe in . —Boston Globs, 1884.
And now the story has crossed the sea, Let some great mind construct the sequel; For sure we are, as sure can be, That 'twill. be bard to find its

Patient: " Dootor, what do you do when you have a cold in the head r—Dootor : "Well, madam, I sneeze most of the time." "Talking about the jaws of death !" exclaimed a man who is living with his third scolding wife. "I tell you they are nothing to the jaws of life !" It is all right to toll a bell, but it makes a difference how you do it. A man once told a belle he would marry her, and it cost him /LOGO because he didn't. Robert Smith, brother of Sydney, and familiarly called " Bobus," was a lawyer and ex-advocate-general, and hap- pened on one occasion to be engaged in an argument with an excellent physician touching the merits of their respec- tive professions. "You mast admit," urged Dr. X., "that your profession does not make angels of men." "No," was the retort," there you have the best of it; yours certainly gives them the first chance." -

COYMUNICATION WITH aNLISALS.—Sit John Lubbock writes to the Spectafro :—Yoa did me the honour, some weeks ago, to insert a leter of mine, containing suggestions as to a method of study lag the pyschology of animals, and a short account of a beginning I had myself made in that direetion. This letter has elicited various replies and sug- geetions, which you will,perhaps allow me to answer; and I may also take the opportunity of stating the progress which my dog Van has made, although, owing greatly, no doubt, to my frequent absences from home and the little time I can devote to hint, this has not been so rapid as I doubt not would otherwise have been the case. Perhaps I may just repeat that the essence of my idea was to have various words such as "food," " bone," " water," " out," to., printed on • pieces of cardboard, and after some preliminary training, to , give the dog anything for which he asked by bringing a card. I use pieces of pieces of carclboaad about ten inches . long and three inches .high, placing a number of them on the floor, side by aide, so that the dog has several cards to select from, each bearing a different word. One correspon- dent has suggested that it would be better to use variously ooloured cards. This might, no doubt, render the first steps rather more easy, but, on the other hand, any temporary ad- vantage gained would be at the expense of subsequent diffi- culty, since the papil woald very likely begin by associating the object with the colour, rather than with the letters. He would, therefore, as is too often the case with our own chil- dren, have the unnecessary labour of unlearning some of his first lessons. At the same time the experiment would have an interest as a test of the colour•sense in dogs. Another enggeation has been that, instead of words, pictorial repre- sentations should be ?lased on the cards. This, however, ocrald only be done with material objects, such as "food," "bone," "water," itc, and would not be applicable to such words as "out," " pet me," a.c.; nor even as regards the former class do I see that it would present any substantial advantage. Again, it has been ruggested that "Van" is led by scent rather than by sight. Ee has, no doubt, anexcellent nose, but in this case he is certainly guided by the eye. The cards are all handled by us, and must emit very nearly the same odour. Ido not, however rely on this, but have in use .a numbec of cards bearing the same word. When, for in- :stance, he has brought a card with "food" on it, we do not put down the same identical card, but another with the frame word; when he has brought that, a third is put down, ,and so on. -For a single meal, therefore, eight or ten cards swill have been used, and it seems clear, therefore, th. 7.4 in „selecting them "Van' must be guided by the letters. eWhen I last wrote, I had satisfied myself that he had learat to regard the bringing of a card as a request, and that ha , could distinguish a card with the word "food" on it from« , plain one; while I believed that he could distinguish be- tween a card with" food" on it, and one with "out "on it. . .

--- I have now no doubt that he can distinguish between different words. For instance, when ha is hungry he will bring a " food " card time after time, until he has had enough, and then ha lies quietly down for a nap. Again, when I am going for a walk, and invite him to come, he gladly responds by picking up the" out" card, and run- ning triumphantly with it before nie to the front door. In the same way he know= the " bone " card quite well. As regards water, which I spell phonetically, 80 as not to con- fuse him unnecessarily), I keep a card always on the floor In my dressing-room, and whenever he is thirsty he goes off there, without any suggestion from me, and brings the card with perfect gravity. At the same time he is fond of a zame., and if he is playful or excited will occasionally run about without any card. If through inadvertance he brings a card for something he does not want, when the correspond- ing object is shown to him, he seizes the card, takes it back again, and fetches the right one. No one who has seen him look along a row cf cards, and select the right one, can, I think, doubt that in bringing a ...,ard he feels that he is making a request, aud that 'he can not only perfectly dis- tinguish between one word and another, but also associates the word and the object. I do not for a moment say that Van thus shows more intelligence than has been recorded in the cue of other dogs; that is not my point; but it does 888111 to me that this method of instruction opens out a means by which dogs and other animals may be enabled to communicate with us more satisfactorily than hitherto. i am still continuing my observations, and am now consider- ing the best mode of testing him in very simple arithmetic. but Pwish I could iinducs others to co-operate, for I fei satistied that the system would well repay more time an Attention than I myself am able to give.

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, tr.o. Feasttets' ENEMlES.,—According te a paper read a few weeks ago at the Rochester Club three seems to be a great difference of opinion as to what birds, animals, and insects are the farmer's friends and what are not. Among the latter the jackdaw and the woodcieeon took the lead, while protection was advised for such birds as the crow, magpie, and jay, which are commonly believed to be destructive and prejudicial to the fareaer'sinterssts, as it was alleged that the good they do by the destruction of insect pests more than counterbalances the loss they occasion by the con- sumption of grain and fruit. Toads, snakes, blind-worms, and ladybirds were all shown to be allied of the farmer, as also were badgers, weasels, and hawks. CHESHIRE AGRICULTCRAL SOCIETY.—The committee of the Cheshire Agricultural Society have accepted an invita- tion from the Middlewich and Northwicti Agricultural Society to hold their next exhibition at Northwich, the local society agreeing to forego their exhibition this year and assist the prize list of the parent society. The prises offered foe the best cultivated farms and cottzgers' gardens are the same as last year. The prizes for cheese are also the same, with the exception of the prize which was given for exhibits where the owners were allowed to bore the cheese. The peizes in ' the horned stock division include three five guinea cups given by Sir Phillip Egerton, to be awarded to tenant farmers. Several alterations have been made in the prize list in consideration of the show this year being only a one day's exhibition. The data has been fixed for Sept. 3, and the local committee are arranging for a dog and poultry show. Tim FRENCH PEASANT PROPRIEVORS.—The current . camber of To-day contains a remarkably able article on Peasant Proprietary in France," by M. Paul Lefargue, in which statements, supported by many authoritios, are made which should be read by every advocate of peasant pro- prietorship. M. Lefargae shows that the French peasant proprietor is a very ignorant man, averse to anything new in agriculture; that he is very heavily burdened by debt; and that his life is an extremely laborious one. The land is lamentably sub-divided where it is owned by the peasants; but it is gradually passing oat of their hands into those of rich men, and the conclusion of the writer is that "a peas- ant proprietary, except under certain special conditions, can only exist in a feudal system of society, but that in the social system of the bourgeioeie it forms (save in the environs of towns) an anachronism that all the forces of capitalist production are tending to wipe away." No doubt M. La- , fargue writes from a socialist point of view; but this does not detract from the weight of the evidence he brings for- ward. SIGNS OF IMPROVEMENT.—As sa sign of the improved condition of agriculture, it may be mentioned that the Mar- quess of Conyngham, who is a large landowner in the eastern division of Bent, has not now a single farm in hand, the last vacant one having been let on Lady Day. Lord Greville has also been very suocessfal in the letting of his farms in the same part of the country. Oa the other hand, the Rec- tory Farm, Welton-le-Wold, near Louth, has been let by auction. The glebe farm consists of a good house and out- buildings, and 350 acres of good land. The lot was put up at a rental of 12s. per acre, and the bidding increased by shillings up to 75., when there was a long pease. The auc- tioneer declared that it was now an open sale and pressed Therefor another ed. per acre. There was no fusilier advance, and the encase:dal bidder was Mr. E. K. Smithson. This sum includes the right to all game, and there is some valu- able shooting. The inventory was estimated at-about £5OO. Several years ago this 'farm was let at 30s. per acre, and the tenant at the time-of letting was paying about 265. per acre. THE DAIRY CONFERENCE.—The fast approaching con- ference on subjects of interest to those engaged in dairy farming, which is to he carried out under the auspices of the Milk Committee of the Gloucestershire Chamber of Agri- culture and the Sanitary and',Economic Association, Limi- ted, is of a most important character. It has been definitely arranged to hold the conference at Gloucester on May 22nd, and two following days. The subjects to be discussed cover a wide field. First comes the question of the selection and breeding of dairy cattle, then covered versus open folds, followed by a consideration of the practice of eneilage with regard to dairy purposes, succeeded in turn by such topics as the relative merits of dairy factories and home manufac- ture, the various modes of cream separation, how best to utilise batterless milk and whey, milk testing and dairy re- cords as essential to successful milk production, aseptic conditions as essential to successful milk conversion, and the needs of dairy farming in view of the requirements of the future in regard to the better training of these engaged in it, better appliances for carrying it on, more effective, means of collecting, testing, and diffusing knowledge of 1 Inew improvements, more combination with dairy farming I of minor subsidiary industries, better protection againstl losses by epizootics, better facilities for distribution of maaufactared productseand better organisation of resources at local centres for the promotion of some of the foregoing objects. Here is a programme which will severely tax the po were of a three-days' conference to deal with. ROYAL AGRICULTURAL COLLEGE, CIRENCESTER,— The spring term of this institution was concluded last week, when the diplomas medals, certificates, scholarships, and prizes were distribuied by Colonel Bingscote, C. 8., M.P., one of the members of the governing body. The report of the principal, the Rev. J. B. Mc.Clellan, showed that the work had been most satisfactory, one of the leading features of interest being that the successful Candidates for the diploma included one of the Indian students who occupy the scholarships founded at the college by the Bengal Govern- ment. In addition to this, several of the other Bengal scholars gained places of distinction on the class list. The diploma of the college was awarded to the following stu- dents :—Jas. H. Dagdale, 9, Hyde Park-gardens, London; Girls Chandra Bose, Bengal scholar; William T. Brown, Wokingham, Berke; Wm. Brier, Bollington, Macclesfield. Duck gold medal, James Henry Dagdale. Scholarships— First, Dalziell • second, Dickson and Reese, equal. The fol- lowing receieed honourable mention, in order of merit : Curry, Chavasse, Cave, Allen, J. T. Davies, B. C. Basu (Indian student), Tonger, Mehta (Indian student), Scott, and M`Donald. The competition for the certificates and prizes in the various classes was very keen. Col.Kingecote, in addressing the students, said that the examination for the diploma of that college was higher, more practical, and more ueeful than the exhibitions Instituted and held. yearly by the Royal Agricultural Society and the Highland Agri- cultural Society. Whether they settled at home. in America, or in the colonies, their training at that college would help them to lay out the money instrusted to them, whether their own or some one else's, in the most remunera- tive manner. THE "Royal? Snow AT Yonn.—The official statement of accounts relating to the show of the Royal Agricultural Society, held at •York last summer, which is now for the first time published in the spring number of the society's "Journal." shows that the total expenditure amounted to £15,544 12s. 5d., and the receipts to £20,834 45., leaving the eminently satisfactory balance of £5,189 us. 7d. added to the funds of the society. The actual outlay for show yard works NYSE £,654, from which, however, must be de- ducted the gam of £5,250 proceeds of the sale of materials used and the work executed for exhibitors, &c., thns reduc- ing the net cost of the show yard works to £4,404. The judges received for their services L 546, of which £477 went to the judges of stock, the balance going to the implement judges. A further eum of £123 was required for the shear- ing and veterinary inspectors and assistants; :!:287 for the foreman, yardmen, grooms, foddermen, labourers, &c.; for the engineering department; while as much as £455 was handed over to the metropolitan and county police. The stewards' expenses, with lodgings for themselves .and other officials, came to £362; and £4lO had to be paid as compensation to the pasture-masters for clearing the Knavesmire of live stock previous to the show on account of the much-dreaded outbreak of foot and mouth disease. The large sum of £919 was expended for the two bulky catalogues of the various exhibits, and £1,725 for printing and advertising; the working dairy cost £288; fodder for the animals reached the surprisingly large total of £1,128 ; and the actual expenditure for stock prizes was £3,775. The last-named amount, it should be noted, is exclusive of ££3so given by the York Local Committee, £295 by the I Yorkshire Agricultural Society, and sundry prizes presented 'by other donors. With regard to the receipts, the largese item is. of course' due to the show yard, which realised £9,837; the next largest amount is £4,453, paid by the im- plement exhibitors for their chedding ; and then comes the ' subscription of £2,000 from the York Local Authorities. By the sale of season tickets the sum of £4.30 was raised, and charges for admission to the stands at the horse ring and dairy brought in £5lO. The sale of catalogues realised , £1,018; upwards of £1,160 was paid by exhilators of live I stock, in addition to £143 levied as fines for non-exhibition. ,iFor entries and advertisements in the catalogues the society I reaeived £663. Altogether the York Show will rank as one of the most brilliant successes yet achieved. AMERICAN CATTLE Diszese.—A Parliamentary Buff Book was circulated among members on Wednesday, containing the official correspondence between the Ministers and Go- vernment of this country and those of the United States from January, 1882, to sth March, 1884, on the various forms of cattle disease existent in the two countries. The correspondence begins with a letter /rota the British Consul ',at Savannah on the outbreak known as pink-eye among J,Ziorses. Reports follow on pleuro-pneamonia in the New York district in the early part of 1882, and on the means taken for the extinction of the disease. The outbreak of Texas fever in September of that year, and which caused a considerable scare in this country at the time, is also dealt with in the correspondence. Notice of footand month dis- ease, which forms the subject of the Bill new before Par- liament, appears to have been first given from Birkenhead, so far as it affected American cattle. Inspector Moore re- ported from that port in January, 1383, that the Kansas!, from Boston, landed 313 cattle, of which 219 were affected with foot and mouth disease. These were slaughtered as soon as possible, and all sanitary precautions enforced. Petrie's day begins at sunrise. goeshis first round, books every arrival, and sets each worker his individual task. After breakfast he goes his second round; helps to move a huge block or two; stirs up the lazy digger; convicts a pilferer; separates gossips; copies inscriptions; or takes photographs, with the sun blazing overhead and the thermometer standing at 94deg. in the shade. So (with the exception of an hour allowed for the people's dinners) the day passes in a perpetual do capo from sunrise to sunset. Writing reports, journals and letters, bookkeeping, the re-copying of inscriptions, the classifica- tion and cataloguing of objects discovered, the drawing of plans, and so forth, occupy the evening hours, and with night come predatory mice and other lees welcome nocturnal visitors. The explorer's bed is not a bed of roses.

div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
Apii3

SOME FANCY VARIETIES. It may be of interest to some of our readers who have thoughts of keeping a variety of fowls for exhibition to know a little as to some of the breeds, and to have indicated in which there are the best opportunities for success. Of course, in nearly every case the individual choice of the poultry keeper has to be exercised, that is, he is more likely to succeed with the breed or breeds he likes best, those which are said to be his "fancy." This is not always so. for many have to "cut their coat according to their cloth," and to keep such breeds as they are able to. For instance, one of the most successful exhibitors of Game Bantams we have known always declares that if he could have the breed he likes best, he would keep Buff Cochins, but as the space at his command is limited, and he could not maintain them with the degree of liberty they require, he is compelled to choose another breed, and consequently has kept Game Bantams for years. Then again, there are some breeds which, in order to win anything like a good position in them, needs a very long purse and plenty of patience, so that many of them who would have them if they could, are obliged to seek some other variety. These are such breeds as Game, Brahmas, and one or two varieties of Cochins, as well as one or two of the Game Bantams. When such gentlemen as Coptain Heaton, of Worsley, and Mr. Lyon, of Liverpool, give £lOO for a Game cock, they knock others entirely out of the running. We are not blaming these gentlemen in any way, and are very glad that specimens have been brought to such perfection and command prices like these, but it makes the winning at first-class shows a very difficult matter. Still it is to be remembered that some of the best birds have been bred by small breeders, and we have known one of the great winners of the year come out of a pitman's back garden. In that case knowledge and skill compensate for money, as it nearly always does when well applied. There are several breeds at present wherein there is a good opening for exhibitors to enter, and when we indicate these, then if they are favourites with readers of The Examiner it will be all the better ; or if there are others they like better, they must use their own judgment as to which they elect to take up. There can be no question but that anyone with a little skill in selecting and mating birds, and persistent effort, can sooner or later win a position in ex- hibiting. Many can do this with the expenditure of com- paratively little money, but the skill required cannot be obtained by anyone—it only comes with practice and the application of a keen judgment to the matter. The first breed we would place in the category is the Leghorn. A few years ago, thanks to the efforts of ,the ' Leghorn Club, classes were obtained at nearly all the shows I for this variety; but during the last two or three years the numbers of entries in these classes have fallen off, and the competition has consequently been less keen, so that an influx of new exhibitors is not only necessary to fill up the classes. but these new exhibitors would find an opening ready to their hands for winning prizes and honour. This falling off is due in the browns, we believe, to the in-breeding for colour, which has affected their laying qualities, and doubt- less also to the change of fashion or taste which is con- stantly going on. The whites have, from their colour, never been so popular as the browns, and with them there is from this cause a splendid opening for anyone. What should be done by newexhibitors is to take up the old style of browns, to get the larger size and squarer bodies, and to regard bril- liant colour as of minor importance. Then the laying qualities would resume their own sway again. We venture to say that anyone taking Leghorns up warmly would soon win a prominent place amongst the upholders of the breed. Both Minorcas and Andalusians also present good openings, but these have not classes provided for them so freely as have Leghorns, and that is the only drawback connected with them; but it is a serious one, for to have any breed relegated to the "any other variety" class means that the chances of successlare very materially reduced, and, what is more, the demand for birds from new exhibitors keeps very small, so long as this is the case. A combination on the part of breeders of these varieties would soon bring about a different state of affairs. Minorcas are not so bad as Andalusians, and at most of the best shows they have classes. All the French varieties present capital openings for new exhibitors, and though Houdans are kept pretty largely, yet there is still plenty of room for work to be done. If an effort can be made to get back to the original characteris- tics of this valuable breed, and not give prizes to the half- bred Creves so mach exhibited, then we are certain both honour and profit would be in the work. Houdans have been getting smaller and smaller of late years, and there wants some new blood both in themselves and their ex- hibitors in order to bring about a change in the matter. floudans, like Leghorns, Minorcas, and Andalusians, have a decided advantage over many other varieties, in that they are very useful fowls, really good layers, and make nice table fowls. Thus both profit and pleasure can be secured. With them there is the question of size and purity to be regarded, and we believe that by a little effort and study in this case also a good position can be secured without very much difficulty. Of Creves the same may be said, and also of La Fleche, though we can scarcely hope that either of these varieties will ever take the position of the Houdans. They deserve to be kept a great deal more than they now are, but only for their table qualities, as they are not first- class layers. Our readers know from what we pave pre- viously said our opinion of these breeds which we regard as about the very best for the table, and they are handsome also, but in Spite of this deficiency in laying qualities, they will, we believe, repay anyone who takes them up earnestly- What is requisite is to maintain size and quality of flesh, and not to develop unduly crest or feather. Hamburghe have their old positions in prize lists, but it is very seldom that we see really large and good classes of them. Often 25 to 30 pens will only gather up:lor five classes. There are many reasons to account for this. In the first place, only those who have space at command can keep them with any degree of success. They do not thrive in confinement, and thus the number of fanciers is necessa- rily limited. Then, again, they are difficult to breed, as there have to be separate pens for producing show cocks and hens, the hens bred from a cock breeding pen being useless for exhibition, and vice versa. And again, we fear that the exhibition of these birds has got into the hands of dealers, whose interest it is to keep them as restricted as possible. These remarks do not, however, apply to the Black Ham- burghs, which ought to be very popular, as they are re- markably good as layers, and do not entail so much trouble in breeding. Size is needed with them, and purity of breed. And even with respect to the other kinds of Hamburghs, anyone with space and persistence could doubtless, in time be able to secure a good position in that section of the fancy. That such a position can be secured, and that Ham- burghs would be all the better for the introduction of a fresh batch of exhibitors, we have no doubt, but probably of all the varieties which offer a position these present the most difficulties in the way. With the other varieties named we do not see why, if right birds are selected for breeding, the ' exhibitor should not be able the very first season to win' prizes with birds 'bred by himself, but with Hamburghs this would be very difficult indeed. SEASONABLE HINTS. In all yards where there are chickens, it is important that at the present time of the year they should have special attention, and the breeder must see that all their wants are attended to if he wishes them to thrive well. They must be regularly fed, be housed in a comfortable manner, and at the same time have plenty of fresh air. The weather is in spite of the east winds, gradually getting warmer, and more fresh air is needed. Too much cannot be given in fine weather, so long as the birds are not exposed to draughts, and it is as dangerous for fowls to breathe the same air over again or to live in a vitiated atmosphere as it is for human beings. A young mother, travelling with her infant child, writes the following letter to her husband at home :—" We are all doing first rate and enjoying ourselves very much. We are in fine health. The boy can crawl about on all fours. Hoping the same can be said of you, I remain, &c., Fanny." THREE LITTLE BLA.CHBIRDS.—One day little Dick Clif- ton found a blackbird's nest with three little ones in it, and the temptation to secure these was so great that he took them home. I do not think he meant to be cruel, still it was cruel to do so; but Dick said to himself that he had a big cage of his own, and that as he would feed them regularly, it could not be wrong. But Dick after a little while found that the little birds were neither well nor strong. And one day when they were in the cage—which was always hung in a tree in the garden—Dick saw a strange sight. The small birds had been traced by their.mother ; and just before Dick reached the tree he found her giving them food which she had brought! Poor little Dick! he was touched to the heart by , the sight, for he at once saw that what the birds had so needed was the food suited to their wants, which only their parents properly understood; and from that moment he resolved never to rob a nest again. And when after a Ml's- time, during which the old bird regularly visited and f them, the little creatures were old enongh to fly, Dick glad i y opened the cage and set them free.—Bo-Peep.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF G ARDIANS. ordinary fortnightly meeting of this Board was held Workhouse buildings on Wednesday morning, Mr. J. ling presiding, There were also present the Rey. G. pberts. Major Cartwright, Dr. Mackie, Messrs. George ton, Wm. ?oughton, John Houghton, William Derby- shire, Thomas Rant, Thomas Jolley, C. Broadbent, George Blackhurst, John Bonnell, John Greenbelt, Jonas Fonder, J .hn Brown, R. Kilsball, E. C. Cooper; and J. C. Sutton (clerk).
THE FINANCE COMMITTEE. It was stated in the minutes of the Finance Committee that Major Cartwright had been re-elected chairman of the committee.—The minutes were confirmed.

THE Bata:nu. In the minutes of the House Committee it was stated that Mr. J. R. Moseley, Her Majesty's Inspector, had visited the school. He said :—" I have inspected the infants' school, which is of course the school in which results in the ordinary sense cannot be looked for. The teaching seems to be fair; attention should be ,nade to discipline." THE VISITING COMMITTEE AND ITS WORK. The Visiting Committee recommended that in future it should be allowed to meet on every alternate Friday instead of every week, as at present.—Major Caurwitionv moved the confirmation of the minutes of the committee. With regard to the proposed fortnightly meetings of the commit- tee, he said as the Workhouse was always kept in such good condition there did not seem to be any necessity for weekly visitations. He believed fortnightly meetings had become the order of the day in other Unions, and he thought they might as well do the same.—Mr. JOLLEY seconded the proposal. They found, he said, that things were soi well conducted at the Workhouse that a fortnightly meeting would meet all requirements.—The Cuing read the Act hearing on the matter, which stated that the Workhouse should be visited once every week at least. The way ke read that was not, he said, that the committee should visit the premises every week so long as they appointed certain persons from their own body to do so. He suggested that two members might be deputed to visit on the week that the committee did not meet.—Major CARTWRIGHT : If the two , members did not attend, comld we get out of it ?—The CLERK: In that case you could.—The CHAIRMAN said the average attendance at the Visiting Committee's meetings was only two members.—A GUARDIAN: One and a half. (Laughter.)—Mr. APPLETON thought the committee ought ' to visit the house once a week.—Dr. MACKIE was of opinion that a visitation of only once a fortnight could not meet the spirit let alone the letter of the law, and if it came to the pass that the attendance was only equal to one and a half member—(Major CARTWRIGHT : That is a joke)—or, even say three members, he would not that it went out to their constituents that a matter like that was left to a visit of once a fortniyht. There was no doubt that at the present moment they had an excellent master, but they could not tell how long he would be in ofice, nor could they tell whe- ther cares and anxieties might not come even upon him. He would suggest that the committee have a meeting on the Board day and another on a suitable day in the inter- mediate week.—Major CARTWRIGHT ultimately moved that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of that relating to the fortnightly meeting. At the same time he expressed the hope that those gentlemen who had objected to the minute would attend the committee's meetings more regu- larly. Dr. Mackie had objected, and he (Major Cartwright) would be very glad if Dr. Mackie would join them at their meetings weekly.—Dr. MACKIE : I will do so with pleasure as often as! can.—Major CARTWRIGHT: And here is my friend, Mr. Derbyshire who does not even know the state of the house; he talks about what it was like four years ago.— The amended minutes were then passed. THE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE —THE BOARD AND ITS PROTEGES.

In the minutes of the Schools Committee; it was stated that Mr. Darbyabirs had been re-appointed chairman, and the Rev. G. F. Roberts, vice-chairman for the ensuing year. —Mr. DAREISTIME moved the adoption of the minutes, and in doing so referred to the Case of a girl who had been hired Out for three years by the Board to a person in Warrington. She had now strved for about 12 or eighteen months, but the committee understood that both parties wished to sever the agreement. The committee did not quite understand what their position was with regard to the contract. It seemed that at the time of the agreement being made the girl's mother was in the Workhouse, but since then had left, and as she wanted her daughter back again she had per- suaded her to be saucy with her master so as to induce him to discharge her. He did not do so, however, and conse-
quently the girl ran away..—Mr. ROBERTS said that as far

as he had been able to gather it appeared that the contract was not binding in its nature. He asked for the clerk's opinion on the subject —The CLERK said that if two people contracted with each other, the one to serve and the other to employ, that contract was binding in common law. It seemed that in some cases, after the masters had trained the

children so that they became useful, the parents wanted them back again.—Major CARTWRIGHT did not think that one of the parties ought to be allowed to break the agree- ment simply because the child had become useful, particu- larly at fusiian cutting, a trade which was very good just now. He believed the children could pick that business up easily, and then make their Sc. or 9s. per.weelc, but it would never do to let a party break the agreement simply on this account. Be hoped the Board would support the rule that as the master had taken the girl for three years he must keep her, and if she would not do what he wanted her to do he had his remedy.—Mr. BROWN said he should not like that Board to insist upon the master keeping the girl under aIL circumstances. She had left him, she had not been sent away by him.— The CLERK said the master could take the girl before the mqgistrates if be wanted to enforce his contract.—Mr. ROBERTS said that what the committee wanted to know was as to what power they had to enforce these contracts. The superintendent told them that they had not the same power as under an article of apprenticeship.—The CLERK : No, it is not as stringent.—Mr. ROBERTS said they wanted to know exactly what their position was with regard to the matter, so that if their power was not sufficient some meansi might be taken to meet the difficulty.—The CLERK said there was no difficulty. The Board could sue the man be- fore the magistrates and have him punished if he did not fulfil his contract.—The matter then dropped.

The Cterac read the minutes of the School Fees Commit- tee, which stated that Mr. Blackhurst had been re-elected chairman of the committee, and Mr. Brown, vice-chairman. —Mr. BLacantrnsy moved the adoption of these minutes, which was agreed to, the Chairman mentioning that he was informed by Mr. Shearer that the school fees were now just about one-half what they were three years ago.—The CLERK also read a statement of the school fees paid during the half- year ending Lady Day, 1884, which was as follows :—War- rington, £57 6s lid ; Latchford, £3 108 3d; total, £54 17s 2d. Newton, £36 19s; Haydock, £2O 19s 6d; Burton- wood-, us 3d; Southworth, £1 4s 6d; Winwick, £l7 2a; total, £6O us sd. Poulton, £2 19s 3d; Rixton, £1 Os 3d; total, £3 193 6d.—Mr. DAREYSHIRE said he did not know how it was that recommendations for the passing of the school fees for Haydock and Newton never came before that Board as the Warrington feesidid. He supposed it WRS be- cause the committee for Haydock and Newton was recog- nised by the Local Government Board. It was time the Board had some information about the matter, because the charges for school fees at Newton and Haydock were larger than those for Warrington and Latchford. They must bear in mind that they were Union charges. Those living in Warrington bad to pay their portion of the school fees of Newton.—The •CLBRK : No; the school fees are all charged against the respective parishes.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE (sitting down): Oh, that will do then. (Laughter.)—Mr. ilLacanunsr : That alters the case.—Mr. firrurrox said he thought they might do as they liked if they paid their own school fees, but he cer- tainly was astonished by the report that had been read. It was a rule, he said, that in the case of a family which was not earning 3s. per head the school fees should be paid. He did not know whether they had the same regulatton in Warrington.—[The CHAIRMAN: That is the rule we go by.] —lf, Mr. Appleton continued, they did the same in War- rington the population there must be far better off than they were in the Newton district—the average earnings muse more per head. In Haydock there was a large colliery population who did not work more than three or fear days a week. He thought it was a very serious matter when Newton district paid more school fees than they did in War- rington.—Dr. MACKIE said there was no doubt that at the present moment it was one of the most serious questions that could engage their minds to keep, should he say, the excellent tax for the edu- . . . .

_ , cation of the people within proper limits. He ad- vised that parents asking for the payment of school fees should be brought before the committee and strictly catechised as to their means.—Major CARTWRIGHT asked if parents who did not send their children to school were ever brought before the magistrates.—Mr. HUNT: They are.—Mr. APPLETON thought some harshness must be used by the Warrington School Fees Committee. ("No, no.")— After some further remarks the matter dropped, Mr. Apple- ton promising that he would attend the Warrington Com- mittee to see how they managed the business of graating fees.

MEDICAL MATTERS AT HATDOCIC. A letter was read from Dr. Watkins, in which lie nomina- ted Mr. John T. Davis, High-street, Newton, as his deputy medical officer.—Dr. MACKIE asked if there was any ex- planation required from Dr. Watkins with regard to the deplorable condition into which his district had fallen in the matter of infant mortality ?—The CHAIRMAN said that Board hal nothing to do with Dr. Watkins except in con- nection with panpers.—Mr. APPLETON : There is a Local Board at Haydock.

Mr. DARBYSHIRE called attention to the; fact t.hat the ex- pensive medicines for pauper patients in the Warrington district were supplied by a druggist, while he was informed that in the Newton district Dr. Watkins supplied the medi- cines himself, and they cost that Board four times as ranch as those for Warrington.—Dr. MACKIE: Newton again.— Major CARTWRIGHT : How do you account for that Mr. Appleton; do expensive medicines include drink? (Laugh- ' ter.)—The CHAIRMAN: It does not include spirituous liquors. I —The CLERK: There are none supplied in Newton to my knowledge.—Major CARTWRIGHT : Or in any district.—The CLERK: No, I exrect not—Mr. APPLKrON said they thought that the cost of the medicines in Newton was exces- sive, but they had no idea they were more expensive than they were in Warrington.—Mr.DARRYSHIRE moved that a return showing the cost of medicines over the whole Union be preparec and laid before the Board.—Dr. MACKIE seconded this proposal, which was carried.

Jragazine a gentleman who took a voyage to AuBtral-40k the hope of being restored to health, relates his experia4, and repeats the opinion that such a journey should be in only the earliest stages of disease. Nothing, he 0.41 could have been more disappointing than the weather iS greeted our arrival at Melbourne. We had come sto 13,000 miles in search of warmth and sunshine, and rescf,,ee Australia in midsummer to find very much the same wanid as we had left behind in England—gloom, rain, and . winds. "A beautiful season, we were told, plenty of which, to English ears, sounded the reverse of encoarageeke However, this did not last bag; and it was not many before we could fully appreciate the beauty of a clol3yet day, and were longing for rain as earnestly as any one. tos persons with weak chests I think the climate of Melba .f must be one of the most trying in the world. Mornings:el' bright, hot sunshine with scorcning wind, change witheo very few hours to afternoons of really biting cold, wheg,,oo strongest are thankful for ulsters or sealskin jackets. rof the hottest days it is a common thing to see people gt heavy coats or rugs, in anticipation of the sudden cheer , that may occur. The whole of the southern coast of Poe tralia and a considerable margin of country inland is, as I was able to lea,-n, subject to like alternations of perature. Very little is known in England, even a°°of- medical men, of the climate of the Australian coloni,,e. rather,l should say, of their many different climates. :dee eons coming out for their health seem very gendrallll;:, 01 , the impression that they have but to reach the shorteig Australia to find a climate ready made to suit !:Tat• particular ailments. Townsend hy- lethecated to the bank quantities of produce, and received Ittd, vances of money amounting to £3,960, but it is alleged oat he then disposed of the goods to other persons and Wrongfully appropriated what money he thus procured. e Wax MURDERS —The Birmingham magistrates on Mon- -731 remanded a labourer named Kelly, who had whilst in- - `°ricated kicked his wife "round the house like a football," tad caused her almost immediate death. The number this time was 103, including neat a dozen families. The emigrants themselves con- towards the expenses, according to their means, thus • Showing that they were anxious to escape from their hitherto Wlealid surroundings. AN INFORMER DISCREDITED.—Ab Shandangon County Cork Session, on Tuesday, Samuel Paul, shoemaker, was returned for trial at the assizes for having on March Bth ;est year murdered his wife. The prisoner was arrested on . the information of John Crowley, labourer, who swore be :!'le the prisoner choke his wife, but as they were on good 7neeer°2B until recently, nojeode9 but the prisoner knew he wit- ! exTeet the occurrence. Stephens has no Itennach for the dagger. _ Womme STUDENTS AT DEFORM—The proposal to admit women students to certain examinations at Oxford, which gave rise to an extraordinary amount of discussion in Uni- !entity circles, is now finally disposed of. Two Congrega- rens of resident professors and tutors have within the past :ow weeks adopted by large majorities the statute giving e ect to the proposal, and a very full Convocation of mem- 'Zs of the University met on Tuesday in the Sheldonian Theatre to give a deciding vote. Mr. Chamberlain is still convinced this is the case, and that the tte!terrient applies to the loss of life reported to the Regis- •wrethneral of seamen as well as to that recorded in the se'lek register. 1:1„ett• O'KELLY, M.P., AND THE Mkuni.—l hear, writes a ' eeZoni correspondent, that Mr. O'Kelly, who has been for DIV time in Egypt, and who was apparently intending to o,e`.;°ed to the Soudan, has been stopped at Dongola. In these circumstance the Egyptian autho- • are acting wisely in relegating Mr. O'Kelly to a career o Peace and inactivity in Lower Egypt. 4.THE SCOTCH CROFTERS.—The report of the Commission ! The commissioners advocate the adjustment ,Of rents by arbitration, but do not find ground for propos- ing a general revision by official authority; nor do they reeommend the concession of permanent tenure except in the ease of occupiers of improving leases. Amongst other "egestions made by the commissioners for the amelioration If the condition of the crofter population, military and naval enlistment are a4vocated ; and the advancement of 112.°ney to fishermen for the purchase of boats, the construe- 'elon of piers and landing places, additional railway facili- "ee, the simplification of the educational system, and in- eree,eanad emigration assisted by Government grants, are —"ong the chief recommendations. .. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. MISCELLANICOUS.—Their 10-dships met at 4-o.—The Royal assent Was given by commission to a number of bills Willett had passed both Houses.—The Duke of RICHMOND read a 'letter from the Duchess of Albany in reply to the address of condolence with Her Royal Highness adopted by their lord- ships' House —Lord NORTHBROOK, replying to Lord Bel- more, stated that certain measures had been adopted by the Admiralty with the object of improving the position of senior lieutenants of the Navy OE half-pay. Their lordships rose at 4-45. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Monoax. The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. Enypr AND THE SonnAte.—lri the House of Commons, Mr. ASHMEAD-BARTLETT had two questions on the paper with respect to Khartoum and Berber, which he supple- mented by several others, put without notice.—The PRIME Mitersnat replied that the Government had no final infor- mation with respect to Berber —ln reply to Mr. Onslow, Lord liesTincrrow said the question of moving a vote of thanks to Admiral Hewett, General Graham. and the officers under their command, for the operations in the Soudan, was under consideration.—Mr. Osistow, *Mid much laughter, gravely intimated that he would himself move a vote of thanks.— Mr. Dawrrav asked whether in the event of a Bum being raised by public subscription sufficient to organise a volun- teer force to proceed to the relief of General Gordon the Government would afford necessarylacilities ? Mr. Dawnay intimated that he had already received in a single sum a donation of £l,ooo.—Mr. GlLAr•aroxis said the safety of General Gordon being the care of the Government, he did think they could fall back upon the assistance of voluntary effort. • Twit FRANCHISI BILL.--At twenty minutes to six, on the motion to go into Committee on the Franchise Bill, Mr. RAMIS moved an amendment providing an instruction to the Committee that they have power to make provision for the redistribution of seats between the existing constituen- cies, and for the representation of populous urban sanitary districts at present unrepresented. The right hon. gentle- man had originally proposed to add after the word "un- represented" "by the transfer to them of seats from the less populous borough constituencies." This, however, he dis- creetly left out. When he rose the House showed its appre- ciation of the proceedings in a marked manner, members rising on both sides, and crowding out till the benches were left almost empty.—Mr. GLADSTONE, following Mr. Raikes, pointed the moral of the situation. The Government, he said, wanted to get forward with the Bill in order that they might follow it up with a measure dealing with redistribu- tion. Mr. Raikes, lamenting that one man would have the ten.thousauttli part of representation, whilst another would have the five-hundredth, added "there- fore I am stopping a Bill which unpassed leaves them without any representation at all." The Government would not, Mr. Gladstone em- phatically declared, play into the hands of gentlemen direct- ing proceedings so fatal to the measure, and he trusted that members on that side of the House would take the same view, a suggestion loudly acquiesced in by the few Liberal members present at the moment. The Lord Mayor had an amendment for the rejection of the Bill. That would lead ta an honest stand-up fight, which the Premier welcomed, and any gentleman who had not an opportunity of deliver- ing their speeches on the second reading of the Bill would find that a much better opportunity than the present one. The question raised by Mr. Raikes had been discussed for seven days on the motion of Lord John Manners, and had been decided by a majority of 130. To bring it up again and propose fresh debate was conduct which threatened to reach a point amounting to betrayal of the trust of members of the Honss.—Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL denounced this speech as an application of the moral closure, and con- gratulated the Liberal party upon being reduced to a condi- tion of servility that would be degrading to a Hottentot Parliament, a remark received with much good humour on the Liberal side. In a House further reduced in numbers Mr. Clarke continued the discussion, and was followed by Mr. Brodrick. who moved the adjournment, on the ground that no speeches were being made from the other side of the House.—Sir W. HARCOURT reiterated what the Premier I had pointed out, that seven nights had been already de- voted to the question. In that time the Liberals had said all they desired to say, and were not inclined to add any- thing now.—Mr. GIBSON and Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTB supported the motion for the adjournment, which on a division was negatived by 108 votes against 71. The making of speeches was then resumed and carried on till midnight, exclusively by members rising from the Conser- vative side. At this hour, to the general astonishment, the debate was allowed suddenly to collapse, and the divi- sion taken, with the result that the amendment was rejected by 174 votes against 147, an accidental and well under- stood reduction of the Ministerial majority which greatly pleased the Conservatives. Mr. Toluratesorr next moved an instruction empowering the coenniittee to provide for the extension of the boundaries of Parliamentary boroughs. The division just taken having shown the temporary weakness of the Liberals in the House, the debate was as rigidly curtailed as (till Liberal members had gone home under the impression there would be no division) the former had been extended. This amendment was rejected by 158 votes against 132. At a quarter to one further proceedings with the Bill were adjourned, the re- maining business was rue through, and the House adjourned at 1-30.

THE NlSERO.—Mesars. Pinkey and Sons, owners of the Riser), have received information stating that the Chinese have declined all monetary compensation for releasing the crew, but demanding principally the restoration of free trade. which existed before the war. It was mentioned the other day that three gentlemen well known in the House of Commons had received a legacy of £2,000 each by a lady who admired their political gifts. , The three gentlemen are Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Dillwyn, and The O'Conor Don, who is not now in the Howie. ARRIVAL OF THE AUSTRALIAN CRICKETERS. Among the passengers who landed at Plymouth, on Tuesday, from the Peninsular and Oriental steamer Sutlej were the Aus- tralian cricketers Bonnor, Murdoch, Bannerman, Cooper, Scott, Palmer, Blackham, McDonnell, Giffen, and Spofforth. The annual spring meeting of the Iron and Steel Institute commenced in Westminster on Wednesday, Mr. Samuelson, M.P., presiding. The reports of the treasurer and secretary were adopted. Bessemer gold medals were presented to Mr. Martin, manager of the Dowlais Ironworks, and Mr. Windsor Richards, Middlesborough. There are now Idle in the ports of the north-east coast from want of employment no fewer than 137 ocean.going steamers, of 150,000 tons gross, valued at over a million sterling, and employing 1,800 men when engaged. This shows an inorease of 13 vessels on the total number idle two months ago. Last week the marriage of Colonel H. Ellis Hicks, of the Royal Horse Artillery, to Miss Legertwood, daughter of the Sheriff Clerk of Aberdeenshire, was celebrated in St. An- drew's Church, Aberdeen. The news was received on Wed- nesday that Colonel Hicks had died suddenly while on his marriage tour. CONSECRATION OF THE BISHOP OF SOUTHWELL.—Dr. Ridding was consecrated first Bishop of Southwell in St. Paul's Cathedral by the Archbishop of Canterbury on Thursday morning, assisted by the Bishops of London, Ox- ford, St. Albans, Norwich, Licpaid, Ely, Lincoln, and some suffragan bishops. Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., presided on Wednesday night at a meeting held at Willesden in favour of the candidature of Mr. W. S. Caine for the county of Middle- sex. Both gentlemen were well received when they ad- dressed the gathering, and resolutions in favour of the last-named and of the Franchise Bill were agreed to. FATAL FIRE NEAR GLisoow.—Early on Thursday morning damage was done to the extent of about £20,000, ad a watchman named William Howie lost his life, by a fire which occurred in the ship-yard of Messrs. Barclay, Curie. and Co., at Whiteincb, near Glasgow. The building in which the fire originated consisted of four storeys, and contained all the manufacturing machinery belonging to the firm. AN IRISH MAIL STEAMER DISABLED.—A telegram re- ceived at Liverpool from the outposts on Thursday morning reported the sighting of the Irish mail steamer Leinster, in tow of two Liverpool steamers. The engines of the Leinster were reported to be disabled. The vessels were making for Holyhead with their charge. The towing vessels were the steamtug Knight of the Cross and the Waterford and Liver- pool steamer Cornerag. THE HIGH SHERIFF OF LLECASIIIRE.—The newly-ap- pointed high sheriff of Lancashire, Mr. Thomas Brooks, entertained about 400 gentlemen from all parts of the county at breakfast at his residence, Crawshaw Hall, Rawtenstall, on Saturday morning. In the afternoon he drove to Bacup in state, being followed in open carriages by the majority of his guests, and thence he proceeded by traia to Manchester for the purposes of meeting the judges of assize. A ROMANCE Or REAL LIFE.—At Pontypridd Police Court, on Wednesday, a young woman was charged with at- tempting to commit suicide. The girl, according to the evidence, bad quarrelled with her lover, and had swallowed a quantity of poison. He had the presence of mind, how- ever; to give her warm water as an emetic, and thus saved her life. He told the Bench he was going to marry the woman at once, and she was discharged on this under- standing. AN EX-MANCHESTER CONSTABLE SENT TO PRISON.—A t Derby Assizes, on Thursday, John Lowe, coal dealer, and formerly a constable in the Manchester police force, was sentenced by Mr. Justice North to six months' imprison- ment, without hard labour, for writing to a magistrate a letter accusing Superintendent Hallam, of the Derbyshire police, with drunkenness and immorality. The judge at first ordered hard labour, but finding it was of doubtful legality, withdrew it. ,‘ Roca" Cocoa.—The Liverpool stipendiary magistrate on Wednesday had a case before him in which Messrs. Jas. and Hugh Feran, grocers, Walton-road, were summoned for having sold adulterated cocoa. It was shown that a quan- tity of "rock " cocoa, which was bought at the defendants' shop, contained 54} parts of foreign matter, including 21 per cent of sager and a considerable amount of starch. The defendants' solicitor called a witness to prove that there was no such thing as pure rock cocoa. THE GREAT FIRE IN LONDON: FALL OF THE RUINS.—AS a number of men were engaged on Thursday morning in taking down a part of the ruins left by the late fire at Mr. Whiteley's, Westbourne Grove, London, one of the walls fell burying them beneath the debris. The unfortunate men were speedily extricated, and some eight or nine of them were conveyed to the Hospital, where their injuries were attended to. Two of the men were found to be very seriously injured, and one is not expected to recover. FRIENDLY SOCIETY CASE —A case of considerable im- portance to friendly societies was commenced at Nantwich County Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Thomas Hughes. Patrick Coleman, a mechanic' of Crewe, claims £5O from , the local Oddfellows' Society for having expelled him from membership. Plaintiff had been on the funds several months, but the club doctor refused to give him further certificates, and he was expelled. The plaintiff then called several doctors to certify he suffered from spinal disease. The case was adjourned. THE USE OF THE KNlFE.—William Thomas, clerk, was remanded at Birmingham on Tuesday on a charge of mur- dering a woman named ilary Hollis, with whom he lodged. Prisoner was jealous of her intimacy with another man, and after a quarrel stabbed her in several places, death resulting in a few minutes. A butcher named William Wood, of Greenfield, Flintshire, was remanded at Holywell, on Tues- day, charged with the attempted murder of his wife, whom he had stabbed with one of his knives. The woman's condi- tion is not considered hopeless. MANCHESTER Caaltnan N Como:um—A meeting of the Board of Directors of the Mancheeter Chamber of Com- merce was held on Wednesday, Mr. J. F. Hutton, the presi- dent, in the chair. The questions of the proposed Congo Treaty, the Turkish import duties, the constitution of the Indian Council, and the provision of adequate consular supervision on the West Coast of Africa were considered. In connection with the last-mentioned subject a memorial was ordered to be forwarded to the Secretary for Foreign Affairs, pointing out how .largely British commerce in the neigh- bourhood of the oil rivers in the Bight of Benin has in- creased, and urging that in view of the fact that merchants from other countrirs have during the past few years been trading there, our Government ought to be adequately repre- santed in that locality. MR. IRVING BISHOP AND HIS PERFORMANCES.—The:busi- ness of the Manchester Spring Assizes was continued on Wednesday before Mr. Justice Cave in the Crown Court, and Mr. Justice Day in the Civil Court. —ln the Nisi Prius Court Mr. Washington Irving Bishop, the "thought reader," sued Mr. Thomas Whiteley, owner of a waxwork exhibition at Liverpool, for £5BO. The plaintiff entered into a con- tract with a man named Gordon to give 19 performances, for which he was to be paid in four instalments of £145 each. The defendant guaranteed the payment of the money providing that plaintiff fulfilled his share of the agreement. After several performances were given a cheque was handed to the plaintiff in payment of the first instalment due, but it was dishonoured, and thereupon the plaintiff declined to give any further entertainments. He had received no pay- ment whatever for the entertainments given, and he now claimed what was due en the 19 performances from the guarantor, Gordon being unable to pay. Mr. Justice Day held that the money would only be due on Bishop's giving the 19 performances, without doing which he could not ful- fil his part of the contract. THE IRISH FRANCHISE.—A. return issued upon an order of the House of Lords has just been published with regard to the Irish Franchise. From this it would appear that in various counties of Ireland there are at present 165,997 re- gistered electors, while the number of lands, tenements, and hereditaments rated at £l2 and over is 242,974; at over .£4 and less than £l2, 266,399; and at £4 and under, 475,376. At the same time the number of inhabited houses rated at £l2 and over is 39,745; at over £4 and less than £l2, 58,216; at over £1 and not exceeding £4, 226,822; and under £1,435,179. In the boroughs of Ireland the number of registered electors is 58,021, of which over one-third (21,805) are in Belfast alone, while another 13,580 are in Dublin. The next largest borough constituency is Cole, with 4,764 voters, no other Irish boroughs having more than 2,000, the nearest being Londonderry with 1,845, and Limerick with 1,916. Four others (Carrickfergus, Galway, Newry, and Waterford) have over 1,000 voters, six having between 500 and 1,000, eight between 300 and 500. and eight 'tinder 300. the smallest being Portarlington with 141, Kin- sale with 207, and New Ross with 255. The number of land., tenements, or hereditaments in these boroughs rated at £4 is 105,712, and at £4 and under, 58,022; while the number of inhabited houses rated at £l2 and over is 36,896; a over £4 and less than £l2, 52,263; at over £1 and not exceed- ing £4 and at £1 and under, 12026. THE CHARITY COMMISSIONERS AND THE MANAGERS OF NATIONAL SCHOOLS AND NONCONFORMISTS.—In a letter to the editor of the Liberator, Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., calls attentio_ to the action of the Charity Commissioners, and the proceedings of clerical managers in the so-called National Schools of the country. "Nonconformists in towns," he says, "are not sufficiently alive to the extent to which these agencies—denominational schools and the Charity Commis- sion—are working throughout the rural districts in opposi- tion to the principle of religious equality. It is high time ' that prompt and decided action should be taken by the Dissenters of the country, and by all believers in religious freedom, to stop the abuses now going on. That action should consist, not merely of complaints against individual managers of denominational schools, and of protests against the proceedings of the Charity Commissioners in individual cases; but it should take the form of a firm demand on the Government itself that these abuses should no longer con finite." With regard to the action of the denominational managers of schools,rhe says, " The only remedy to be found for the evils which admittedly exist is in the establishment of universal School Boards, elected by the people them- selves." Another correspondent says, "There can be no doubt that the object is to crush out Dissent in the rural districts: and elementary education will never be satisfac- tory until Government grants are withdrawn from denomin- ational schools, and education is taken out of the hands of the priests and placed in the hands of the people."
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDIa. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. MisceLLawzons.—The Duke of Marlborough took the oath and subscribed the roll on his succession to the title. —The Married Women's Property Act, 1882 (Amendment Bill was, on the motion of Lord SALISBURY, read a second time.—Lord DERBY explained the circumstances attend- ing the appointment of the Chief Secretary of Malta as Lieutenant-Governor of the Island.—Speaking on a resolu- tion introduced by Lord Castletown, Lord KIMBERLEY said the Government were sensible of the necessity of amending the purchase clauses of the Land Act. so as to increase tbe number of freeholders and enable landlords to dispose of their estates on favourable terms.—Their lordships ad-

him what became of them.—After some remarks from Mr. Kennard, Mr. I. Rogers. Mr. Wartcn, Mr. Findlater, and Colonel King-Harman, the House divided, and the second reading was refused by 149 votes against 79. THE halm LABO ACT—At five o'clock Mr. PICK- SON rose to move the second reading of a Bill de- signed to extend the advantages of the Purchase Clauses of the Irish Land Act of 1881. Mr. Parnell supported the Bill. Mr. Trevelyan, who had only five minutes to speak in stated that the Government had prepared a Bill on the subject which he expected would be satisfactory to all con- cerned—an expectation rather encouraged by the speeches he bad just listened to. He hoped in about a fortnight to be able to lay the Bill on the table and explain its prin- ciples.—The House adjourned a few minutes before six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TitIIRSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock. —Lord North took the oath and his seat on the death of the Baroness North, a peeress in her own right.—The Birkenhead Corporation Bill and the Hull, Barnsley, and West Riding Junction Railway and Dock Bill were reads second time. ENGLAND AND h nvvr.—The Marquis of SALISBURY called attention to the Premier's statement that the coven- ants under which this coantry had been acting in Egypt were made by the late Government, and complained of the interpretation placed by Mr. Gladstone on the despatch of the 19th September, 1879, which gave the result of a con- versation between himself (Lord Salisbury) and M. Wad- dington. The agreement come to, he said, was not with the Khedive but with the French Government, but ever since the bombardment of Alexandria the course of Her Majesty's Government had been adopted in deference to the Freoch Government or in pursuance of any agreement with them.— Earl GR.ANYILLE considered the desptach as a most complete declaration on the part of the two Governments to give sup- port to the Egyptian Government. He thought it impos- sible, however, that the Prime Minister should not also have taken into consideration the fact that it was the late Govern- ment who with France forged the late Khedive to resign and placed the present Khedive in his place, subject to the con- dition that he should follow their advice in all important particulars. That was the real origin of the position in which we now were. The noble Marquis had repeatedly de- clared that England VMS bound in honour to support the present Khedive by the engagements which they themselves had entered into, and by those which they had inherited from their predecessors. The House adjourned at twenty minutes past five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TEWILSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Chancellor of the Exchequer 'made the announcement that a bill to provide for the main- tenance of Cathedrals generally is in a forward state. Lord E. Fttzmaurice informed Mr. Houlsworth that the new treaty with Portugal contained not only full security for the suppression of the slave trade, but new stipulations for that purpose. The chiefs in the African territory had not been consulted in the matter. The case cf Mr. O'Kelly, M.P., the correspondent of a London paper, who had been stopped at Dongola on his way to the residence of the Mandi, was brought before the House by Mr. Labouchere. The reply of Lord E Fitzmaurice was to the effect that the Egyptian Government acted entirely within their right.. Mr. O'Kelly had been stopped on public grounds, having reference to the relative position of Mr. O'Kelly, the Mandi. and the British Government. THE FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE.—The PRIME MINISTER informed Sir S. Nerthcote that the Government had pro- posed a Conference upon certain Egyptian affairs, which proposal had been accepted by the Powers in full, except- ing that France had expressed a desire that there should be some communications before the Conference meets between the French and English Governments. No answer had yet been received from Turkey. The financial situation of Egypt required attention, and from that attention the law of liquidation could not be excluded. It was proposed that the Conference should meet in London or Constintinople, and the invit.tion was limited to finance. In the course of the evening the PRIME MINISTER intimated that next day he would propose that until th,.. end of June the House should meet on Tuesdays and Fridays at two o'clock. IRELAND AND THE FRANCHISE BILL.—The debate on the motion to go into Committee on the Franchise Bill was resumed by Mr. Alderman Fowler, who had an amendment on the paper for the rejection of the bill. He, however, declined to move it. Mr. Chaplin was expected to move his amendment declaring that it is at the present time inex- pedient to largely increase the electoral privileges of the Irish people, but he withdrew it, and contented himself with a strong protest rgainat a measnre which, he said, would facilitate the repeal of the Union, and promote and encourage the separation of Ireland and England. He declared that the bill was the price which the Government were going to pay for the Irish vote at the next elec- tion. He found that the Irish and Radical members were banded together against him, and he considered it was not the Policy of a wise general to court overwhelming dot eat.— Mr. GLADSTONE considered the statement just made one of the most remarkable he had ever heard, proceeding from a wise general who bad undertaken to marshal the party op- posite, and at the last moment had remembered that pru- dence was the better part of valour, and had announced that after all he did not intend to fight. The hon. gentleman said he withdrew his amendment because he should have against him the whole Irish party and the whole Radical party. He (Mr. Gladstone) believed there were other reasons, and among them was the ad- vice the hon. member received from the most prudent and perhaps the most experienced and influential of those who sat on his side of the House. As to the Act of Union with Ireland it was impossible to maintain that union except on the principle of giving equal rights to those who were included in that Act. He put it to Mr. Chaplin if he did not think that the refusal to meet the Irish people on a footing of justice and equality would have a far stronger tendency in the direction he so greatly deprecated than could be anticipated if the people of Ireland found them- selves fairly an 4 frankly dealt with.—The debate was con- tinued by Mr. Newdegate, Mr. R. Power, Mr. Sullivan, Mr. R. Yorke, and several Irish members. Soon after eleven o'clock the motion that the Speaker do leave the chair was agreed to without a division, and the Bill was put into Com- mittee amid cheers.—Mr. GLADSTONE at once moved that progress be reported.—Sir H. D. WOLFF opposed the mo- tion, which, however, was azreed to.
