div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. ABANDONMENT OF BERBER. CAIRO, BAxtrat,Ax.—The reply of the Britiah Government to the proposal to send an expedition to Berber has been received. It says that such an expedition is impossible at present and could not, in fact, start for four months hence. This decision has been communicated to Hussein Pasha Khalifs, Governor of Berber, and at the same time he has been told that he may withdraw from the town if be is in a , position to do se. Troops had arrived at Berber from Shendy, having suffered trifling loss on the way front attacks of the rebels. This disproves the report of the Shendy massacre announced on the 20th instant. . .

Cana°, SIINDLY.—There is news from Assouan that Col. Duncan has passed 1,008 refugees from Khartoum and the south, with pay and provisions, on to Lower Egypt and to their own villages. There was a telegram from Berber, yes- terday, dealing only with petty affairs, but making no men- tion of the general situation. Canto, SllNDAY.—Despatches have arrived from Berber stating that the troops there have fraternised with the in- surgent Arabs. The inhabitants are taking flight, and in a few days the place will be deserted. There is no news from Khartoum.

CAIRO, MONDAY.—Mr. Cuzzi telegraphs from Berber as follows :—" It is useless trying to send messengers to Khar- toum. They refuse going for any amount. Berber will shortly be a waste. All the troops are leaving. I shall leave to-morrow, and will come to Cairo as quickly as pas- sible, when I shall be able to explain the actual situation. Four Sanjaks of Scingkea have joined the rebels with 500 soldiers. The Sanjaks came from Khartoum. The steamer Moncrillonia that was at Shendy was much damaged. The position is most despernte." This message arrived at mid- night.-11S4 p.m.; Baker Pasha left to-night on three months' leave. A large assembly, among whom were Mr. Gertoia, General Stephenson, and other influential personages, were at the station to bid him farewell. A further telegram from Mr. Cuzzi, the British Agent at Berber, states that he left there to-day for Korosko. Already the rebels were entering the houses on the outskirts of the town on the south and east. Many of them are fraternising with the Egyptians, but those of other nations have fled, except one or two who have been playing into the rebels' hands. The Egyptisn officers at Aesouan have received letters from the Mandi's lieutenant giving them notice to quit within ten days, and stating that otherwise they will be annihilated. Colonel Duncan has received a similar epistle.—. Daily News. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—The last telegram received from Hussein Pasha Kbalifa, Governor of Berber, reached Cairo this morning. In it the Governor reiterates his demand for reinforcements, and begs earnestly that he may not be aban- doned. Nothing has come through since, and it is assumed that the telegraph clerks have left the town. The Ist Battalion of the Cameron Higelanders left Cairo for Alexandria this evening, to replace the Royal Marines, who embark to-morrow for Suakin to relieve the 60th. Telegraphing on Tuesday night, the Standard correspon- dent at Cairo says :—Mr. Egerton this morning received a telegram, dated from Berber at five o'clock last night. His correspondent reports that all his efforts have failed to ob- tain the delivery of a letter to General Gordon; that the town is in a state of revolt, and menaced alike from within and from neighbouring villages, all of which have joined the cease of the Mandi. He concludes by saying that he in- tends to leave Berber to-day for Cairo. We can, therefore, scarcely expect any further news from the south for some time to come. Preparations for the despatch of Egyptian troops to Assonan continue. The heads of the departments and military authorities are sitting in council, under General Stephenson, to deliberate on the best method of supplying a force of 5,000 men and 500 horses. The chief points of consideration are whether such a force should be despatched as a whole or in detachments of 500 men each, and what would be the best means of ensuring water supply along the routes from Suakim to Berber, or from lorosko to Abon Hamad. The spirit of revolt is sensibly increasing both in Upper and in Lower Egypt. The exche- quer is almost empty. The Cairo correspondent of the Daily News received the following telegram from a correspondent at Berber, on Tue.- day morning :—We are leaving to-day. We find it impos- sible to communicate with Gordon. Every village between Berber antl Khartoum is in open rebellion. The rebels have surrounded Barber, and are enteriag it. Every village is occupied by the Mandi's men. OSMAN DIGNA AGAIN. SUAIIM, SUNDAY —A spy just returned from the rebel camp, where he had been detained for ten days, states that. Osman is at Hashertin with 2,000 fighting men, besides old men and children. ADEN, MONDAY.—Osman Digua is reported to have sent a message to King John of Abyssinia, by the principal Sheikhs of the hostile tribes in the vicinity of Massowah, in which be threatens an attack unless all the Christians in Abyssinnia become Moslems. THE PROPOSED CONFERENCE. PARIS, SATURDAY.—A Council of Ministers was held this morning, at which the proposal for a conference on Egyptian affairs was under consideration. At the termination ef the Council M. Waddington. conferred with M. Ferry. The Republique Fran guise to-day states that as soon as the pro- posed Conference upon Egyptian affairs meets the whole Egyptian question will de facto be submitted to the arbitra- tion of the Great Powers. PARIS, MONDAY.—lntelligence received here states that the Italian Government agrees to the British proposal for a Conference in the general terms in which it is formulated. Russia is expected simply to announce her assent. It is added that Austria and Germany have not yet replied, and that the former is reported to intend demanding that the objects of the Conference be limited to the financial affairs of Egypt. The Porte strongly urges that the Conference should be held at Constantinople. VIENNA, WEDNESDAY.—The Presse says it is informed on good authority that Austria, Germany, Russia, and Italy have accepted unreservedly the proposal for a conference within the limits of the programme defined in the English invitation. Turkey and France have not yet sent their replies.

THE QUEEN AT DARMSTADT. DARMSTADT. MONDAY.—Last night the Crown Princess if Germany and other members of the Battenbarg family dined with the Queen and Grand Ducal family at the New Palace. This morning the Crown Princess of Germany visted the Queen, who, a little later, visited the Grand Ducal dairy. In the afternoon the Queen paid a visit to Princess Charles. and afterwards took a drive in the country. The wedding presents are now on view at the New Palace, and are very costly and numerous. The Queen's presents Include two diamond and pearl stars for the hair, a silver tea service, and some Indian shawls. A bracelet presented by the late Duke of Albany is also among the wedding gifts. The Court Circular says :—" Though the Queen will be present at the marriage of her granddaughter, she will not, in account of her deep mourning and recent terrible be- reavement, be present at the banquet afterwards, or at any of the festivities. The serenade which will take place in honour of the eveat will be performed at Prince Alexander of Hesse's palace, and not at that of the Grand Duke." The Prince and Princess of Wales and family left Charing Cross by special train at 6-15 on Monday evening, proceed- ing to Port Victoria, where they embarked on board the royal yacht Osborne for Flushing, travelling thence to Darmstadt. OPENING OF THE ITALIAN NATIONAL EXHI- BITION.

TURIN, SATIIRDAY.—fi-e—ltilian National Exhibition was opened to-day by the King and Queen. The ceremony was attended by all the members of the Court, the Ambassa- dors of Germany, Austria, Turkey, Russia, and France, to- gether with the Ministers. The proceedings were opened by the Duke d'Aosta. Signor Villa, a member of the Cham- ber of Deputies and Vice-President of the Committee, lay- ing stress on the special object of the exhibition, declared that henceforward Italy would seek only to conquer in the grand contests of labour and civilisation. Signor Grimaldi, the Minister of Agriculture, then, in the name of the King, declared the exhibition open, and on behalf of His Majesty said it behoved the Government to study it in all its aspects in order mere effectually to ensure the prosperity of com- merce, industry, and agriculture, together with the well- being of all classes. THE REVOLUTIONARY MOVEMENT IN SPAIN. MADRID, SA.TURDAT.—The Spanish Government is re- parted to have obtained further information with respect to the revolutionary movement being plotted in various pro- vinces. A major in the Spanish army and eleven civilians have been arrested in Barcelona, and two emissaries of Zo- rifle were arrested in Cadiz, papers and money being found , on them.

div.head: DESTRUCTION OF PUBLIC PROPERTY.
div.p: DESTRUCTION OF PUBLIC PROPERTY.

MADRID, TRURSDAY.—Two insurgent bands have ap- peared in the provinces of Lerida and Gerona. They have cut the telegraph wires between Lerida and Seo de Urgel, and between Gerona and Figneras, and destroyed a bridge on the railway connecting the two latter places. Troops have been sent in pursuit, Further details are wanting up to the present. PARIS, MONDAY.—A. telegram from Bayonne to the Temps states bat a certain agitation exists on the Spanish frontier. The Spanish Customs office for Valcarlos has been destroyed by a band of insurgents of some sort, but it is not known under what political flag they are assembled. -
- - FALL OF A. RAILWAY BRIDGE AND LOSS OF LIFE.
MkMUD, SUNDLY.—Yesterday evening a serious railway accident occurred a short distance from Ciudad Real. A

....--.., —,..,_ train was passing over abridge, when the structure gave way, and all the carriages, with the exception of the guard's van, were precipitated into the river below. Several pas- sengers were killed, and twenty others seriously injured.-- LATER —There is good reason to believe the fall of the Alendia railway bridge was not accidental. It has been dis- covered that one of the supports was cut through MADRID, MONDAY.—Little doubt is now entertained that the Alcudia railway bridge was cut intentionally. The train was composed of an engine and tender, several luggage vans, and eight carriages of all classes, containing over 170 pas- sengers, includinz a large number of soldiers returning house after completing their term of service. Up to the present, 33 bodies have been got out of the river. It is feared that the loss of life will prove greater than was at first believed. In some quarters the deed is attributed to the enemies of public institutions, and as an act of revenge for the dis- covery by the Government of the revoltitionary movement, but this must be accepted with reserve. MADRID, TUESDAY, 7-15L.711.--UP to the present 38 bodies have been recovered, victims of the railway bridmecident at Alcndia, the victims being all soldiers. Thirtnersons were injured. One account states that 110 passengers are

reported to be missing. The Ministerial papers persist in attributing the deed to the revolutionary petty. NIADEID, TUESDAY, 10 15 P.M.-1 tie West par!icuhrs regsrding the railway accident near Ciudad Heal stste Mit altoge•her 49 bodies have been recovered rip to the present. It is calculated, however, that there are s. ill about 20 in the water. About 60 of the passengers escaped unhurt. In their °facial report the engineers express the opinion that the rails bad been raised, but the belief is gaining ground that the catastrophe was due to accidental causes. The Ministerial papers, however, state that the telegraph lines were cut a short distance from Grenada, THE BRIBERY CASE IN ONTARIO.

Tottovro, SATURDAY.—True bills have been returned in each case against the four persons who are charged with offering bribes to members of the Ontario Legislative As- Oembly to induce them to vote against the Government. UNITED STATE.—DESTRUCTIVE EXPLOSION.

- - . - - - NEW YORK, MONDAY.—Inte ligence from Michigan an- nounces that forest fires have occurred there, causing im- mense damage along the line of the Grand Rapids and In- diana Railway. Several small villages have been burned. Jamestown, Ohio, have been visited by a cyclone, by which two-thirds of the town were destroyed and six persona killed. —5 pin.: Later intelligence received here testifies to the appalling nature of the cyclone in Ohio, especially in the southern parts of M. ntgomery and Greene counties. The destruction of property is wide-spread, and mush loss of life is believed to have been caused. Senor Zaldivar, President of the Republic of San Salvador, has arrived here on his way to Europe. .Nnw YORK, TUESDAY.—A despatch from Panama states that a fire has occurred there. Several buildings used for storing spirits, gunpowder, and petroleum have been des- troyed. The loss is estimated at 500,000 dols. NEW YORK, WEDICESDAY.—Further intelligence received from Havana states that the explosion yesterday afternoon occurred at the San Jose powder magaaine. All the gaso- meters in the vicinity were destroyed, and an explosion of gas ensued, which caused a second and heavier shock. The casualties are not yet known, but several corpses have been found. It has been ascertained that the magazine contained 20 soldiers and one artillery officer, who bad been engaged for several days removing powder to the military hospital at San Ambrosio.

NEW YORK, TKIIRSDLT. - Intelligence received here from Havana states that up to the present it has been ascer- tained that 21 persons were killed and 79 injured by the explosion at the San Jose powder magazine. STOPPAGE OF A BANK IN MEXICO. NEW YORK, THLTS+DAY.—A despatch received here from ' Mexico. of yesterday's date, announces that the National Bank of Monte de Piedad. the oldest financial institution in Mexico, has been closed. There had been a run on the bank for several days previously, owing to an expectation that the Government would demand assistance. Yesterday morning a peremptory demand was received from the Government for an advance to a large amount. It is an- nounced that the establishment has been closed to protect the legitimate creditors, and that it has ample means at its disposal.

div.head: FATAL COLLISION AT SEA.
div.p: FATAL COLLISION AT SEA.

NEw YORK, TUESDAY.—A collision has occurred off the banks of Newfoundland between the French flushing-boat Paquebot and the barque Venus, bound from Liverpool. The former vessel sank and 12 persons were drowned. CANADA.—ATTEMP r TO BLOW UP A PARLIA- MENT BUILDING. TORONTO, THURSDAS.—Some powerful dynamite cart- ridges were discovered under the Crown Land Office in Parliament Buildings yesterday. A careful search was made, which resulted in the discovery of another cartridge under the steps leading to the Speaker's Chamber. The cartridges had apparently been placed yesterday in the positions where they were found. They had wire fuses at- tached, and, if they bad exploded, were sufficiently power- ful to have blown up the whole of the building. The greatest excitement prevails here in consequence of these disclosures. FRANCE AND CHINA.—RECALL OF THE MARQUIS TSENG. PARIS, THIIRSDAY.—The Marquis Tseng has ceased to represent China at Paris. According to a despatch re- ceived here from Berlin, Li Fong Pao, the Chinese Minister to Germany, who is a confidential friend of Li Hung Chang, will leave this evening for Paris accompanied by two secre- taries. The same despatch adds that the Chinese Govern- ment has spontaneously put an end to the Marquis Tseng's mission, and appointed Li Fong Pao to act provisionally as his successor in order to open preliminary negotiations with the French Government for a final understanding between France and China on the Tonquin question. RUSSIAN AND AUSTRIAN SOCIALISTS.

YIENNA, TCESDAY.—Further intelligence from Cracow eoncerning the recent dynamite explosion at the police station in that city states that police investigation has suc- ceeded in tracing a connection between the perpetrators of the outrage and the Anarchist conspirators at Warsaw. Up to the present four individuals, all from Russia, have been handed over by the police to the provincial tribunals on suspicion of complicity in the outrage. This is the first instance of complicity between Austrian Socialists and the Russian Nihilists of which conelusive proof is stated to have been obtained. STRIKE AT THE DIAMOND FIELDS.

CAPETOWN, MONDAY.— A general strike, accompanied by disturbances, has broken out at the Diamond Fields, on ac- count of the enforcement of regulations for searching men at the close of the day's work. CAPETOWN, TDESDAY.—Despatches from Kimberley state that tbe disturbances among the men employed in the Diamond Fields who have struck against the " searching " regulations continue. The police were compelled to firs sin the rioters, several of whom were killed and wounded.

div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

CONGREGATIONAL CHI:TECH.—The annual aermens on be- half of the Sunday school funds were preached on Sun- day by the Rev. Alfred Holborn, M.A., of Bradford (formerly the pastor at Huyten). The church was well filled morning and evening, and was prettily decorated with plants, flowers, and foliage for the occasion, the pulpit, font, and choir hiving a specially attractive appearance. Extra accommodation was provided for the Sunday school festival choir, who assisted in the musical portion of the service. The rev, gentleman took for his text in the morn- ing," And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free," John viii. chap. 32 v., and in the evening "Crown of thorns," John xix. chap. sv. A special ser- vice was held in the afternoon, Mr. E. S. Eccles, the super- intendent, conducted, and rewards were distributed by Mr. J. B. Leach for regular and punctual attendance during the past year. Collections were made at the close of each service, and the total amount realised was £2l ls, being an increase on the amount collected the year before of £4 Rurron QUARRY IRON CHAPEL.—Referring to a state- ment that the congregation of "the fluyton Quarry Wes- leyan Chapel were obliged to conduct their worship outside the premises owing to the action of the trustees, who had refused permission to worship in it until a sum of £5OO was paid for the church," we may explain that the iron chapel was erected by public subscription on the understanding that it should be held for undenominational purposes. When the owners found they were unable to arrange for the continuance of services unconnected with any denomina- tion, they came to an arrangement with the Wesleyans for a lease of the premises, giving them the option to purchase for £5OO. After this had been arranged, the Wesleyans took possession under the agreement for a lease, but when the document had been drawn up and approved by their own solicitors they suddenly declined to sign it; and they have not paid the rent due or fulfilled the conditions agreed upon. Under these circumstances the owners had no alternative but to re-take possession of the premises, as they are by the terms of their holding under obligation either to retain the chapel or use the proceeds, in case of sale, for unde- nominational purposes Ample notice was given to the tenants that the terms of the lease must be fulfilled or the premises relinquished, and so far from their being compelled to hold services in the open air, we understand that the use of a room in the immediate neighbourhood was offered to them by one of their friends. On Sunday morning services were commenced in t'.e roam mentioned, under the auspices of the Huyton Quarry Mission (undenonainational), who have secured the services of a gentleman from Liverpool. The Wesleyan authorities of Grove-street Circuit (Liver- pool) having, at a meeting held last week, decided to give up the cause at Huyten Quarry, though modified terms were offered to them by the trustees. What is to be done with the building is puzzling the neighbourhood, provoking com- ments on all parties concerned. TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION —A special meeting of the above was held in the Hayton Park Schoolroom on Tuesday evening, when addresses were delivered by the Revs. A. Holborn. M.A., of Bradford, and T. Keyworth, of Liver- pool. Mr. E. S. Eccles, who presided, said they were met that evening to welcome the presence amongst them of the founder of their association. Mr. Holborn, on rising, met With a cordial reception. He spoke of the various agencies at work in the temperance cause at Bradford. The latest movement, the formation of a temperance choral society, he commended to their notice. Speaking a the Blue Ribbon Mission, he said 6,000 persons joined it in Bradford. After a lapse of three months a committee was formed for the pur- poses of visiting the members, and the result reported, wa that 6 per cent, only had broken the pledge. Their Liverpool taverns were also successful, and, same as the , crreoved the use of Company, paid 10 per cent. dividend. MANCIIESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. The Select Committee re tesern led on Monday morning, the Duke of Richmond sg,in presiding.—Captain Graham Hills, marine surveyor to the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, who was under eximination when the Committee adjourned on r'riday, was further ex mined by Mr. Bidder, Q.C. He expressed doubts as to the fessibility of navigating the low-water channel at night, but had no cases in point from experience of similar works on the Tyne and Tees. . He was closely cross-tx Amine(' in reference to the silting-up 6 process which the petit uners auticipate as a result of these works.

On Tuesday Hills was further cross-examined by anneal for the bill. He said he could not name a single river trained by training walls in which accretion had not followed. He was satisfied that this scheme would Injure the bar of the Mersey.—Mr. Thomas Stevenson, engineer to the Northern Lighthouseßoard and the Fishery Board for Scotland and te tbe Conservancy of the River Dee below Chester, who claimed that he and his brother had had the largest expe- rience in the world in regard to river improvements, was next called by the opponents to the bill, fie said be had no doubt that if this work was C irriM out the estuary of the river would silt up and be covered with grass Sooner or later. It was, in his. opinion, little better than madness to interfere with the bar at Liverpool. The Mersey was ore-eminently a river in which training walls should not be made. On Wednesday Mr.Rebert Norris Dale, examined by Mr. Squarey, said he was an underwriter carrying on business at Liverpool, and had had many years' experience in under- writing in London and other places. He had made himself acquainted with the features of the whole scheme. There would be a great many dangers to navigation in consequence of the training walls. Large steamers approaching the channel in foe or against tide would be in danger of getting on the training walls. There would be considerable danger. also, of collision in the channel. These risks would naturally lead to an increase of the rates of insurance. There would also be higher rates to Manchester through' the canal an compared with Liverpool.—Professor Vernon Harcourt, cross-ex anined by Mr. Bidder, said he had had large ex- perience o: dealing with tidal estuaries, and had ne ide a special study of the Mersey. He was net aware et any other river that had a configuration like the Mersey. He agreed with previous witnesses that the proposed •corks would lead to the increase of the bar and the silting up of the upper estuary behind the training walls. In his opinion, I as an engineer, the scheme of the Bill was not a feasible one. He had arrived at that conclusion after careful in- vestigation. He would admit that the scheme would pro- bably improve for a time the 'navigation between Runcorn and Garston.—Captain John Parsons, Staff Captain in the Royal Navy, was examined by Mr. Squarey, and stat,d that he had had charge of the Admiralty surveys for the last 27 years. He made a survey last year of certain portions of the upper estuary of the Mersey. The tides were very stung, and the sandbanks in the estuary were continually shifting. He found no analogy between the Mersey and the Tyne, the Clyde, or the Tees.

A WARRINGTON REPORT IN QUESTION. Mr. J. Woulie Barry, C.E., of London and Westminster, examined by Mr. Aspmall, said he had made himself ac- quainted with the estuary of the Mersey. Be did not know any other river where the channels altered so frequently aid so rapidly as in the Mersey. The scheme for the promoters would interfere with those natural ceases, and thus do dam- age to Liverpool.—Mr. Michael: Since we have had the pleasure of seeing you in the last inquiry, you have been employed as an engineer to report on the deeirability of con- structing training walls in a portion of the estuary ?—Yes ; for barge traffic —Did you sav thie in your report to the Warrington Corporation: "The recent inquiry before Par- liament into the proposed Manchester Ship Canal has suffi- ciently indicated the nature and extent of the difficulties connected with making a channel navigable for large vessels between Garston and Runcorn. In view of these formid- able difficulties, and the very large cost of such a work, I think we may dismiss from consideration as an undertaking for Warrington alone any proposal for making any such im- provement in the Lower Mersey as would admit sea-going ships of a large slze up to Warring- ton. I do not, of course, wish to be understood as suggesting that a Ship Canal (such as was proposed this session) would not have been a benefit to Warrington, but merely to point out that it is too large an undertaking to be practicable for the trade or for the re- sources of Warrington alone. . lam of opinion that by dredging and by the use of low training walls such improve- ments of the river elay be undertaken at a reasonable cost as will afford a depth of nine feet at Runcorn and of eight feet at Bank Quay, Warrington, at high water of a neap tide rising ten feet at Liverpool above the Old Dock Sill, and I think such an improvement would fairly meet the require- ments of the case." Would those training walls you suggest inflict any injury upon the estuary ?—Witness: It is a ques- tion of de minimi. This is a small affair. The tidal cap- acity of the Mersey above Runcorn is so small that I thought I was justified in talking about training walls be- tween Warrington and Runcorn.—Did you also say, "I beg. therefore to recommend that a more or less hew channel should be made by excavation and dredging. protected by training walls made of stone (or if it be more cheaply pro- curable, of slag) in the course shown on the enclosed plan, or as near thereto as circumstances will permit." Now, are these training walls the settle as ours?—Yes.— Is this also in your report; "I think, when the works are finished, the river will itself easily maintain the depths which I have recommended • indeed, I consider that in all probability the depths will be increased by the scour when properly directed by training walls; but for the first few years there may be some expense in connection with the training walls until they have taken their bearing throughout." The effect of your training walls would be to increase the scour and not to diminish it? Yes, between the walls.—And no danger would arise? A great deal may be said about the question of accretion, but I do not think between Runcorn and Warrington it is of sufficient impor- tance to be considered. I intend to carry my walls above the sand. The depth of water was so small between War- rington and Runcorn that I would be justified in recom- mending the adoption'of training walls for a barge canal. —Witness, in answer to further questions, said the scour would be increased between the training walls.—Mr. Robert Manning, chiet engineer to the Board of Works in Irelan& was of opinion that the proposed works would seriously damage the estuary and increase the bar.—Mr. J. E. Wil- liams, C.E., said he had had 20 years' experience of river dredging and training walls. From that experience he was able to say that the proposed works would lead to accretion, to the diminution of the tidal scour, and to the sitting up of the upper estuary of the Mersey.—The Committee then ad- journed. . .

On Thursday Mr. G. F. Lyster, engineer to the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, was examined by Mr. Sullivan. He claimed a large experience in the construction of dock and harbour works, and be was responsible for the expendi- ture upon the Mersey alone since his appointment in 1861 of twelve and a half millions of money. The entire real estate of Liverpool and Birkenhead covers 1,583 acres, and comprises 51 docks, 30 of which have direct communication with the river. The docks were provided with sheds and warehouses wherever such accommodation was required. The sheds were necessary adjuncts, but the board did not now consider warehouses of their own indispensable. In further examination the witness stated that the total expen- diture on dock works, plant, had been from 20 to 30 millions. His objection to the abip canal scheme arose from - his belief that the proposed interference with the river would Involve physical resuls which would go far to destroy the condition of the dock estate and injure the approaches to the Mersey.

SION CHAPEL—On Sunday anniversary sermons were preached at Sion Chapel, Cherry-lane, to good congrega- tions, by Mr. W. Sanderson, of Liverpool. The collections realised £7 4s 2d. THE ALLEGED CONCE&L3fENT OF BIRTH. At the Chester Assizes, on Saturday, the grand jury ignored the bills against Mary Forrest and Sarah Forrest, who were in- dicted for concealment of birth at Derryn.—ln charging the Grand Jury his lordship (the Hon. Sir Archibald Levin Smith Knight), made reference to the case, remarking that Mary Forrest was indicted for having unlawfully disposed lof the body of her child in November 1883. When inves- tigating the case they would probibly find that there was strong evidence,but it was circumstantial and mostly founded upon suspicion as to her condition. It was not until some time had elapseelthat the body of the child was found in the soil pipe and the privy. There must be some actual disposi- tion of the dead body after the child had been brought into the world,and in considering-the case he would ask whether there was any tangible evidence against the prisoner having committed the crime with which she was charged. She was living with her sister, and he would make the r,mark • that it seemed egnally consistent with the case for the Crown that the sister inight have secretly disposed of the body. If they did not fad any tangible evidence as to the disposal of the child it would be useless for themto re return a true bill, tor he would have to direct the jetty that was no evidence for a c tea to Lro to them.

The installation of the Very Rev. J. Oakley, D.D., as Dean of Manchester, took place on Wednesday, at tha Cathe- dral. The Dean was afterwards formally admitted to the Cathedral Chapter. Mar Hume, the Liberal candidate for Maidstone, ad- dressed a meeting on Wednesday, and condemned the pro- posal to send a relief expedition to Khartoum. A resolution of confidence in the Government was passed. Mr. Anderson's Cruelty to Animals Bill will now be with- drawn from the Commons, and a bill with the same object —the prevention of pigeon-shooting matches—will be in- troduced in the House of Lords by Lord Balfour of Bur- leigh. On WednesdAy the Duke of Cambridge, who was acecrro- panied by Lord Wolseley„ made n .insp- Id h t of the troops of all arms in Sir Archibald. A is,on's command. The total force was about 6.000 men, with I,ioo horses and 52 guns. El:16118h TFavreaernm,"telines Rwaarsl The annual grand festival of held on Wednesday night at Feeemasons' of Carnarvon prosiding. At the subsequent banquet chair was taken ay Viscount Holmesdale, Provincial Gratd Master of Kent. Tawhiao, the Maori Kim's, who is now on his way to Eng- land, Is accompanied by twelve chiefs and influential men. The expenses of the mission will be defrayed by a subscrip- tion raised among the native tribes. Several thousand pounds have been contributed.

Loogrtm Arms His SUPPER. John Heath, a bottle hand, was charged at the Town Hall, on Monday, with stealing nibs of bacon value 3s sd, the property of James Rimmer, provision dealer, Liverpool-road. Shortly after nine o'clock on Saturday night an assistant to Mr. Rimmer, named Lewis observed the prisoner examining a lump of bacon at the slop door. While Lewis had his head turned another way the prisoner disappeared and the bacon was missed. Lewis followed the prisoner and found him 20 yards away with the bacon in his possession.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and said he did not know what he was do- ing as he was under the influence of drink at the time.—He was fined 30s, including costs, or, in default of payment, one Month's imprisonment.
By Mr. W. ELLIS.

• SATURDAY, MAY 3, 1884.

THERE is a great deal of curious and strangely contradictory talk just now as to what will be the effect of the proposals of the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER with regard to our gold coinage. Recognising that it would be unwise to do other than keep the sovereign up to its real value as a gold coin which is accepted almost the world over, he makes it part of his Budget to call in all half- sovereigns light in weight, and replace them by issuing a ten-shilling piece which should cost nine shillings only. Replacement, whe- ther as to loss by "wear and tear," or by the expense of minting, cannot be .accom- plished without the cost being met in some way. It would be an easy matter, in Tory fashion, to take money from the taxpayer whenever it is wanted, or, more characteristic still, incur the expense and leave a succeed- ing Government to meet the bill; but Mr. CHILDERS believes in paying his way as Treasurer to the Nation, and he thinks, too, that the re-issue of coinage should be made to pay its way. It is not doubted that the plan he propounds will be successful so far as its obvious intention is concerned; but the question is raised whether what is . called " debasement " of the gold coinage would not have an injurious effect upon commerce and current exchange. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL says it would, and if he may be believed, which in such a matter is asking a great deal, the working-class of this country are about to be robbed of ten per cent, of their weekly earnings by a Liberal Govern- ment He says :—" The immediate effect of Mr. CHILDERS' proposal will be felt almost entirely by the working-classes ; it will be found in practice that the new half-sovereigns will be largely used for the payment of weekly wages, if they should ever get iato circulation.

THE Warrington Liberal Association have lost no time in dealing with the letter ad- dressed to them by Mr. MCMINNIES, the borough member, in which he announced that, consequent upon the state of his health, it was not his intention to come forward as a candidate at the next General Election. As will be seen from the particulars given in an- other column, a well-attended meeting of the General Council of the Association had the matter under consideration on Tuesday even- ing, and a Committee was appointed to make preliminary inquiries as to suitable candidates and report at the earliest opportunity to a future meeting of the party. It was felt that it would be useless, and indeed cruel, to urge upon Mr. MC MINNIES to reconsider his deci- sion, and an enthusiastic vote of thanks for the invaluable services he has rendered was formally passed, coupled with the earnest wish that there may speedily be such an im- provement in health as will permit of his as- sisting the Liberal party with his presence and advice. It is satisfactory to note that, apart from the depression caused by sympathy with the borough member, there i 3 every sign in the Liberal party of the strength and unity which will, in a short time, enable them to tide over the present difficulty by selecting a candidate who will win at the next ' election. With a register undoubtedly favour- able, and a party earnest and united, there need be no fear as to the result, especially if the Conservatives can do no better than "totter to their fall " by clinging as hereto- fore to the frail coat-tails of Sir GILBERT GREENALL. The meeting did not, as has been erroneously stated, discuss the merits of several gentlemen ; it was felt that such a course would at that stage be out of place. The only name mentioned by the meeting was that of Mr. JoHN GROSFELD, and that was done incidentally—just as it cropped up spontaneously at the public meeting in the Public Hall on Monday night, when it was received with an outburst of applause which was strikingly suggestive of popular opinion as to the natural successor to Mr. McMirasnEs. But Mr. CROSFIELD does not seek parlia- mentary honours, though, unless the diffi- culties in the way are insuperable, we are quite sure he is too good a Liberal not to place himself, if he should be called upon, in the hands of the party for which he has done so much for so many years. Their organisation isthorouglq lated, assuming he is in the right, on finding democratic, and they must allow it to do PI! himself in so happy a position ;he has already work that devolves upon it now that the tira. made this question especially his own, and for action has come. The Committee whial holds the fate of the Ministry n the hollow has been appointed has not to decide aari of his hand; he can at length say with "Shy- thing : its business is to report, and the fina lock "—" Now, infidel, I have thee on the decision will rest as it ought to rest with th,ee hip ;" • for he has only to restrain himself duly accredited representatives of the who until the working man is "on the strike" of the Liberal electors of Warrington. against this latest form of reducing wages. Meantime, as we are not all " RANDOLPH " mad, it may be as well to exercise a little common sense in reflecting that, as wages have not been in the least degree affected by what with equal propriety, or lack of pro- priety, may be called the debasement of silver coinage, it may be that the new half- sovereign will in this respect be equally harmless. It is pretty well known that the half-crown, for instance, does not represent one-eighth of 'a pound in silver; in fact, taking the coin on the average—that is in- cluding short weight from "wear and tear" —it is reduced in real value at least twenty per cent., and, according to the reasoning of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, a pound paid in half-crowns should not be worth more than sixteen shillings. But does anybody find in every-day life that this is so ? Where is the workman who complains of a reduction in wages when he is paid in half- crowns; and where is the house-wife who finds she can get more bread and butter for one sovereign than she can for eight half- crowns? So long as, under the law, eight half-crowns, or ten florins, can in this country be converted into a sovereign, it is sheer nonsense to talk about a reduction in the actual value of either coin being equivalent to a reduction in wages. And so with the proposed ten- ' shilling piece; so long as two of them, when they come into circulation, can be ex- changed at the bank for a' sovereign of the full value of on pound sterling, so long will they do their work as tokens of exchange without in the remotest degree affecting wages. If, indeed, there were anything in this new theory of " reduction," bank of Eng- land notes would be worth no more than their cost of production, the five-pound note being worth, say, a penny, and the thousand- pound note another penny—and not a fraction more. No doubt Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL when he fingers pension money wpuld like to be paid in this way ; but we fancy he will be content, so long as he can get them, to re- ceive crisp bank of England notes, and take them at the value stamped upon them. There will be a "reduction "—perhaps an entire stoppage—before long of the pension to the CHURCHILL family, but it will not be.the re- sult of debasement of either silver or gold, but of an elevation of the moral sentiment of the nation. If our coinage were throughout in international use, it would be a serious thing to bring its nominal much below its real value, and that is why the Government do not propose to interfere with the sovereign, which finds its way all over the world. But this does not hold good as to the other coins, and hence the proposed application to the half- sovereign of a principle in minting which has been found to work so well with silver. It may at once be admitted that if tokens were brought into use representing a considerable sum, although costing a mere trifle, it would be a bad thing; but this would not he because wages would be affectei in the same ratio, but because it would put an enormous pre- mium on spurious coinage. There is no such premium, however, under the proposal of the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER; he seeks merely to do business in a business-like way, and will not be deterred from doing the right thing through fear of being overwhelmed with what a metropolitan Conservative organ not inaptly describes as "quite a flood of nonsense." Lord_ RANDOLPH CHURCHILL for the moment rides on the flood ; it will be interesting to observe where he is when the flood subsides; if he is right he will be found at the "top of the tree," but if the Govern- ment are right he will be found lying on his back—in the mud.

CRESTER CORPORATION BILL —The Improvement Bill Promoted by the Cheater Corperation came yesterday before the Select Committee of the House of Lords. The bill pro- Poses to consolidate all the various parishes within the city, to fres the Dee bridges from toll, and to enable the Corpora- tion to increase their borrowing powers for special improve- ments from £lO,OOO to £75,000. It is further proposek convert the Corporation debt into stock, in accordance with the practice of other towns. The sum of £28,000 has been contributed to the freeing of the bridges, including £lO,OOO from the Duke of Westminster. The Chester Tramways Company oppose the bill on the ground that they should be relieved from their present contribution to the maintenance tf the bridges. COTTON DISTRICTS CONVALESCENT FUND.—At a meeting the Governors of the Cotten Districts Convalescent Fund, held at the Westminster Palace Hotel, London, on Wednes- day (the Earl of Derby in the chair), the Hospitals and purposes Committee reported that they had revised `ta'a allotment of beds at Southport, Buxton, and Cheadle, to 1„elt the special needs of the various hospitals, and so as to -'-mde the infirmaries at Bolton Warrington, and Roch- dale' rne total outlay for land, buildings, fixtures, furni- luta for the new home at Southport had been £46,753 10s Pd, Including ,C 11,391 19s Sd still outstanding, being £439 108 'n. eXeess of the sum authorised by the Charity Commis- toners. The total invested capital of the fund was now Merninally £92,578, aid had cost £101,1170 producing a 'revenue of about £3,700 per annum, and that the current selling r,rices of the stock were higher than the cost. The demand for beds at the disposal of the Governors was greatly OD the increase, and funds were urgently needed to cope therewith. The floepitals General Purposes Committee were requested to consider the whole question of ways and means, end to report to the July meetingef Governors. AMUSING SCENE IN RUNCORN POLICE COURT.—At Run- Corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Joseph Jackson, a rough- "king young fellow, was brought up in custody charged With having en the previous night refused to pay his fare .Cross Runcorn Bridge, and also with having assaulted Joseph Thomas Nickson, a lawyer's clerk, living in Lord- ,u,tteet.—Mr. Preston, junr., of the solicitors' department, '''me-street Station, prosecuted on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company.—The charge against the Prisoner of refusing to pay his fare was not gone into. .Prom the evidence of Samuel Inglesfield, the ticket ool- metor, and Mr. Nickson, it seemed that about nine Velock .etr Sunday night the prisoner went past the collector'seabin .ithOut giving up a ticket or tendering his fare. The col- lector pursued him, and on reaching him he said he had no tneneY, and if he (the collector) wanted the fare he must Re to With the object of detaining him the collector !eized the prieoner, and a struggle took place. Gaekell, sen., and Mr. .1. Brook, William Galihnore, a grey-haired old man and Mrs. Alice Jane Philburta, his daughter, were charged with as- %tilting Michael Doran. Mr. Knowles, solicitor, appeared 10r complainant and stated that on Monday, the 21st nit., 415 client was annoyed by two boys throwing stones into his stable. • Ruscome VOLUNTEERS.—Messrs. Unsworth Brothers, of High-street, Runcorn, have again been successful in obtain- log the contract for the Runcorn Volunteer clothing and helmets. The corps wore their new clothing at the Parish Church on Sunday last. WIDNES BATHS.—These baths were re-opened for the summer season on Saturday, when 154 persons availed them- selves of a "dip." The interior of the building has been thoroughly cleaned and painted, and the swimming bath is supplied with Pot Hill water. POOR RATES IN THE RUNCORN UNlON.—fit Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the magistrates (Captain Elazle- burst and James Handley) signed a poor rate of 90 in the £to realise £153 12s fid for Clifton, and a poor rate of 10d in the £ to realise £29048 8d for Norton. Fuer SUNK IN THE RlVER.—Yesterday afternoon a flat belonging to Weaver Navigation Company was sunk in the river whilst crossing from Ditton Iron Works to Weston Point. The craft was laden with slag. The two men who were in charge were rescued by a passing boat. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORII.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the following persons were sum- moned by the School Board for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—William Harrison, Martin Rourke, Mary A. Howse, Mary Murphy (two cases), John Keenaghan, Patrick Britt, Henry Burgess, Agnes Holden, Patrick Hyland, Anthony Armstrong, Jacob Cauft, Peter Riley, William Osman, James Handy, Chas. Fitzpatrick, John Keating, Michael ohn Keough, Wm. Fallon, Peter McCafferty, Thomas Quinn,gpruce, Richard Glassey, and Henry Whitfield.—Mr. G. IT. Denby appeared to prosecute, and a fine of 6d, and costs 4s 6,1, was imposed in each case. A VIOLENT Yonne} MAN AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Austin Young, a respectably- dressed young man, was charged with assaulting Sarah Bennett, the wife of a cattle dealer, living at Appleton Mr. Knowles appeared for the complainant. It was alleged that on the 15th April, while Mrs. Bennett was engaged in removing fodder from the hayloft, the defendant threw large stones at the kitchen door of the house, and also at a dog which was chained up in the yard. Mrs. Bennett de- scended to see what was the matter when the defendant used some vile language towards her and threatened to kill her. He also threw a large " clinker " at her, but fortunately it missed its mark, or, Mr. Knowles added, she would not have been in court that day.—After hearing the evidence, the Bench bound the defendant over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each. THE HEAVY CLAIM AGAINST WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.— The ease of Jeffries a,. Widnes Local Board, came on for hearing yesterday afternoon, before Mr. Justice Day and a special jury, at Manchester Assizes. The plaintiff in this case, Mr. Jeffries, contractor, claims for damages for loss of work, material, Sm., a sum amounting to almost £5,000, from the defendants, the Widnes Local Board. 'fbe plain- tiff was represented by Mr. Ambrose, Q C., and Mr. S. Tay- lor and the defendants by Mr. Gulley, Q.C., Mr. Collins, Q C., and Mr. Sutton. The only witness examined was Mr. Hunt, the foreman of the plaintiff. At the close of his ex- amination, it being then about a quarter past seven, His Lordship remarked that the case was likely to last a long time, and he would, therefore, excuse the special jury from attendance to-day (Saturday) in order that he might get on with the shorter cases. The further hearing of the case would be adjourned till Monday morning, or until the last special jury case bad been tried. PRESENTATION TO THH VICAR OF HALTON.—On Wed- nesday last, the anniversary of his birth, the Vicar of Hal- ton called together his parish workers, numbering some 80 ' persons, when a very pleasant evening was spent. After supper the churchwardens, on behalf of the congregation, presented Mr. Lockwood with a handsome cassock of the first quality from a London firm, and the choir and teachers . with a beautiful clock and aneroid baremeter, as a mark of their regard and esteem. The presentations were made by ChnrclayfardenS T. F. Acton an J, Yapp, wIo 4a11111.11 etilogiffed the leak' ilbon hang such a band of 'helpers, and for the very efficient manner in WhiCh the affairs of the parish were carried out. In ronly, the Vicar feelingly expressed his sincere gratitude for the many tokens of the kindly good fee,ling which existed towards him, and took that opportunity of opening a parcel received that day, which contained the Easter offering of a brass altar desk, the gift of Mr. ex-Churchwarden Thomas Wright. CONJUG.iI. INFELICITY AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Luke Feeney, a labourer at the Smelt- ing Works, was charged with having threatened his wife Ellen Feeney.—Complainant stated that she had lived apart from her husband since Christmas, in consequence of his violent conduct. Since then she bad got her own living by washing for families. On Monday, the 213 t April, the de- fendant met her, and accused her of having been walking , out with two soldiers. She explained to him that she was only taking two boys belonging to the Indefatigable to her ' mistress, but he called her a liar, and attempted to strike her several times, at the same time tlreatening farther violence. —Ellen Cook, a domestic servant, corroborated.—The de. fendant said his wife last Christmas sold all tbe furniture in the house, and "chocked him out." He alleged that since then she had misconducted herself, and he had simply ex- postulated with her.—A, man named Leathwood, foreman over the defendant, stated that the cemplainant on one occa- sion went to the works, and was so abusive that he had to eject her from the premises.—Captain Hazlehurst said it was clear the defendant had had a great deal of provocation, and had suffered much unhappiness since Christmas. His remedy was not, however, to threaten his wife, and he would have to pay 14s 6d costs, and be bound over in his own recognisances to keep the peace for six months. TRADUCING THE DITTOS POSTMAN—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, senr., and Mr. J. Brock, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Squire Heyes, a middle-aged man, having the appearance of a blacksmith, was summoned on a charge of using defamatory language to James Turner, the postman for the Ditton district.—Mr. Knowles appeared for the com- plainant, and Mr. J. O. Swift for the defendant.—lt was alleged that on Easter Monday the complainant called in the course of his round at the Hammer and Pincers public- house, Hough Green. The defendant was there, and paid for the complainant a couple of glasses of beer, and then ac- cused him of having signed a certain document belonging to a society, following it up by the declaration that he was a thief and a rogue. The complainant stated this language was calculated to injure his character.—The Chairman said the case seemed to be a very paltry affair.—Mr. Knowles offered to accept an apology and lOs costs from the defen- dant, and Mr. Swift advised his client to accept these terms. —The Defendant: I am not sorry at all for what I said be- cause he knows its true.—Elizabeth Moss, the daughter of the landlady at the hotel was called.—Mr. Swift character- ised the affair as a mere squabble ovar a glass of beer.—The Chairman observed that the defendant's conduct in court had aggravated the case, and he would be bound over to keep the peach for three months, himself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each. 6TY/IMT OESTRUCIRON AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John Quinn, a youth, was fined 2s ekl and costs for Obstructing the footpath in Gerrard- street, Simm's Cross, on the 12th April.—Samuel Porter. a yotrig man, and William Roberts, a youth, were charged with having, on the nth ult., obstructed Waterloo-road. P.C. Laing said on the night in question the defendants were in charge of a small handcart, which was drawn up to the footpath opposite Mr. Edward Johnson's shop. A crowd of people assembled, and the defendants were selling fish. Many persons bad to leave the footpath during a period of twenty minutes. The defendant Porter stated he was hawk- ing his fish in the ordinary way. Mr. H. Gaskell said the Bench di I not wish to interfere with him hawking fish in the place, brit hawkers had no right to stop in the street in- terfering with the traffic, and with the custom of the trades- men's shops about. Porter was fined 2s 6d and costs. The boy, who was acting under his directions, was discharged with a caution.—Jobn Hedgepck was charged with obstruct- ing Peelbouse-lane by leaving his horse and trap there for 15 minutes. Defendant stated he was transacting business in a house. Mr. Gasket' said the defendant most under such circumstances leave some one in charge of the horse. Defendant wae 'fined 2s '6d and costs.—Fer obstructing Albert-road, on the 17th ult., by leaving a horse and cart there an unreasonable time, Joseph Murphy was fined -2s 6d and oosta—A similar penalty was imposed upon Richard Abram far obstructing Churcb-street. CHARGE AGAMT A WIDNES POLICEMAN.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr.tH. Gasket!. sen., and Mr. I. Brock, Joseph Hampsen, a constable in the Widnes police force, was summoned for using defamatory language towards James Cowley, grocer, Ann-street West, Widnes. The Chief Constable for the County occupied a seat on the Bench.-Mr. Knowles appeared for the complain- ant, and Hammon was defended by Mr. 1. 0. Swift.-4ror the complainant it was stated that in January last he sold the defendant's mother a pig and some fowls, payment to be made in three weeks. Payment, however, was net made, and on the:23rd ult. the corplainant, attended by a man, and bis son, went to the defendant's mother's house with the intention of removing the pig. The complainant got inside the pig sty, ;and some conversation took place be- tween him and Mrs. liampsoc, who refused to allew the animal to be removed. Whilst this was proceeding the de- fendant, who enad been in bed, came into the yard, and call- ing Cawley an Irish Fenian and an Invincible ordered him off the premises, and ran at him three times to strike him. The mother, however, prevented him. —The complainant corroborated these facts, and stated the defendant pushed him out of the yard.—Mr. Knowles said be had no other witnesses, as the man who had accompanied the plaintiff had left the place.—Without waiting for any defence, Mr. Gaskell said the Bench were of opinion that the complainant had no right whatever to go to Mrs. Hemp- son's house and remove her property. The defendant had interfered in behalf of his mother, and for a few angry words used under great provocotien they were asked to bind him over. The Bench would bird no man over for using angry words under these circumstances, and the case would be dismissed.—Mr. Swift said he had three witnesses who entirely denied that the words stated were used by the de- fendant.—Mr. Gaskell.: We thought there was no case on the evdence of the plaintiff. We acted simply as if the de- , fendant had not been in the police force at all.

This is, it is stated. 1.,%ne only Order which Lord Derby possesses.

The fust meeting of the new Board was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present: The Revs. Canon Bar- clay, J. Lockwood, J. W. N. Tanner; Messrs. W. Handley, J. Stokes, T. Norman, R. Ashton, J. Challener, P. Speak- man, E. Aaron, J. Warburton, R. T. Lowe, W. Whitlow, W. Fisher, W. Whittaker, J. Weir, J. Derbyshire, W. Pickering, J. G. Hamilton, J. Campkin, J. Mclntyre, W. Neild, George Whitlow, E. A. Wallington, P. Hall, S. Rowland, Jos. Smith, J. Knowles, R. Ashton, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN' AND VICE-CHAIRMAN.— In a few congratulatory remarks Mr. J. Ashton proposed the re-appointment of the Rev. Canon Barclay as chairman.— Mr. Mclntyre seconded the motion, which was carried with acclaination.—Ou taking the chair, the Rev. Canon Barclay thanked the members for this renewed mark of their cont. deuce, and hoped the proceedings of the ensuing year would be conducted as harmoniously and satisfactorily as in the past.—On the proposition of the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, seconded by Mr. P. Speakman, Mr. J. M. Ashton was ap- pointed vice-chairman. , APPOINTMENT ov CoinsurEEs.—The ftst business was the appointment of committees, and Mr. G. Whitlow advo- cated the introduction of some "new blood." Ihe com- mittees in the past had been an extravagant lot, increasing salaries, iec., while the farmers sat there like the lot of duffers that they were. (Laughter.)—Mr. Robert Ashton denied that the committees had been extravagant, and re- ferred to the large amount of work they had to perform. He would gladly allow any member to take his place on the committees.—Mr. J. Dlrbyshire hoped those persons who allowed their names to be put on the committees would attend the meetings. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Aaron complained II that Weston was not represented on the Assessment Com- mittee.—Mr. P. Speakman observed that Weston was the 1 third highest ratepaying district in the Union, and agreed that it ought to be represented. He therefore moved that Mr. Aaron's name be added to the Assessment Committee. Eventually the committees were appointed as follows : Assessment Committee (ex-officio guardians): E. A. Wright, Esq., Charles Reynolds, Esq., Alfred Thomas, Esq, W. C. Jones, Esq. (elected guardians) Messrs. John Weir, John Challoner, Henry Neild, James Derbyshire, William Hand- ley, Robert Ashton, Thomas Norman, Joseph Knowles. Finance Committee: Rev: Canon Barclay, Mr. John Ashton, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. John Lockwood, Messrs. J. Mc Intyre, Thomas Norman, William Handley, James Darby. shire. Relief Supervision Committee r Rev. Canon Barclay, Mr. John Ashton, Rev. .1. Lockwood, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. S. Rowland, William Fisher, John Campkin, Chas. Rigby, James Warburton, E. A. Wallington Robert Ashton, William Whittaker, George Whitlow, William Jackson, Thomas Norman, John Challoner, P. Speakman, John Weir, E. Aaron, William Pickering, F. G. Claudet. School Atten- dance Committee (ex-officio guardians): E. A, Wright, Esq., Alfred Thomas, Esq., W. C. Jones, Esq., Charles Reynolds, Esq, (elected guardians) Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. John Lockwood, Messrs. John Ashton, E. Aaron, W. Pickering, Joseph Knowles, John Weir, John Challoner. Visiting Committee.: Rev. Canon Barclay, Mr. John Ashton, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. John Lockwood, Messrs. James Derby- shire, John Mclntyre, William Jackson, John Highfield, John Challoner, W. Whittaker, Joseph Knowles, Peter Hall, Charles Rigby, E. A. Wallington, John Campkin, Thomas Norman, Philip Speakman, Joseph Smith, Robert Ashton, Joshua Midwood, John G. Hamilton, E. Aaron, G. Whitlow, James Warburton. rrta OFFICIALS' SALA-RM.—Mr. Warburton gave notice that at the next meeting of the Board he would move that a return be made and a copy supplied to each member, of the salaries and emoluments of the officials for the year ending March 25th, 1884.
The Board then went en with the relief business.
TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION AT WIDNES

The annual demonstration of the— Widnes branch of the Church ot England Temperance Society took place on Saturday afternoon and was as successful as in former veers. The members of the various sections, numbering between five and six bundredonet at Waterloo-road echools shortly after two o'clock, where they formed in the following pr.°. cessional order ;—The band of the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen, the banner of the St. Paul's section, the juvenile members, and then the new band of the Widnes Church of England Temperance Society, followed by another banner, and the adult members. In this order they proceeded along Waterloo-road, ltictoria-road, and Widnes-road, to the boundaries of the parish, returning to the ground on the south side of the unfinished Church of St. Paul. Here the 'near (the Rey. J. Wright-Williams) delivered a short address. He asked theta to remember that that church was a workingmen's church, and there would be no rent charged for pews whatever. Any man or woman could enter and take possession of any seat they liked, ex- cept, of course, the reading desk or pulpit. (Laughter.)— Mr. L. lailcross ales spoke a few words. The procession then wended its way to West Bank, and returning, to the parish church, where a sermon was preached to a large con- gregation by the Rev. F. A. Bartlett, of Liverpool. As the weather, though rather dull and tiweatening, was fine, large numbers of people lined the streets to watch the procession, which, we may state, was accompanied by the Rey. J. Wright Williams. and Mrs. Williams, 'Mr. and Mrs. Foley, Mr. and Mrs. Cave, Mr. Kilcross, Mr. Farrant, Mr. T. Atherton, Mr. Richards, Mr. Bruce, kc. Mr. and Mrs. Thomas were in charge of the St. Pact's branala of the society. At half-past 'five tea was provided in Waterloo- road schcol, and so numerous was the attendance of members that there was a scarcity of provisions, bct steps were taken to satisfy the wants of all. The ladies who presided at the tables were Mesdames &law, Bruce, HuntaFairclough, Bate, Atherton, rones, Bott, eurver, Eves, James, Smith, and Hackney; Misses Whittle, Mason, Eva Davis, Elizabeth Pardoe, Purvin, Bella Feirley, Shakeshaft, Annie Briscoe. Thou who assisted in 'the preparation of the tea were Mesdames Williams, lU:cross, Cave, Thomas, Pemberton, Davies, Miss French, and Miss Woods. Sabsequently a public meeting was held uader the presidency of tha Vicar, who was supported by Mr. Clarke Aspinall, 5.P., of Liver. pool, Mr. liilcross. W. Shaw (seamen's missionary, and others. The Chairman, who was cordially received, observed that that was the third birthday of the adult section of the society, and -referred to the presence of their good friend Mr. Shaw, of that worthy institution the Mersey missions to seamen, who was always ready to place his hand at their disposal. Speaking •ef Mr. Asmnall, he stated that that gentleman's praises were heard in all the church e, from. John-O-Groats to Land's End. (Applause.)—Mr. F. Cave (the secretary) read the third annual report of the commit- tee. Heartfelt satisfaction was expressed at the progress of ' the local branch, and of the temperance cause generally in Widnets. Since the last report presented in October last, the society had been doing a good work in rescumg nonal)era of their fellow-townsmen and women from the downward road to ruin, induced by indulgence in strong drink. Although some members of the society bad broken their good reeolu. Cons, the majority of these bad been prevailed .upon to re- join, and the same good result was bopod for m the other

Reference was made to the excellent manner in which the weekly meetibgs had been attended during the winter months, and it was Et tted that owing to the kindness of the Star of Temperance brass band they were enabled to hold open air meetings with a fair share of success. This , year with the help of their own brass band they hoped to do even more, and on that occasion they proclaimed that the band was not formed for money-making purposes but for the glory of God and the furtherance of His work. They trusted their numerous friends would help to pay for the instruments with which the members of the band had been supplied. The Tontine Society, under the secretaryship of Mr. Peter Hewitt, was in an even better position than last year, and the Family Dispensary Club was making fair pro- gress, while the coffee still established last year was quite an institution and a great success.

Mr. Clarke Aspinali, who was received with loud accla- mation on nein to address the audience, said he haft heard Widnes spoken of in terms of the kindest solicitude by their reverend diocesan' and he honestly thought there was no community in the diocese of Liverpool, in which the Bishop of Liverpool was more interested and mere anxious aboett than Widnes. (Applause.) Perhaps no one knew better, than he (the speaker) was obliged to do what a fearful curse drink was. It utterly devastated and ruined family and personal life from one end of the kingdom to the other. He did not know any platform upon which he liked better to stand than that of the Church of England Temperance Society, but he would be a very narrow, uocatholic. and very sectarian Christian if he did not frankly and gladly acknowledge that they had a great mtny earnest, ardent, God-fearing. and 1 God-loving workers outside of the Church of England alto- gether. So far as he could co-operate in any good work with his Nonconforming brothers and sisters, he did so with all his heart and soul. He perhaps tried morn people for I drunkenness. and held more inquests in his capacities as magistrate and coroner than any person they could point to, and this experience naturally forced upon him a great fund of information. It would be absurd and utterly untruthful to say that all the inquests he held were the result of drink; bat he maintained that he should hold fewer inquests if they had less excess of drink. (Applause.) They did not need to be told that drink was doing a devastating work in the homes of the rich and the poor outside of pane statistics and magisterial and coroners' inquiries. There was a very considerable percentage of drunken reprobates, ne'er-do-well folk, in all classes of society, who never by the particular I development of drunkenness swell what were called police statistics. Where the police locked up one man, how many did they coax home. (Laughter.) The speaker then re- ferred to the squalor and wretchedness existioe,r amongst the Door in large cities, and maintained that drunkenness was the cause. He hoped that a compbrensive Sunday closing act would be introduced and passed in the immediate fitters, and suggested that something ought to be done with the ob- ject of opening public houses later in the morning, and clos- ing them earlier at night on all days of the week. He ad- dressed some observations to workingmen and women, and said he was glad to find they had in Widnes so large a society for the suppression of the enemy of English hearts and homes. (Applause.)—On the proposition of Mr. Kil- cross, seconded by Mr. Richards, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Aspinall for his address. During the evening the band of the society and the band of the Mersey jVlissions to Seamen performed selections of music.

NEW DOCKS AT WIDNES,. In a few days there Will be opened for use what is termed an extension of West Bank Dock, but which in reality is an entirely new and magnificent harbour for vessels, and will vastly improve the already admirable water facilities of the town. The old West Bank Dock Wee nkned in 1864, and proved a source of advantage to the trade of Widnes, but not to such an extent as was contemplated by the pro- moter and owner, the late Mr, J. Hutchinson. Subsequently tow, g,sntretrian drew out plans for the enlargement of the dock, but he did not live to see the scheme commenced, and it was only about two years ago that the work was under- taken: The contract was given to Mr. R. B. Matthews, while Mr. Routledge was selected to superintend the en- gineering operations, and it is gratifying to record that the work has been accomplished without any accidents involv- ing injury or loss of life to those engaged in the operations. Major Cross, as acting trustee to the Hutchinson estate. has exercised a general supervision. The magnitude and importance of the new dock will be best understood by a comparison with the old, and it will be seen what greater facilities will be afforded for the transhipment of goods from the numerous works in the im- mediate neighbourhood. Being 90 yards in length and 35 yards in width, the old dock had a total area of 3 000 square yards. The new dock is at least 15 times this size. The old entrance has been removed and a new one of massive masonry constructed upon the edge of the river bed, with gates of the most approved description. This leads into a basin of considerable area with stone walls, and branching to the south is a dock having an area of 10,058 square yards, and to the north the old dock has been extended 26,544 square yards, the entire area of the dock now being 50,727 square yards, or between ten and eleven statute acres. The increased accomodation will be more apparent when we state that whereasthe old wharfage was only 8,000 square yards, the wharfage now is estimated at 88,451 yards. The quay space has also been enlarged from 280 yards to 3,000 square yards, and there will be brought within easy reach of the waterway the works of the following firms :—Messrs. Hall Brothers and Shaw, Widnee Metal Co., the Phcenix Vickers' Sulphur Phosphate Works, Golding, Davis, and Co., Neild, Mathieson, and Co., and Mort Liddel and Co. Hitherto these works have been compelled to send their goods by rail to the dock, but now it will simply be a question of wheeling them to the wharf and shipping them forthwith. With the excep- tion of the basin, the sides of the dock are formed of some kind of clay in a sloping direction, the vessels being reached by substantial wooden stages. It is almost needfess to add that the dock will have sidings connected with both the London and North-Western and the Sheffield and Man- chester Railways. Owing to the improved entrance, the sill being 71t. 6in, upon the Liverpool old dock sill level, vessels of a much larger tonnage than formerly will be able to enter the docks. Previously, the dock would only ac- commodate vessels of 150 tons, but in the present dock ves- sels of between 350 and 400 toss will find safe anchorage, and it is anticipated that many vessels which now enter Garaton will pass that port and enter West Bank Dock, tines increasing the trade and importance of Widnes as an inland port. We understand that the dock will be opened without ceremony of any description; in fact at the present time it is filled with water, and has been for the past week.

div.head: WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB: ANNUAL MEETING.
div.p: WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB: ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the members of the Widnes Foot- ball Club was held on Saturday at the Norton Arms, Lugs- dale-road, and there was a good attendance. Mr W Ireland presided, anti amongst those present were Messrs E M Davies, J Burnes, S 11 Kenrick, J J Latham, W Rogerson, Corys, ii Stirrup, T ilingley, E Id Harrison, W Smith, H Cooper, A Brown, J H Smith (hon. sec.), F Smith (assist- ant sec.), and H W Cookson (hon. treasurer). The minutes of the last meeting having been read and passed, The SECRETARY (Mr. T. H. Smith) read the annual report , of the committee which stated that the first team had played 29 matches, of which they had won 15, lost 10, and drawn 4, the scores being Widnes 20 goals, 29 tries. and 134 minor points, against 14 goals, 14 tries, and 47 minor points. The second team had played 16 matches, of which they had won 10, lost 3, and drawn 3 The committee were of opinion that these comparatively nsatisfactory results were mainly due to the dilatory manner in which members had turned up to play in matches when chosen, and this tended to lower the prestige of the club, and was no encouragement to a secretary to make efforts to arrange a good hat of matches. They trusted in the coming season to see a change for the better. The foregoing remarks applied more particu- larly to the first team, the second having held their own as in former years. Twe matches had been played with strong teams from Manchester and district, kindly broueht down by Mr. T. E. Sutton (Athletic News), the first of which resulted in a victory for the visitors, and the second in a draw. In addition to the above, two other matches had been played, one in aid of the Widnes Accident Hospital, and the other on behalf of the Star of Temperance Brass Band, in recognition of their many voluntary services. An import- ant feature in the events of the year had been the amalga- mation with the True Blues, which had considerably strengthened the playing powers of the club. (Applause.) Mr. El. W. COOKSON, the treasurer, made a statement as to the finances of the club. There was a balance in hand at present of £l5 .e 3 lid, but subscriptions amounting to about £44 had yet to be collected, and the balance would be increased-to that extant. The expenses had been very heavy indeed, principally caused through the loss on extra matches. The ,club had given to the Widnes Accident Hospital-the proceeds of a match, £44s, and the sum of £1 6s 4d, the proceeds of the charity match of the True Blues, whilq the Star of Temperance Brass Band had been presented with £6 iSs. The 'gate money" for the past season amounted to £49, which was £6 in excess of last year; the -fares of players had cost LK, being £7 in excess of the previous season. Mr. Cookson said he was not in favour of continuing the extra matches in the present financial condition of the club, because the loss was greater than any advantage the club derived from the matches. unless the committee practised economy next season the balance would dwindle down, and the club would lose the first-class position which it occupied in the football world. He thought the full fares of the players ought to be paid as soon as theclub mild afford it. Mr. &Atones moved the adoption of tlie report and be.l- ance sheet. Mr. PULING seconded the motion which was carried. The CHAIRMAN read a letter from Mr. C. E. Barlow, a vice-president, who thought it would be a good thing if Association football could be played in Widnes in conjunc- tion with Rugby, as he felt sure greater interest would be taken in the pine. If the club arranged a team to play Association he would subscribe a guinea.—Tiae meeting took no action upon this suggestion.-1 committee consisting of , Messrs. Davies, Burgess, and Rogerson was appointed to con- sult with Mies Dewnie, as to how the money raised for the ' Hospital should be spent. There were several motions made that the dress sbovid be changed, but, by a large majority, it was decided that it should remain as at preaent.—On the motion of Mr. E. AI. DAVIES, seconded by Mr. 1. 11. SMITH, Mr. H. W. Deacon was re-elected president with acclama- tion. The following gentlemen were appointed vice-presidents: —Rev.
