APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER. The Rev. J. Lockwood said in rising to move the appointment of a medi- cal officer of health, he begged to expfess his very great regret, and he was sure also that of the Board, at the cause of the vacancy throdgh the illness of Dr. Bride, who for some 3 years had been the Authority's worthy medical officer of health. About seven months ago Dr. Adams was appointed his deputy, and from what be (Mr. Lockwood) had heard and eeen that gentleman was a most worthy and suitable person to succeed Dr. Bride. (Hear, hear.) The members had heard Dr. Adam's testimonials read to the Authority, and he (the speaker) had had communications from the Principal of Edinburgh University, who spoke of him as knowing him personally, and his abilities. At the last •meeting of the Authority it was unanimously decided that there was no necessity to advertise for a successor to Dr. Bride, and he had, therefore, great pleasure in moving that Mr. Joseplr Adams be appointed medical officer of health for the Union at the same salary as Dr. Bride, namely £l2O per annum.—Mr. Challoner thought he had had as much to do with Dr. Adams ai most people, and he had always found him courteous and gentlemanly. He had understood the work, was really an efficient man, and if the Authority ad- vertised a hundred times he did not think they could get a better officer. He had great pleasure in seconding the motion —Mr. C. Rigby: I think we ought to try him at £2O a year less.—Mr. H. Lowe: For a start ?—Mr. Rigby: Yes. There is a lot of money going in salaries every year. —Mr. Lockwood said the salary at one time was £l5O a year, but it was reduced by £3O when Dr. Bride was ap- pointed.—Mr. Rigby: It wants dropping again.—Tbe motion was carried unanimously.—Dr. Adams was then called into the room and informed of his appointment by the chairman.—Dr. Adams said he was much obliged to the members for the confidence they had reposed in him. He would perform the duties to the best of his skill and ability. WESTON NUISANCES: A POLLUTED BROOK AT KINGS- LET.—The Medical Officer presented a report on the sewer- age of Weston and the pollution of Kingsley Brook. On the former question the Medical Officer suggested the ap- pointment of a committee to inspect the premises in the district. At Lunt's Row, Weston Point, the outfall sewer required improvement, especially at the lower end opposite to the cottages at Wright's Dock. The Medics! Officer was of opinion th it the Ki n 3.14 li.oeit was polluted Vcloti eeWage froul a few cottages On its banks, but he was ; g-IVea io 'understand that the inhabitants did not drink the water from the brook, there being special supplies for drink- ing purposes distributed by continually running spouts. One of these he tested and calculated the yield to be at the rate of 22,000 gallons per 24 hours. The village was well supplied with these springs and spouts, and their analysis had been reported to be most favourable. At the time Parker died of typhoid fever at Kingsley last year he (the Medical Officer) applied to the Authority kr an analysis to be made of the water from the brook (of which Parker had freely drunk by mistake) but the Authority con- sidered this to be unnecessary. He now begged to suggest that an anilysis should be made in order to definitely determine whether the water was really as dangerous for drinking purposes as it was reported to be, as it was impossible to prevent anyone from drinking the , water who wished to do so. In the event of it proving an ' impure water handbills should certainly be distributed through Kingsley and posters put up in conspicuous places along the coarse of the brook warning anyone against drink- ing the water.—A committee, consis.ing of the Rev. Canon Barclay, and Mee3rs. Aaron and Stokes, was appointed to inspect and consider the sewerage arrangements of Weston. —'in the motion of Mr. Challoner. seconded by Mr. Rigby, it was decided by nine votes to eight that the consideration of the pollution of Kingsley Brook be deferred for six months. A PAROCRIAL COMMITTEE FOR PRODSHAM.—In accord- ance with the notice he had given, Mr. J. Ashton moved that Messrs. Charles Roynolds, A. Thomas, John Aelaton, 'rhos. Andrews, John Challoner, Robert Ashton, and Edmund Wal- lington be appointed a parochial committee for Frodsham under section 202 of the Public Health Act, 1875, and that I thcre be delegated to that committee all the powers which I the Authority could exercise in the said township. Several years ago there was a similar committee in Frodsham, which worked very well, and there were various important matters to deal with at the present time which such a committee as he had proposed could do better than the Authority.—Mr. Challoner seconded the motion, which was carried unanim- ously, it being pointed out that the committee would have to submit its proceedings to the Authority for approval.— Mr, Ashton moved, and Mr. Challoner seconded, a similar resolution with regard to Frodsham Lordship, and it was carried unanimously.—This concluded the businees.

div.head: WARRINGTON CORPORATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON CORPORATION.

A meeting of the Warrington Town Council will be held in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening next. The business to be brought forward includes the return of the election of a councillor for the Latchford Ward, a reso- lution expressing appreciation of the valuable services ren- dered by the late Councillor Woolfall to the borough daring r a period of thirteen years and the receipt of letters of ac- knowledgment of the addresses of condolence forwarded by the Council to Her Majesty and the Duchess of Albany on the death of the late Prince Leopold. The various committees recommend the payment of ac- counts as follows, viz.:—Watch Committee, £258 28 9d; Finance Committee (including accounts of gas department), £3,930 Is 10d; Paving and Sewerage Committee, £4lB 8s 10d; School Attendance Committee, £5O 103 3d Museum, Library, and Arts Committee, £2l Is 8d ; Cemetery Com- mittee, £23 lOs 2d; Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee, £l2 lOs 3d; Markets Committee, £22 12s; Sanitary Com- mittee, £635 4s 8d ; Gas Committee, £1,289 Os 4d; Fire Engine Committee, 103; General Purposes Committee, .£9 The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee recom- mend that the plot of laud containing 755 square yards required by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Company, Limited, for the purpose of re-erecting the Roebuck lon in Bridge-street, be sold to them for the sum of three pounds per yard, in consideration ef their having surrendered the lease for fifteen years of the existing Roebuck Inn without payment. The Paving and Sewerage Committee recommend that the sewer in Lord Nelson-street be continued as far as is necessary to sewer the houses built by Mr. W. S. Pierpoint ; that the tender of Mr. John Lunt, for excavating Oliver- street, Mill-street, and Lime-street, be accepted; and that the tender of Mr. C. H. Cartwright for the delivery of bur stone in the streets mentioned be accepted; that Mr. Alder- man Davies be appointed the deputy chairman, and Mr. Councillor Marsh a member of _the committee.

The Inspector reports to the School Attendance Com- mittee that 53 cases have been inquired-into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 47 cases for 98 children; that 26 cases have been taken before the magi- strates, and fines inflicted in 23 cases, two adjourned, and one warrant ordered. The committee recommend that a grant of ten guineas be given to the managers of the Ship Clio, in which several boys from the borough are being maintained free of charge. Thirty-nine cases were brought 'before the committee and dealt with, The average attend- ance at the different schools during the month of March was 6,878, and for the corresponding period last year 6,267 —increase 611.

The report of the Curator of the Museum. Library, and Arts Committee is as follows:—Visitors to the Museum 2,059, a decrease of 35 per cent, as compared with March, 18S3; volumes issued to subscribers 2,522, a decrease of 9 per cent.; velumes issued to readers 1,334, an increase of 29 per .cent.

The Cemetery committee recommend that Thomas Stockton be appointed gardener at the cemetery, to reside at the lodge, at XI. per week, in place of his father resigned. The Bathkeeper ,reports to the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee that the income from the baths for the past six weeks was L2lSs Bd,and for the corresponding period last year £l:5 108. The committee resolved that the Borough Surveyor be requested to prepare a plan and estimate of an extension of the present carriage way at the front of the Town Hall, so as to make a circular walk, the present mound being levelled, the wall to Sankey-street removed, and an ornamental palisade on stone base placed in lieu thereof.

The Sanitary Committee recommend that the sum of .£3OO be paid to Mr. Samuel Broadhurst for a plot of land adjoining the Manure Dept at Longford, containing about 1. 3r. Ip., required for the extension of the depot, and that that the common seal of the borough be affixed te the con- Yeyance ; that the tender of Mr. William Winstanley for the painting, c., of the Infectious Diseases Hospital be ac- cepted; that one of Johnson's patent drying machines be purchased and fixed at Longford, and that Mr. Councillor Greening be appointed deputy chairman of the committee. The Gas Committee recommend that the tender of Messrs. Newton, Chambers, and Co., Limited. for the supply of 200 common socket pipes, delivered at Warrington sta- tion, be accepted. The average illuminating power of the gas for the past four weeks was equal to 19 candles at both works. _

The Fire Engine Committee recommend that the tender of Mr. William Winstanley for the painting of the 7,fre Engine Station be accepted, and that fireman Isherwood be allowed the sum of £8 as compensation for injuries receiVed by him while in the execution of his &Op at the fire at the premises of Mr. Monnfield on the 4th March.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

The most interesting debate of the week took place yester- day, the subject being, the not particularly attractive one of cremation. It was, however, mach a real pleasure to emerge even momentarily from the heated atmosphere of political controversy, and the speeches sere so full of information that a new grace was given to the ghastly subject. On these occasions Sir Lyon Playfair is a host in himself. He takes evident delight in lecturing the House as he used to lecture his class at Edinburgh, and the House, I fancy, en- joys it much more than the young Scots were wont to do, the pleasure being of rarer occurrence. Dr. Farquharscn, who seconded the motion for the second reading of the Bill, created some sensation by producing the remains of a cow contained in a very small bottle. The House was as pleased' and interested with this as the gathering of boys and girls at the Polytechnic with some of Professor Pepper's practi- cal experiments. The two Home Secretaries, Sir R. Cross and Sir W. Harcourt, joined hands in opposing the motion, but it must be admitted that the weight of argument and of eloquence was on the side of the cremationists, who polled a surprisingly large number considering the novelty and delicacy of the subject. As for general business it continues to get" no forrader." Conservatives still dissemble their love for the Franchise Bill, and spare no effort to kick it downstairs. They are now concocting a fresh vote of censure, the real object of which is to occupy time and imperil the chances of the Franchise Bill, The Government, save for occasional ex- plosions on the part of the Premier, remain very quiet, in- dulging neither in complaints nor threats. This is an at- 1 titude due, as I have before mentioned, to the consciousness ' that they held in their band the trump card in the game to which the obstructionists challenge them. They mean to pass the Franchise Bill, tite Government of London Bill, the Merchant Shipping Bill, and one or two other measures. It would be more convenient and more regular that they should be passed in time for the House to rise on the 4th or 1 7th of August, as was its wont in times not long gone by. If it is to be, then the House must sit through September, or, if necessary, October. What is quite certain is that before the prorogation the appointed work will have been done. The danger that in issuing private circulars one or more may get into the wrong hands is a very real one. Only the other day the enterprising secretary of an association called "The Church of England Working Man's Society" got I out in hot haste a circular headed "Private and Confiden- tial," addressed to all the members, in which he instructed them forthwith to write each men to his parliamentary re- presentative and implore him to be in his place to resist Mr. Broadhust's resolution on the question of marriage with a deceaUd wife's sister. "Be careful," this ingenious circular proceeded, "not to mention your connection with this society or any other. Write to your member entirely on your own account." A copy of this instruction to the Church of England working- man fell into the hands of Mr. Broadhurst, and will doubtless be read in the House of Com- mons when he makes his speech. A more recent but less compromising instance of misad- venture is in the matter of a circular just issued by the London and Counties Liberal Union, of which Sir John Lubbock is President. It sets forth "Fifteen reasons why all Liberals in the Some counties should support the Union." A copy was inadvertently addressed to a well , known Conservative member of the House, who under the title wrote in red ink, "One reason why I should not: Be- ' cause I'm a Tory." IThis circular summarises some important facts with res. I pent to the representation of the Home Counties. It shows that out of 27 representatives 26 are Conservatives, the odd Liberal being the minority member for Hertfordehire. This is a falling off from 1868, when the Home Counties re- turned eight Liberals, a downward movement more remark- able since the Liberal strength in the election of 1880 was ' generally gathered in the counties. In Lincolnshire, Che- shire, and Yorkshire, 34 Liberals and 50 Conservatives were returned at the election of 1874. At the last general elec- tion the number of Liberals was increased to 58, and the Conservatives reduced by almost 50 per cent. In the mid- land counties the movement was even more remarkable. In 1874 33 Liberals and 37 Conservatives divided the repre- sentation. At the election of 1880, 46 Liberals were re- turned, the Conservative force being reduced to 24. Much is hoped for both in the Home Counties and elsewhere by the working of the new Corrupt Practices Act which will check that lavish expenditure that from the time of Boling- broke downwards has been the mainstay of Conservative predominance in the counties. At the' last general election the Conservatives spent nearly a sovereign to every ten shillings disbursed by the Liberal candidates. The exact figures, shown by the election returns, are—Conservative expenditure, £82,708: Liberal expenditure, £44,034.

• Last night the Speaker held his second Parliamentary dinner, which was largely attended. The scene both at the dining table and at the reception which followed is a very picturesque one, all the dinner guests being arrayed in court uniform. Mr. Peel, following the practice of his predeces- sor, will continue to bid batches of the Parnellites to the feast, and they, also in accordance with recent practice, will continue with more or less politeness to decline. It is, how- ever, a mistake to suppose that the Irish party never graced the'Speaker's dinner with their presence. It was only in 1876, when they were at daggers drawn with authority that they began haughtily to decline the advances of the Speaker. In the spring ~f 1874 no less a personage than Mr. Biggar, arrayed in velvet coat, velvet broeches, silk stockings, shoes with glittering buckles, and sword by his side, sat at meat with the Speaker. What is more, Mr. Biggar after the fes- tivities went home in a twopenny 'bus. He is now anxious to explain the circumstance on the ground that being new to Parliamentary usages he believed that the acceptance of the Speaker's invitation was peremptory, and of course the costume was indispensable; bat that he went to the dinner, and also went home in a 'bus, are facts vouched for by high authority.

It is not generally konwn that the State is a newspaper proprietor, and by no means.the least prosperous in the coun- try. It owns three papers, the London Gazette, the Edin- burgh Gazette, and the Dublin Gazette. According to ac-i counts made up for the past year, the London Gazette shows, a nett profit of £25,714 19s 41; the Edinburgh Gazette is a I trifle over £3,000, whilst the Dublin G azettc is a paltry £429. The editorship of the London Gazette (worth £BOO a year) is one of the very few sinecures which dangle as prizes be- fore the English journalist. In the United States as under the French republic, a journalist may aspire to be a Minis- ter of State or an Ambasiador to Foreign countries. In England he may by rare luck become editor of the Lou. don Gazette. The present incumbent of the office is Mr. Walker, formerly editor of the Daily .Ye:cs. Falking about the political advancement of journalists in foreign countries, there are two men whom I knew very well in journalistic work who are now holding high diplomatic position. One is Mr. Russell Young, United States Minister to China, the other M. Barrere, French Minister in Egypt. It seems but Yesterday that Russell Young was London editor of the lireve York Herala, located in a dingy room with entrance up a court and window overlooking Fleet- street. Nine years ago M. Barrere,who is still a young man, vfas knocking about London in search of edd jobs with his pen. Mr. Gowing, then editor of the Gentleman's Magazine, was one of his earliest literary friends, and found him some work. It is said that when Garabaldi first came to England there was sonic talk of his marrying a wealthy widow mach devoted to his cause. Ob- jection was taken that Ile was married already; What

The exhibitions at the Grosvenor Gallery are always de- lightful through the many varied forms of artistic feeling that Sir Coutts Lindsay manages to call together under one roof. In the present display, of which the private view has just taken place, everyone will find something congenial to his taste. Those who delight in Mediasvalism will be satis- fied with Mr. Borne Jones's "King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid," and "a wood nymph" clad in green amid green leaves; Miss Evelyn Pickering's beautiful love idyll, full of refinement and rich colouring; Mr. J. M. Strudwick's "Story Book," and his finer work the "Ten Virgins," which in the lovely tones of blues and reds remind one of old, Italian art. Mr. Whistler is a little less eccentric than usual in his one contribution, a portrait of Lady Archibald., Campbell, of which the kindest thing one can say is that to hope she is satisfied with it. She looks rather as if she were flying from the ghost of her former self. One of the gems of the East Gallery is a charming head of a little child called "Dorothy," by Mr. J. Hanson Walker, who has some other children'a portraits worthy of being well studied and appreciated.

The International Health Exhibition is to be opened next Thursday, the Duke of Cambridge performing the ceremony on behalf of the Prince of Wale!. Encouraged by the remarkable success of the Fisheries Exhibition a last year, • neither trouble or money has been spared CO make this a 'worthy successor. Among the exhibits, food will have a prominent place. Products have been brought from all parts of the world. There is to be a real Koumiss Establish- ment, with mares and peasants from the Steppes of Siberia, so that people who hanker after mare's milk can have it fresh. In dress there is a series of English costumes designed to trace the history of fashion from the time of the Con- quest. There will also be an international collection of dresses and uniforms. In respect of dwellings, models will be shown of improved and industrial houses, sanitary appli• ances, and internal decorations and fittings. There will also be practical illustrations of healthy and unhealthy houses on the principle of the pictures in the advertise- ments, showing on one side a gentleman with a bald head and on the other the same personage, almost unrecognisable under a luxuriant crop of hair as he appeared "after six months use of the Rising San Stove Polish." Perhaps not the least attractive feature in the Exhibition will be a com- plete reproduction of a section of the City of London in the olden times, with its gateways, churches, houses, shops, and vistas of streets.

div.head: ROYAL WEDDING AT DARINISTADT_
div.p: THE ROYAL WEDDING AT DARINISTADT_

_ The marriage of Princess Victoria of Hesse with Prince Louis of Battenberg, was celebrated on Wednesday after- noon. The weather .throughout the day was fine and warm, and the town wore a most animated appearance, every house displaying Hessian, German, or British flags. The streets were thronged with sight-seers, especially in the neighbour- hood of the Palaces, and the whole town was en fete, the principal point of adornment being the Luisenplatz. As the time fixed for the ceremony approached large crowds col- lected in the streets between the chapel and the residential palace:the way being kept clear by the military and police. A guard of honour was stationed at the entrance to the residential palace, where the royal guests began to arrive at half-past four in State carriages. At a quarter to five Queen Victoria, accompanied by the grand ducal and bridal party, arrived in a State carriage under a small mounted escort. At half-past friar the various personages who had received special invitatioes :assembled in the private chapel of the residential palace. Among those who had thus been invited were the mediatised nobles, the mem- bers of the diplomatic body, the presidents of the two legislative chambers, the Cabinet Ministers, the genera: officers in the grand ducal arely) the Chief Burgomaster of Darmstadt, and ether iditctionaries and officials. On each side of tho chapel are galleries, which on this occasion were reserved for the holders of invitations, and at the end of the building facing the altar is the grand decal gallery, which is furnished with windows and curtains. Over the altar is the organ, and on each side of that were the places for the choir. At a quarter to five the royal and princely guests met in the saloons of the palace, and as soon as all were assembled Princess Victoria entered, led by the Prin- cess Charles, mother of the Grand Duke, and followed by her ladies in waiting, the procession being headed by the Master of the Ceremonies and several chamberlains. In the presence of the assembled guests and Ministers of State and the Minister of the grand ducal household, the marriaze by civil contract was then performed, upon the conclusion of which the Grand Duke gave the signal for a movement to be rcade to the chap el& The first procession, headed by the Chamberlains, Ince-Chamber- lains' and other Court functionaries, was composed of the Ducal Court, the Queen leading Prince Ernest and Princess Alice of Hesse by the hand, followed by Princesses Louise, Victoria, and Maud of Wales, following whom came a large number of royal visitors. Then followed Prince William, Princes Henry and Francis Joseph of Battenburg, Count Erbach Schrenberg, and the mediatised nobility, the mem- bers of the suite of the bride and bridegroom, and ladies and gentlemen in waiting on the Royal guests. The bridal procession came next. The bride was conducted by the Grand Duke and Prince Alexander, and after them the bridegroom, who walked between Princess Charles and the Princess of Battenbarg, his mother. Before the bride was carried a handsome bouquet presented by English officers and army students resident in Darmstadt. The procession moved through the White Saloon, down the grand stair- case, into the inner court oT the palace, and thence into the chapel, at the entrance to which the Court chaplains were in waiting to receive the bride and bridegroom. The Grand Duke and Prince Alexander then led the bride to the left hand aide of the altar' whilst Princess Carl and Princess von Battenberg led the bridegroom to the right hand side. Their respective suites arranged themselves behind on either hand, and the marriage service commenced. Herr Bender, the Court chaplain officiated. The moment the bride and bridegroom exchanged rings the first of a salute of thirty-six guns was fired. At the con- clusion of the marriage ceremony, and when the blessing had been pronounced, Her Majesty embraced the bride and bridegroom. The Queen was dressed In black and white. The bride's dress was of white satin, the veil, which did not cover the face, being the same 85 worn by the late Princess Alice on the occasion of her marriage. The ladies in attendance on Her Majesty were dressed in black, but the rest were in white, except some of theladies in waiting, who wore coloured dresses. There were no bridesmaids.

After the ceremony a grand banquet was given in the Kaiser Baal of the New Palace, at which all were present except the Queen, the Marchioness of Ely, and the young Princess Alice, who dined alone. The table was in the- form of a horseshoe. On the bride's right heed sat the Grand Duke. next to whom were the Princess of Wales, the Crown Prince of Germany, and Princess Bea- trice. On the left of the bridegroom sat the Princess Charles, next to whom were the-Prince of Wales and the Crown Prince of Germany. Prinse Alexander sat opposite the bride, and the Princess of Battenberg opposite the bridegroom. No speeches were delivered, and the only toast proposed was in the following words: "To the health of the newly-married couple." A flourish of trumpets fol- lowed, and the toast was drunk. The bride and bridegroom taking leave of the Queen, left at nine o'clock for Sugen- helm, being enthusiastically cheered while passing through the streets. The town is again illuminated to-night in hon- our of the- occasion.

In commemoration of the marriage, the Grand Duke has Pardoned a number of prisoners who have not yet served their full term of imprisonment. rho Crown Prince and Princess of Germany proceeded to Heidelberg on Wednesday morning on a visit to the Empress of Austria, returning to Darmstadt at neon.

ELECTION Irrramaciarecs.—The Hon. H. F. Cowper has definitely announced his intention of retiring from the, representation of Hertford at the end of the present Parlia- ment. The Liberals intend to bring two candidates forward at the next election, one of whom, Mr. Frederick Seebohm, of Hitchin, has already been selected. ACCIDENT Alf to RAILWAY Ciaossuen..—A woman named Elizabeth Bantum, and a girl named Martha Alexander, while passing a level crossing, on Tuesday, on the North London line at Bolto Bridge, Acton, were knocked down by a train. The woman, who died on Wednesday morning, sustained serious internal injuries, and the girl had her foot cut off. It is stated that the man in charge of the gates shouted to them to stop, instead of which they crossed, and In the hurry both fell. CHOLERA IN A, BRITISH TROOPSXIP : SIX DEATHS.— Indian troopship Crocodile, from Bombay, anchored Off Spithead on Tuesday morning with several cases of cholera on board. She was ordered into quarantine, and Dr. Fletcher, fleet surgeon, of the Crocodile, subsequently sent his report ashore. It showed that six cases of cholera had occurred on board, the first on the 15th inst. and the bet on the 20th, and that three deaths had occurred from cholera and two from secondary fever after cholera. The remaining patients were progressing favourably. The three convales- cent cases are so far cured that it is believed there is no pos- sibility of danger. On Wednesday morning, Her MarjesfY's Indian troopship Crocodile went into Portsmouth harbour, having completed her gearantine. THE Carrraer..Naws V. Tun EASTERN TELEGRAM Com- PANY.—The action brought by the Central News against the Eastern Telegraph Company and others was continued on Wednesday, in the Queen's Bench division, when An- nette Georgio Biancordi, formerly employed by the Eastern Telegraph Company, stated that Mr. Smith came on board the Chiltern at Alexandria while the Burleigh message was being despatched, looked through the message, and gave orders to clear the line. He then sent through a service message briefly describing the battle of Tel-el-Kebir. In cross-examination, witness said he was applied to by the representatives of the Central News to gvre information, and was promised if he would come to London and tell the truth his expenses would be paid, and a situation would be found for him if he lost his place in the Eastern Telegraph Company. This closed the plaintiff's else, and the Attorney.. General was addressing the jury on the part of the Eastern Telegraph Company when the court adjourned. A REMARKABLE WOMAN.—One of the best known char- acters of the last century was Mrs. Mapp, the bone-setter, who, after leading a wandering life for Some time, settled down at Epsom. The remarkable strergth with which she was endowed, together with such knowledge as she had ac- quired from her father (himself a bone-setter), mainly con- tributed to the success which, in many cases, undoubtedly attended her operations. She journeyed to town twice a week in a coach-and-four, and, at the Grecian Coffee House, operated on her town patients, carrying their crutches back to Epsom as trophies of her skill. During one of these visits she was called in to the aid of Sir Hans Sloane'a niece, and the success she met with on this occasion became the talk of the town. Many remarkable cures effected by her are noted in the pablic journals of the day, and there is no doubt that she was in the receipt of a very large income. In 1736 she was at the height of prosperity. In the Decem- ber of the next year she died, "at her lodgings near the Seven Dials, so miserably poor that the parish was obliged to ! , bury her."—Prom Cassell's"Greater London" for April.

FOOTBALL : THE EARLESTOW'N JUNIOR CHALLENGE Cup: SEMI-FINAL TlE.—The semi-final tie in connection with the Earlestown and District Junior Challenge Cup Competition was played at Wargrave Moss, on Saturday afternoon last, the competing teams being the Earlestown (2nd) and Wanderers (Ist). There was a large attendance of spectators, whose excitement caused them to encroach upon the field of play, in consequence of which the game was several times stopped. The Wanderers won the toss, land in the first half chose to play with the ground in their favour. Both teams were cheered on by their supporters, land the play was fast and pretty even. Before half-time 'Shaw stored a splendid goal after making a capital run with the leather &lin the field. In the 2nd half the Earlestown 2nd strove hard to equalise the score, but they were pre- vented by the good play of the opposing backs. An ex- citing game thus re.sulted in a win for the Wanderers by one goal to none. The losers afterwards protested against the tie being awarded in favour of the Wanderers on the ground that the play was several times stopped by the spectators. The protest was considered at a meeting of the committee OD Monday morning but it was overruled. The Wanderers have thus to meet the Newton St. Peters in , the final tie. STRUGGLE WITH A POILICE-CONSTABLE AF NEWTON.— special sessions. adjourned from the previous Saturday, was held at the Newton Town Hall, on Tuesday last, when the magistrates on the Bench were Messrs. R. leogghton, T. J. Gillespie, and A. C. McCorauodale. James Singleton, a young fellow, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Newton, on Saturday night, and also with assaulting P.C. Spencer at the same time.—P.C. Spencer deposed that about a quarter-pat eight he saw the prisoner drunk in High-street, and he afterwards went into Rob-lane, where he became very disorderly. He repeatedly asked him to go home, but he refused to ao so, adding that he had already had to serve 18 months for him (witness), and he could do another but he would have his revenge. Witness attempted to take him fiat() custody, and prisoner thereupon became very violent, and in the struggle both fell to the ground. They struggled for about ten minutes, when two men came ' to the officer's assistance, and prevented the prisoner getting :away. With considerable difficulty the haudraffs were placed on the prisoner's wrists, but he still behaved very violertly all the way to the police station, and kicked the officer twice.—For being drunk and disorderly he was fined 59 and costs, and for assaulting the constable be ITSB further fined 13s and costs. DEATH OF MR. C. E. DRIFFIELD.--The announcement of the decease of Mr. Charles Edward Driffield, who for over a period of 31 yeare occupied the position of coroner for the West Derby division of the county will be read with much regret, not only by a large circle of friends,.but by the public generally, as he was well known and universally esteemed throughout the entire division. During the period he occupied the coronership, Mr. Driffield faithfully and judicioasly discharged the onerous duties which' devolved upon him. He was elected to the position which he so worthily tilled for so many years on the 18th of July, nu, in succession to Mr. John Reyes, but previous to that year he had for some time acted as that gentleman's deputy. Mr. John Blundell, a solicitor, of Liverpool, was also a candi- date for the vacancy created by the death of Mr. Reyes, but eventually withdrew from the contest. Pravices.to his ap- pointment as coroner, Mr. Driffield practised at, it solicitor at Preseot, where, we understand, he served his articles, anal where the Driffield family were held in high respect. 'The deceased gentleman, who was 61 years at axe, had been in declining health for some few years past, and on the 11th of December, 1882, he formally resigned his office, on that day a petition being presented by him at the Liverpool Chancery Courtepraying to be relieved of the appointment. He was attended by Dr. George Woods up to the time of his death, which took place on Monday morning, at his residence, 36, liesketh-street, Southport. ALLEGED BURIAL SCANDAL AT NEWTOIL—On Sunday and early in the present week considerable talk was occa- sioned in Earlestown and Newton by the alleged refusal of the eficar of Newton to allow the body of a prominent Non- conformist to enter the church prior to interment. It was stated that the Vicar (the Rev. H. Monk) had absolutely objected to the body of the late Mr. Goldwortby (Wesleyan Methodist) being conveyed into the charch without any reaeon being assigned, and much indignation was expressed thereat, even by Churchmen. Not only so, but it was also stated that the Vicar had curtailed the lament service, simply reading at the grave side the tame' " eve side" portion of the service, while for the interment Of. Church- man shortly afterwarda the Vicar went through the service in a proper and complete manner. A. paragraph referring to the matter appeared in a Liverpool ccntemporaryeand the Vicar, in writing an explanation of the affair, says no disrespect was intended; it all arose through both funerals not being at the church at the hour fixed. He adds :—" Had this been the ce.se no difficulty whatever would, have oc- curred, both funerals would have hem taken together, and both would have been treated in all respects alike. Teie was my expectation until the first funeral arrived at the church, and I was for the first time informed, on advancing to meet the bodies, that only one nad arrived, as the hearse had to be despatched to fetch the other. Explaining in a few words to the widow's brother, the r lative is charge, the difficulty in which I was thus placed, he kindly offered to wait till the hearse eould be despatebed and could return with the second funeral. Doubtless to have adopted this course, and to have taken the large Concourse mean- while into the church, would le?.ve beets the best if I had had time to reflect; but not wishing to detain so Many people, I said, I will do which you like' (so much for my I alleged 'refusal to take the body inside), • but I would suggest to you the course ef taking the first funeral to the grave while the other is -tot route, and after taking the see. vice in church (which is surely for the msolation of the living) with the friends of both, Jean then take the'secona body to the grave.' The brother-inaaw acquiesced, and, with a word of explanation to the widow, this order was carried out."

THE EARLESTOWN CHURCH SCANDAL. POLICE COURT PROCEEDINGS: OFFICERS OF THE CHURCH FINED. The Newton Town Hell was crowded on Saturday, when the summonses arising out of the recent scenes in Earles- town Church were heard. Never did such an amount of interest appear to be taken in any previous case at that court and throughout the six and a half hours occupied in the hearing the inclination of the sympathies of those present was evidenced by occasion el applause at any state- ment, which appeared to be against the vicar. Of course, these manifestations were immediately suppressed, and on one occassion the Chairmen of the Bench gave orders for those guilty of such conduct t) be turned out. The charges were as follows :—Matthew Birkhead (who Has appointed vicar's warden by the ptriehioners at the vestry meeting), Henry James Darman (organist), and Thomas Nevitt (sides- man) were summoned for that they "did molest and disturb the Reverend Thomas Robert Matthews, a clergyman in holy orders of the Church of England, minietering at and celebrating divine service in the Church of St. John the Baptist at Eerlestown," on the 10th March; Nevitt and Birkeead were further summoned for being "guilty of vio- lent and indecent behaviour in the church," on the eth April; and Nevitt, Duman, Birkhead, and Benjamin Cor- lett (late people's warden and now sidesman) were also further charged with "riotous and indecent behaviour in church" on the 13th April. The defendants, who were represented by Mr. Cottingham, barrister. of Man- chester, pleaded not guilty; and Mr. J. Galleon (the Bishap of Liverpocl's legal adviser) appeared to prosecute. The magistrates on the Bench were R. Houghton, .1. G. Gilles- pie and A. C. McCorquodale, Esqrs , but Mr. Gillespie re- tired before the case was concluded. When the cases were called Mr. Cottingham said he had to. take a techuial objection to the summonses. He maintained that the charges of inde- cent, violenteand riotous behaviour were separate offences, and ought to have been eoecified as such. Mr. Gamon said he did not preen' for a conviction in all the Cases. He would only take thet for the 13:h April, as the others bad been taken out only to show the occur- rences that led up to the disturbances on the date men- tioned. Mr. Garnon said the circumstances under which the sum- menses were taken out had originated in a dispute between the churchwardeus and the incumbent of St. John's, Earles- town, with retarence to the powers or control over the. or- g *let and choir of the church. He appeared in that case by the direction of the Bishop of Liverpool, acting as his secretary, and ii was not the wish of the Bishop that any such proceedings should have been taken. Very great efforts bad been made to adjust the dispute in au amicable and friendly way, and many proposals had been made by the Bishop, who had been intervieWei by both parties, and he had given the beet advice he could in the interests of peace and quietness. It was very reluctantly that they came for- ward in order, as they believed, to put down mob law, which was likely to prevail at Earleatown. The disturb- ances had commenced as far back as last December, and with some intermissions they had gone on up to last Easter landay, increasing in violence till they culmintted in the scene which he should bring before them in evidence. It was thought that it would be a disgrace to the civil power as well as to the ecclesiastical law if it was allowed to go on any further. Whatever rights or claims might be set up there were many ways easily suggested to secure them, and Mr. Matthews had shown every willingness to adjust the dispute in a proper manner. It was not for them to take , the law into their own hands and disturb a place of worship in the mincer they had done, practically depriving the parish from worshipping in their parish church. He read the section of the law bearing on the appointment of war- dens,, and said if there was one thing more clear than another it was that the churchwardens office was one of ob- servation and complaint, and he geestioned whether in any case except in extreme instances they had any right to interfere with the celebration of the services, such as the minister should direct. At all events if there was one duty which was laid down emphatically it was that the wardens had to keep order in the church, and where they thought any wrong had been done to apply to the Ordinary of the Bishop for hiedirecttons. With regard to the particular Point in dispute-the conduct of the services by the minis- ter and the control of the organist and choir he would refer the Bmch to the case of Wyndham v. Cole ite the Court of Arches in 1875. Eie maintaiqed that according to the decisions in that case the minister of a parish had full control over the organ and the organist whether or not he was elected by the charchwardens and parishioners or whether or not he was paid by them. He contended that only wardens were recognised by the Act and that eidesmen had no legal authority whatever. They were merely deputy wardens, and whatever authority they • had could only be derived from the wardens. The distur- bances at St. John's Church in relation to the playing of the • organ had gone en so far that the church had on One occasion to be closed to prevent further disturbances. A new organist named Mr. Thomas Pemberton was provided by the incum- bent for the Easter Sunday services, and the defendants • CJrlett, Nevitt, and Bit-I:Mead went up to the organ and drove awn' the men appointed as organ-blowers. Nevitt sat on the floor, placed his shoulder against the organ-pole, prepping it in such a way as to prevent it being used, while the defendants also brought a form and put it under the handle to still further prevent it being used by anyone, The incumbent remonetrated with them upon the proceed- ings, but Corlett gave inatructims as Hilo was the man in authority, telling the others what they ought to do, and en- couraging them in their proceedings. He even went so far as to threaten to put Mr. Mitthewe out from the church, and to turn out Mr. tatty -b?.catge he was a man deputed to blow the organ. Mr. Pemberton, who was deputed to play the organ, was removed from the seat near the organ and Du,- Irian was put in his piece, and the latter began to play. Then the Vicar's churchwarden (Mr. Shinn), by he direc- tion of the Vicar, told Mr. Darman that he was not to play, but he replied that he would, and he went on playing. When the clergymen came

into the church to proceed with the service they saw Mr. Birkhead in the chancel with a hymn paper ready to give out hymns of his own in opposition to those directed to be sung by the incumbent. Upon that Mr. Matthews seeing that he could not possibly proceed with the service; that Mr. Darman persisted in playing the organ, and that there was a very unruly atmosphere in the church, gave notice that he should be obliged to close the service. The defendant Darman played a voluntary, then played the Hallelujah Chorn4, which was snag by the choir in contempt, and he would say contrary to the direc- tions of the incumbent. After that Birkhead came to the chancel steps and made a speech to the people; atter which he gave out hymns of his own free will, four hymns in all, which were sung. and they then sang the doxology. The defendant Durman then played a wedding march. There was much hooting and noise in the church, and most unruly proceedings in the church. Ile contended that if those things were proved the defendants were guilty of violent, riotous, and indecent behaviour, that they were banded to- gether with others aiding and abetting them, whom they had not thought necessary to bring before the court. They did not want a multiplicity of cases or to unduly press that action, all they wanted was that the parishioners of St. John's should be able to enjoy worship in their parish church decently and quietly, and that the vicar shou'd be allowed to exercise the right which belonged to him of say- ing whether or not the organ should be played; who or who should not play it, and celebrating the services quietly and orderly, and that he should say what hymns should be given out and sung during service. The Rev. Thomas Robert Matthews was then sworn. He said he had been the incumbent of St. John's Church, Earlestown, since it was consecrated on the 6th January, 1879, and in the May following he had the district assigned to him by the Ecclesiastical Commissioners. He had never had any dispute with the wardens previous to the com- mencement of December last. It continued for some time, until the death of his wife and his own illness put a stop to them. On Easter Sunday there was an early celebration of the Holy Communion, which was a quiet service. For the forenoon service he provided an organist—a Mr. Pember- ton, of Liverpool. Ile (the vicar) furnished him with such hymns as were to be sung on that day, and gave him cer- tain directions about playing the organ. He (the vicar) got to the church about ten o'clock, and saw that there was a determination on the part of certain Cottingham: Don't speak of determinations—speak to facts.—The Rev. T. R. Matthews (continuing) saw Corlett, Nevitt, and Birk- head walking up the aisle' and making their way towards the back of the organ. He ' believed Mr. SIMI], Mr. Atty, and a Mr. Barton were there at that time, and they were displaced by the defendants. Mr Nevitt sat down on the floor, and put his shoulder under the blowing pole. The next thing he saw was a form placed under the organ-pole so that it could not be used. He asked what they were doing there, and they said they were there under Mr. Corlett' direction, and that no one should blow unless it was for Mr. Durman.—Mr. Gamon : Did they use any threats 2—Mr. Cottingham : Don't suggest to the wit- ness.—Mr. Gamon : I don't want to suggest or lead the wit- ness in any way. After that Mr. Atty came into the vestry, and Mr. Barton was driven away from the organ, Mr. Corlett also came in the vestry, and, he believed, laid hold of Mr. Atty, and ordered him out. Witness told him he was not to leave, that he was there by his (the vicar's) invitation, whereupon Mr. Corlett threatened to put him (the vicar) out. He threw open the door, but witness shut it, locked it, put the key in his pocket, and asked him to put him out. Corlett, however, walked away. He (the vicar) gave certain orders to Mr. Shinn, and afterwards went into the church, where he siw Mr. Darman at the organ and Mr. Birkhead close to with a paper in his hands, and most of the singers in their places. He did not give any directions to the singers about their places. When Darman stopped playing the volun- tary, he (witness) got up and announced there would be no service, and he and Mr. Smith (the curate) went into the vestry. Mr. Durman struck up the Hallelujah Chorus, and the choir joined in singing it. Mr. Birkhead then caste forward, and, standing on the chancel steps, made a speech to the people. Hearing him in the vestry, he (the vicar) walked oat into the church, whereupon Mr. Birkhead said, "Yes, I'ra here," and witness returned to the vestry. Mr. Birkhead proceeded to give out four hymns, which were sung, as well as the Doxology.—Mr. Gamod: Was any authority given by you to give out hymns 2—Witness : None whatever. The Rev. Henry Elwell Smith (curate) said : I was at the service on the 13th April and was present in the chancel with the Vicar. I have heard what hat; been stated by him, and I corroborate the cardinal features of what he has stated.—ln reply to Mr. Cottingham, witness said: I was present in the vestry when Mr. Corlett came in after the announcement that there would be no service. He asked Mr. Attv what business he had there, and I think Mr. Afty said it was at Mr. Matthews's invitation. He ordered Mr. Atty out, and then I think Mr. Matthews interfered, and then I think Mr. Corlett said "I have more power here than you have," and then he told him (Mr. Matthews) he was the means of the row, and would put him out. I understood from what Mr. Corlett said that he had more power as our officer than the Vicar. I did not personally sea any dis- sorderly conduct en the part of the defendants. There was plenty of hissing on the part of the congregation. The hymns given out were properly sung by the choir and pro- perly played by Mr. Darman. , Mr. Cottingham then proceeded to address the Bench on behalf of the defendants. He said that before he called any witnesses he would take the opinion of the Bench whether or not there was any case to answer. They were charged with being guilty of violent, riotous, and indecent behaviour, and he sehmitted there was no evidence to show that any of the defendents were guilty of it. He also main- tained that anything done by the defendants did not con- stitute an offence under the statute under which the sum- monses had been issued. Mr. Darman refusing to give up his place to the appointee of the Vicar did not constitute A riot or indecency, or in any way tend to interrupt the congregation or the services. With reference to the case quoted by his learned friend, it would be noticed that it was only an Ecclesiastical offence —that of playing the omen before or immediately after I divine service contrary to the vicar's directions; but in this case there was no intention on the part of the vicar to pre- 1 vent the playing of the organ, but to prevent a certain in- diyidual—a salaried organist, exercising his customary functions, and that they should be supplanted by a stranger. With regard to the other defendants, they were not guilty of any offence. There had been a great deal of disorder in the church, but they had the Vicar to thank for that, and no one else. It was admitted that but for the Vicar attempt- ing to remove and dismiss Mr. Darman therm never would have been the slightest disturbances in the church. He was bound to perform the services, and had a sacred duty to perform; but simply because he was annoyed with Mr. Dar- man, not because he was incapable of performing his duties, but because Mr. Matthews said "You shan't per- form. I will have another," he punished his parishioners by refusing to allow any service. A more illegal or more un- justifiable act a clergyman was never guilty of. Here was a Christian clergyman on Easter Sunday who refused to perform his duties in a most unchristian spirit because the organist insisted upon his right to play. Before continuing his defence he would the magistrates whether they thought that there was a case for him to answer.—After a short consultation, the Clerk said : The Bench wish you to go into the merits and facts of the case.—The Chairman : Most decidedly —Mr. Cottingham then proceeded to criti- cise the evidence at considerable length, maintaining that it went to prove that the defendants took no part in the hoot- ing, hissing, or other demonstration in the church. He re- marked that public opinion was that the Vicar's conduct was high-handed, tyrannical, and cruel, and though a large num- ber of meetings bad been held, at which the Vicar's con- duct bad been condemned, there had not been a eingle gather- ing in his favour. It was a most unenviable and deplorable condition of things for any clergyman to be in, and the parishioners had only acted as Englishmen generally did, and that was resent high-handed and tyrannical proceedings. Of all tyrannies Englishmen had always resisted that of one man, clothed with a spiritual authority which he tyran- nically abused against his parishioners.

Sr. JOSEPH'S Sonoma, "'EASLEY CROSS.—A tea party and entertainment in aid of the church and school fund were held in St. Joseph's School, Peasley Cross, en Monday even- ing. About 500 persons sat down to an excellent tea; after which an entertainment was held. The selections by the Excelsior Glee Party were mach appreciated, and Mr. S. A. Hollingworth created much amusement with a "Stump speech" The Rev. Father Byrne occupied the chair, and in the course of the evening heartily thanked the ladies and , gentlemen who bad contributed to the success of the even- ing's proceedings. I POLICEMEN as Bown-sarrnits. The great practical value of the work done by the St. John's Ambulance So- ciety WAS illustrated at Chester Police-court on Monday. I Two young Irishmen were charged with seriously injuring ' their brother in Boughton, an Irish quarter of Chester, on Saturday. night. As the climax of a long-standing family I feud, they knocked him down breaking his leg and disloca- ting his ankle. Acting-sergeant Gallagher, holding a certi- oate of St. John's Ambulance Society, actually set the man's I leg in the street and conveyed him to the infirmary. The doctors say the operation was properly performed. I MAY-DAY AT ST. HELENS.—There was very little observ- able in St. Helens on Thursday to denote that the "merry month of May" had made its advent. About nine o'clock Messrs. Greene'', Whitley, and Co., the well-known brewers, turned out their splendid stud of animals attached to drays laden with casks of ale. Both horses and men presented a smart appearance. At noon the horses and carts belonging to the Corporation appeared in front of the Town Hall, as were also a number of the members of the Fire Brigade, I under their superintendent, Mr. L. Birchall, mounted on the , steam fire engine and hose and reel. They were subjected to ' a critical inspection. The streets were paraded for a short time, notwithstanding the drenching rain. div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

Strom; DEATIL—Mrs. Pratt, the wife of Mr. Pratt, Market-place, was found dead in bed on Wednesday morn- ing. She appeared to be in her usual health on Tuesday I night, and in good spirits. An inquest will be held.—An inquest was held by Mr. F. Smith, coroner, on Tuesday, at the King's Arms, on the body of a child named John Travis, son of John Travis, Beacondeld-street. The child WAS very delicate, and Mr. Green was called in, who advised the parents to take the ehll4 to Dr. Ball. While waiting in the surgery the child died.' 'The jury returned a verdict of "Died from natural causes." Bosun or GUARDIANS.—The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held at the Union Work- house, VVhiston, on Thursday forenoon' when there were present: Mr. J. T. Hall (in the chair), the Rev. T. Chambers, the Rev. J. Barnacle, the Rev. Father Finegan, and Messrs. J. Jackson, Leatherharrow, T. Dobell, J. Lowe, W. Birchall, J. Fisher, J. Fidler, E. Syder' T. F. Hill, H. Hulme, J. Matthews, W. Newsome, and S. H. Hartley (clerk).— Vote of Condolence: Mr, Meadows moved that a letter of condo- lence be'sent to the family of the late Mr. James Penketh, whose death they all regretted. Mr. Fidler seconded the motion, and in doing so commented upon the unseemly haste with which some gentlemen wished to fill his place.— The vote of condolence was unanimously passed.—Relief Statistics: The Clerk reported ,that the number of inmates of the Workhouse was 427, against 447 in the preceding week, and 500 in the cor- responding week last year. There had been 64 vagrants relieved daring the week; and there were 173 boys and girls in the Kirkdale Schools. Of the number in the House 261 were in the hospital ward.—Alleged Informal Com- mittee Meeting : Mr. Fidler drew attention to an alleged in- formal meeting of certain members of the Building Com- mittee, and maintained that a slight had been put upon other members of the committee. Mr. Hill explained that he had arraLged with the chairman of the Building Committee, the chairman of the Beard, and the chairman of the House Com- mittee to meet at the House and make themselves thoroughly conversant with the details of the plan. Nothing was at all intended in the way of a slight or insult. The matter dropped. The Rev. T. Chambers drew attention to a recommendation of the Visiting Committee that a screen should be purchased for use in the Workhouse Chapel to hide the Church of England communion table or the Romah Catholic altar, candlesticks, dm., during the set vice of either denomination, and strongly condemned the suggestion as the stirring up of strife and enmity, and spoke of it as a species of malice, hatred, intolerance, and he would go so far as to say bigotry. The RA'. J. Barnacle agreed with the suggestion that there should be a screen provided. The Rev. Father Finegan said he was always very reluctant to say anything upon a matter of that kind, bat he could see no objection at all to allowing things to re- main as at present. By a majority of 8 to 4 the Board decided to expunge the minute referring to the screen, after which the minutes were passed.—The Removal of Children from Pantasaph : This question was again discussed upon the clerk reading a letter from Mr. T. W. Reynolds, of Wool- ton, asking for an explanation with respect to the removal of school children from Pantasaph, and requesting the Board to receive a deputation on the subject.—The Rev. Father Finegan ultimately moved that the deputation be received at the next meeting, and Mr. Fisher seconded the motion, which was carried by 7 to 5.

ANOTHER ARREST. There was again, as previously, a large attendance at the Birmingham Police Court on Saturday, when James Francis Egan, charged with conspiring with John Daley, alias Denman. to cause an explosion in the United Kingdom likely to endanger life and property, was brought up on remand. Mr. Poland came down specially to prose- cute on behalf of the Treasury, and was accompanied by Mr. Cuffs, the Treasury solicitor. Mr. O'Connor again rip. peered for the prisoner.—Mr. Poland said: I propose to-day to prefer a charge against the prisoner of treason felony, and I propose on a subsequent occasion to place by his aide a man named John Daley, so that they may both be charged with this offence.—Mr. O'Connor (interrupting) said the charge was completely new, and was far more serious than the charge previously preferred. He had not had any notice of it, and he considered it scarcely fair to his client.—The magistrate said they had better hear from Mr. Poland what the evidence was likely to be.—Mr. Poland then said he should show that the prisoner and Daley (apprehended on Good Friday at Birkenhead) had lived together and been on the most intimate terms at the present prisoner's house at Sparkbrook, Birmingham. On Daley being arrested three destructive nitro-glycerine shells were found in his pockets. The present prisoner on being apprehended on Good Friday denied that he knew Daley by name, which must have been false, as he had letters signed by Daley. In the present prisoner's garden had been unearthed a tin can containing doeuments (produced) purporting to provide for the consti- tution of an Irish Republic. Books, labelled as if belonging to an assurance company, were found providing for the collec- tion of money for arms in the use of which the Irish Repub- lican Brotherhood were to be trained. In John Daley's bed- room there was found this document :—" Arms got from 1879 to 1881: rifles 2,844, revolvers 702, making 3,546; prevlously in hand, muzzle holders 1,194, shot guns 1,656, revolvers 1,808; total—old 4,748, new 3,546, making a total of 8,294." Then there is a memorandum, "The above is a record of arms in the hands of members of good standing." A penny levy was exacted from members of the Brother- hood, and a letter dated Sept. 11th, 1871, from 0, Waterloo- street, Kidderminster, and written by a man who signed himself " John Moran," mentioned that the Brotherhood were growing stronger in Lancashire, there being "a good Centre, a vety energetic fellow at Bury," whose address, however, was in Ramsbottom. The present prisoner ap- peared to have acted as clerk to a highly-respectable gentle- elan by day and as a Fenian at nights.—Egan, who showed confusion on hearing of the discovery of the documents, was remanded till Saturday.—At Liverpool on Saturday, Daley was brought up and formally remanded till Thursday. He asked whether it was necessary for him to be shackled, and the Stipendiary said it was a matter for the police. On Thursday morning at two o'clock Thomas Daley, who, during his remand from Birkenhead, has been incarcerated in Chester Castle, was removed to the former place. Since his confinement there Chester Castle has been closely guarded by seven county policemen in addition to the ordinary prison officials. On Wednesday night Daley went to bed at half-past seven, and at half an hour after midnight he was awakened, and informed that he was shortly to be conveyed back to Birkenhead. At half-past one o'clock Detective-sergeant Murphy, of the Chester city police, De- tective-inspector Moore, and Detective-inspector Hughes, of Birkenhead, together with another officer, arrived at the castle, and Daley was handed into their custody and hand- cuffed, and taken to the railway station in a cab. Daley wore a light felt hat, light overcoat, or dustcoat, and black trousers. He also had on a pair of light kid gloves. The train left for Birkenhead at 2-45. The officers in charge of he prisoner were armed with revolvers. On Thursday, Daley, Egan's lodger, was brought up again at the Birkenhead Police Court. Colonel Majendie, chief inspector of explosives, described the experiments he had made at Woolwich with the bombs found upon the piisoner when he was arrested at Birkenhead railway station, and said these bombs were of a character very formidable to human life, and he could come to no other conclusion than that they were intended for use against human beings. Dr. Dupre cuToborated Colonel Majendie's evidence, and said the shells could only have been intended for the purpose of killing or injuring human beings by being thrown into a room or among a crowd. Daley was committed for trial at the Chester Assizes. United Ireland publiaises long extracts from a correspon- dence which took place in 1877, between Mr. O'Connor Power, M.P., and Daley, in which they mutually accuse each other of being traitors. The dispute arose in consequ- ence of a party of Fenians under the charge of Daley break- ing up a meeting Mr. O'Connor Power was addressing at Dumbarton and Hamilton.

div.head: ABHIEST CF A PUBLICAN.
div.p: ABHIEST CF A PUBLICAN.

At the Birmingham Police Court, on Thursday, William McDonnell, 34 years of age, manager of the Royal Oak, King-street, Wednesbury, as brought up on a charge of treason felony. The prisoner was apprehended at his resi- dence late on the previous night by Detective-Inspectors Stroud and Stephenson, Birmingham, and Superintendent Holland, Wednesbury, and brought at once to Birmingham, arriving at midnight. Mr. Farndale, in applying for a remand until Saturday, said it was necessary, in order that the prisoner might be brought up with Egan and Daley, who was at present in custody at Birkenhead. His worship would recollect that Mr. Poland, in his opening speech on Saturday morning, referred to a letter foand in the canister, buried in the garden at Egan's horse, from William McDon- nell, of Wedoesbary, who signed himself "district centre." In consequence of that letter, and other letters from the pri- soner found at Egan's house, he (Mr. Farndale) proceeded to McDonnell's house on Wednesday morning to investigate , the matter. He was assisted by Superintendents Black and Holland, of the Staffordshire Constabulary. After having I an interview with the prisoner and several other people in Wednesbury, he communicated the result of his investiga- tions to the Home Secretary, and on Wednesday night, from i a telegram received from the Home Office, he ordered ' McDonnell's arrest. He was requested to apply for a re- mand until Saturday, in order that he might be brought up with the other prisoners.—The Stipendiary (to thh priso- ner) : Have you any reason why you should not be re- ' manded ?—Mr. Corbett said he appeared for the prisoner, and he had no objection to a remand until Saturday. Ile, however, applied for bail, the prisoner being a most re- spectable man and well known.—Mr. Farndale said Captain Congreve, chief constable of Staffordshire, was present, and also the superintendent of Wednesbury. They had known the prisoner for some time, and after consulting them he must oppose the application.—The Stipendiary: On such a charge as this I should not be justified in allowing bail. You will be remanded until Saturday. In Birmingham considerable importance is attached to the arrest of the alleged dynamitard, William M•Donnell, a Wednesbury publican. It is stated that Daley, during the time he was watched was followed on several occasions to SPDonnell's house, which, it is believed, was a favourite meeting place of the Fenian brotherhood in the Black Country. The documents which were found at Egaa's house are very compromising in face of this fact, as many of them are dated from M‘Dennell's house, and he has had several documents addressed to him by EgAn. The arrest , has caused great excitement throughout the Black Country and in Birmingham, more especially as it is believed other arreste will follow. Numerous persons have been constantly i watched by the police for weeks past.

A Dublin correspondent states that an action by a young lady ef 21, who has been a ward of Chancery; with an in- come of £3OO a year, has been commenced against an octo- genarian Irish connty court judge for breach of promise of marriage, the damages being laid at 18,000.

LIMIT.-COLONEL GREENALL AND TIIR VOLUNTEER ORLEBRATION.—It is proposed to celebrate the 25th year of the existence of the volunteer force by a banquet on Her Majesty's birthday, the 24th May, at which Colonel Viscount Renelee), K.C.8., will preside. Only officers still serving whose commissions date prior to let Januaty, 1860, will be eligible to attend. Lient.-Colenel Greenell, 9th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers, has the matter in hand, and may be addressed at the Volunteer Service Club, 32, Dover- street. Piccadilly. FALL OF A BUILDING.—On Saturday night part of a three-storied building, situated in Cloth Hall-yard, Bank- street. collapsed, and fell with a loud crash, causing con- siderable consternation among the residents of the vicinity. The debris fell on an old maltkiln, and some of the brices were projscted as far as Trow-lane, where several doors and windows were damaged. The building is old and dilapida- ted, but no immediate danger had been apprehended, and the upper storey of the part that fell had been occupied until two o'clock on the afternoon of the same day by a number of fustian cutters, who are in the employ of Mr. Thomas Hunt. It is fortunate that the fall occurred so late in the evening, as a number of young children had been playing near the property about two hours before. LECTURE AT DADISHEAD.—The Rev. E. A. Telfer de- livered a lecture on Tuesday evening, to a very appreciative audience, in the Wesleyan day school, on "Canada, with Memories of Mighty Niagara." The lecture was comprehen- sivetillustrated with a map showing towns, cities, villages, lakes, rivers, and forests, as well as climate, temperature, fertility, and productiveness of soil. With graphic power he pictured the wonders of Niagara, warning the young by way of ill astration of other rapids in this life which lead to destruction. As for emigration, he knew of no place to compare with Canada. Wherever he bent his steps he saw a prosperous and a well-to-do people. The chair was occu- pied by Mr. Hopewell, of Cadishead. A very hearty vote ad thanks was given to the rev. gentleman for the rich treat he had afforded the meeting, the chairman too being cordially thanked for his services. NEWS INDEED!—It is said one should go from home to , bear news, and so the Liverpool Evening Ezpress tells us in a " special telegram" that the "Warrington Conservative Association" had a meeting on Tuesday night at which hearty votes of thanks were passed to Mr. McMinniee fer his past services." Can it be that the Conservatives have really been showing sons ble regard far the Liberal member for Warrington, or is it that mit contemporary is getting " mixed" ? Perhaps some one has been "playing tricks," for the paragragh goes on to refer to "the merits of several gentlemen,' —ell of whom are Liberals—being discussed by this, the Conservative Association, with a view to their being "probable candidates." There was a Liberal Meeting in Warrington on the Same evening, but the " special tele- gram" can hardly refer to that, unless the sender has been drawing on his imagination as to a discussion of names which were not even "mentioned as probable canuidates." iletancrserrAL DISTRICTS, WARRINOTON.—The Queen has approved of Colonel W. de W. Thackwell, half-pay, being appointed to eommaad the Bth and 40th Regimental Dis- tricts at Warrington, vice Colonel H. J. Bell, retired with honorary rank of major-general. In losing Colonel Bell the volunteers of this district part with an officer who has done much in his short term of office to bring all volunteer corps to a high state of efficiency. Colonel W. de. W. Thackwell was formerly in command of the old 38th Foot, now better known as the let Battalion of the South Stafford- shire Regiment, with which regiment he served through the Crimean campaign, including the siege and fall of Sebas- topol, for which he holds a medal and clasp, the stk class of the Medjidie, and the Turkish medal. Colonel Thackwell leas the reputation of being a very smart officer, severe when necessary, but, according to an old colour-sergeant of his late regiment, an officer who takes great interest in his command, and very popular with his men. This will make the seventh change in the command of the Bth and 40th Regimental Districts since the death of Colonel Jones in 1876, the other officers who have held the command b.ing Colonels A. C. Robertson. De Montmorency, D. Berry, Sally Flood, De Renzy Pigott, Harry J. Bell, and Thackwell. • Womemzer's Carne—On Monday evening, the nineteenth and last family party of the season was given at the Work- men's Club, Warrington, when Mr. Hall, of Manchester, gave a number of selections from various authors, which were highly appreciated by a numerous audience. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. Yonge, who was supported by the following gentlemen, viz. :—The Mayor (Alderman Harrison), the Rev. C. C. Harrison, Alderman Davies, Dr. Mackie, and Messrs. Wright, Bennett, T. Birchall, T. Robin- son, .1. Potter, J. Roberts. and Davey. The recitals given by Mr. Hall included selections from the following : Hamlet, act 3, scene 2, and act 5, scene 1 ; Longfellow's "Psalm of Life ;" Cornwall's " Life," " Ferdinand and Elvira ;" Dicken's "Richard Doubledick;" "The charity dinner ;" "Bridge of Sighs ;" and "Love in a balloon." Miss F. Baker gave several pianoforte selections previous to the recitals, and was very well received.--At the conclusion the Mayor proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Hall, who, he remarked, had made great and thoroughly successful efforts to please his audience.—Mr. Birchall seconded the pro- position, which was carried by acclammation.—A. vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, on the motion of Alderman Davies, seconded by Mr. Bennett, and was suitably acknowledged.—Dr. Mackie proposed a vote of thanks to the committee for their labours during the winter season in organising such attractive entertainments ; they had, he said, had the best chairmen and entertainers that could be procured, ant the committee deserved their best thanks.—The motion was seconded by the Rev. C. C. Harri- son, and carried unanimously, after which the meeting broke up. A WELL CONTESTED RACE.—On Saturday afternoon, George Wilcock and James Walsh, both of Warrington, met at the Star Inn Grounds, St. Helens, in order to decide their engagement to run 130 yards, on level terms, for £25 aside, but the affair ended in a fiasco. The match created no small amount of interest amongst the respective partisans of the men, who are well-known pads. in their native town, and "there would be at least 1,000 persons present. Wilcock was trained by J. Harrison, of Newton Common, at Lowden, near Newton-le-Willows, and Walsh, by A. Williamson, of Charlestown, from the Central Hotel, Warrington, and each was in the pink of condition. The betting, which was pretty brisk, opened at sto 4, and closed at 6t04 on Walsh. The race was a moee desperate one, each doing his very utmost from start to finish. After some needless waste of time at the mark, the pistol was fired to a very good start, Walsh, if anything, having just the best of it, and he held a slight lead until about a dozen yards from home. Here Wilcock made a determined effort, and getting level in the last two strides, made a dead heat of it. The referee gave his deci- sion accordingly, and theta followed a most disagraceful scene. Each claimed to have won, and a mob gathered round the referee and abused him in the most shameful manner; indeed, it was a wonder that he escaped with his life. In the opinion of many present, the decision was an honest and proper one. and they interfered on behalf of the official named. If each rowdyism is to be continued at the Star Inn Grounds, St. Helens, it will become a very difficult matter to find either a stake-holder or a properly qwalified man to act as referee in the fature. Mr. J. Candow' of Sheffield, in the absence of Mr. T. Wilkinson, officiated as Starter, and Mr. J. Clarkson, of Manchester, as referee. It is expected that Wilcock and Walsh will ran off their dead heat this (Saturday) afternoon. CELEBRATION OF LORD WINMARLEIGH'S BIRTHDAY.— On Saturday last this venerable nobleman entered upon the 83rd year of his age and the event was fittingly celebrated at his seat, Winmarleigh Hall, near Garstang, though his iordship was absent, having left about 10 days ago for Lon- don. When Lancashire returned only two members to Par- liament (previous to the Reform Act of 1832) Lord Win- marleigh (then Mr. John Wilson-Patten). was returned unopposed along with Lord Stanley; but though he voted for the second reading of that Bill, and by his vote carried it, he found himself tenable to concur with the whole of the details of the measure, and he resigned his seat when the Government appealed to the country shortly after its intro- duction in 1831. Mr. Benjamin Heywood become Lord , Stanley's colleague for a short time. Under the Reform Bill ef 1832 Lancashirewas divided into two northern and southern divisions, each to return two members, and Mr. Heywood having offered his services to another constituency, Mr. Wilson-Patten again came forward as a candidate for the representation of the northern division, and was unani- mously elected along with the Right Hon. E. G. Stanley (the late Earl of Derby) at the nomination, which took place at Lancaster, on the 17th December, 1832. Up to 1874 the hon. gentleman continued to represent the northern division, which was again divided under the Reform Act, 1867. He had therefore been one of the representatives of the county in nine Parliaments, his services in that capacity extending over a period of nearly 44 years. He was highly esteemed in the House of Commons, and was Chairman of Committees of the whole House from November, 1852, till April, 1853; Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster from J0ne,..1867, till September, 1868, and for a short period was Chief Secretary for Ireland. In 1874, on the accession of the Conservatives to power, Mr. Wilson-Patten, the then senior member for North Lancashire, was raised to the peerage, on the recommendation of Mr. Disraeli, and took his seat in the upper House as Baron Winmarleigh, of Winmarleigh. From 1842 till 1872 he was Colonel of the 3rd Royal Lancashire Militia, served with that regiment at Gibraltar during the Crimean war, and was ap- pointed on his return one of Her Majesty'e aide-de-camps. On the death of the Duke of Bnceleuch he became senior aide-de-catup, and is still honorary colonel of the third and fourth battalions of the Loyal North Lancashire (the new nomenclature of the 3rd Royal Lancashire Militia.) Among his tenantry, both at Warrington and Winmarleigh, Lord Winmarleigh has always been held in high esteem. His lordship was a prominent figure in the celebration of the Preston Guild of 1882, when he was in his 81st year, and has been present at four guilds. Lord Wininarleigh took a very active and important part in the Ship Canal Scheme in 1883. Lord Shaftesbury is just two deem younger than Lord Winmarleigh, and reached big 83rd year on Monday.
