NON-EFFICIENr VOLUNTEERS—Yesterday several mem- bers of the 9th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers were sum- moned at the Warrington Borough Police Court by Ser- geant-Major Fennelley for non-efficiency.—ln respect of Sidney Smith, a labourer at Dallam Forge, the sum of Ll 103 was claimed.—Defendant said that he stopped r way under the impression that he had made up the required number of drills.—He was ordered to pay 5s a month.— Thomas Chadwick was summoned for £4.—He said that he

had been ill for two years. and produced a doctor's certifi- cate dated July, 1883, which he said-he thought would tie sufficient. He had belonged to the Volunteers for twenty years.—The case was adjourned for 14 days to allow him time to make arrangements, or produce a certificate of a later date.—William.Corbett' who had been a volunteer for 15 years, was ordered to pay £1 103 at 58 a.month for non- efficiency, and James Turner was similarly dealt with. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending Saturday, April 26th, 1884. The mean temperature was 37.8 Fahrenheit, and therefore a degree wanner than the precedir g week. The maximum temperature 52 Fahrenheit, was netorded on the 23rd inst , and the minimum temperature 21 Fahrenheit on the 25th inst. The rainfall measured inches. The general direction of the wind was easterly. Daring the week, which was the 17th of the current year, 44 births and 19 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal te 214 per 1,000, against 161 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 317 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 2 from diarrhcea, 1 from old age, 2 from brain disease, 1 from hydrophobia, 5 from lung disease, 1 from heart disease, and 1 from liver disease. Two cases of typhoid fever were reported under the require- ments of the Act of Parliament. Jolter H. GonNaLL, medical officer of health. THEFT AT A BEER-HOUSE.-011 Tuesday, at the Warring- ton Borough Police Court, Martin Higgins, a brewer labourer, was charged before Major Cartwright and Alder- man Webster with stealing four bottles of porter, the pro- perty of William Partington, beer-house keeper, Friar's- green, on the previous evening.—The Chief Constable (Mr. Hata) said that the prosecutor was the landlord of the Old House at Home beer-house, Friar's- green, and the prisoner was a labourer at the brewery in Dallam-lane. He was a single man, and , lodged at the Star and Garter, also in Friar's-green. On Monday evening Mrs. Partington left the bar to draw a quart of beer, and during her absence the servant saw him remeve from a shelf four half-pint bottles of porter, three of which he put in his pocket, giving the other one to a man named John McCue, who was in the room. The servant told her mistress what she had seen, and Mrs. Partington asked the prisoner to give back the bottles to escape any further trouble, but he strongly denied having taken them. Whilst she was speaking to him the bottle given to McCue exploded, and Mrs. Partington, noticing the bulky appear- ance of the prisoner's pocket, snatched two bottles of porter out of it. The prisoner then made his escape, and was after- wards arrested.—He now asserted that he had paid for the porter, but the Bench disbelieved him, and sent him to prison for 14 days, severely censuring McCue for the part he • took in the affair. AN ABSCONDING POLICEMAN.—At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yesterday, before the Mayer (Alder- man Harrison) and Mr. John White, Richard Hastens, a member of the Borough Police Force, was charged with ab- senting himself from duty, on the 18th of April.—The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said that the prisoner joined the Borough Constabulary in March of the present year, and he might say that he should not desire to recommend to the Watch Committee a man with a better character than the prisoner had. He was a native of Warrington' and had been in the army, having claimed his discharge in February last after nearly 14, years' service, and having left with a good character. The prisoner. on joining the force, was provided with the necessary clothing and accoutrements, and ap- peared to make a good constable, indeed, he (Mr. Hunt) took an especial interest in him, as he had been accustomed to discipline, and had seen something of the world. On the I 18th April he received his weekly wages, and should have paraded for duty at ten o'clock at night. He failed to do so, land it was ascertained that he had left the town. A war- mut was issued, and he surrendered himself on Thursday. He (Mr. Hunt) wished to be merciful, but he had to be just, and be simply brought the case before them and left it in their hands.—Prisoner said that be had met some friends from Liverpool, who persuaded him to have some drink and then to go away with them. The same night he got his face smashed, and was ashamed to come back.—Prisoner's wife said that he had always been an excellent husband.— Fined £2 and costs, or one menth. MAY DAY.-0 wing to climatic influences, the May Day of 1884, if one of the merriest days of the year, could hardly be described as being one of the most genial. The traditions and associations connected with May Day are always remembered with pleasure, although fortunately, perhaps, in some respects and unfortunately in others, the pageantry and mirth that in olden times were the order of the day that ushered in the month of flowers and blossems, have now almost en- tirely disappeared, or, at any rate, are only repre- sented on a very diminished scale; fortunately, because the May Day celebrations of former days were often accom- panied by revelry such as the people of the present day would scarcely tolerate, and, unfortunately, because the in- nocence and purity of the welcoming of the coming summer are also in so great a measure lost. There still remains, however, and especially in Cheshire, the custom of de- corating the horses, and in some parts of the county a fairly successful attempt is made to revive the May Pole and the crowning of the May Queen. In Warrington the observance of May Day appears each year to be less recognised, and on Thursday the only noticeable observance was the pretty attire of some of the horses, whose drivers had done their best to make them as attractive as possible. The violence of the weather, and the heavy rain that fell during the day, detracted considerably from their appearance, and no or- ganised effort was made to focus a procession. The proces- sion not being held is probably to be accounted for by the fact that this year it was found impossible to give the usual prizes. The brewery and railway horses were nearly all de- corated, however, and presented a cheerful aspect, even amidst the dullness of the weather. About the most noticeable was a horse and waggon driven by Geo. Daven- port, in the employ of the London and North-Western Rail- way Co. At the front of the waggon, on a raised pedestal, was placed a stuffed monkey, surrounded by an arch bear- ing the words "Success to the Lon& i and North-Western Railway Co," and holding in its banes a pair of ribbon reins and in its mouth a clay pipe. This novelty in the way of May Day decorations caused no little amusement. Another horse, driven by John Hulse and belonging to the same Company, was very prettily adorned with artificial flowers and ribbons. Maim LOCAL BOARD.—An ordinary monthly meetiol of this Board was held in the Board-room. Lymm, on Thure• day evening. There were present—Messrs. Cameron (in the chair), Dewhurst, Rogers, Wooley, Forster, Gibbon, Thoma- son, and Appleton; Mr. Ridgway' (clerk), Mr. Mullard (assistant clerk), and Mr. Wilson (engineer).—The Sewer. age Works: The Clerk, referring to the inquiry held on the 3i'd April by Mr. Harrison as to the Board having authority to borrow £1,650 for the purpose of constructing sewerage works, :.‘ald he had received a letter from the Local Govern- ment Board enclosing an official sanction t, borrow that amount. —The Chairman: That shows that the inquiry has been satisfactory so far as the Government inspector was concerned.—The Clerk said it would be necessary to pass a resolution authorising the getting in of tenders for the carrying out of the work, and also a resolution to authorise the borrowing of the money.—The Chairman: We begin de note now as far as the work is concerned ?—The Clerk: Yes.—lt was agreed that a special meeting of the Board should be held to consider the plans, &c., which would then be submitted by the engineer.—Alleged Nuisance: The Chairman read a letter from Mr. 'T. Richardson calling the attention of the Board to the great nuisance which existed In the neighbourhood of Booth's Hill, owing to people standing about the footpath, using bad language and insult- ing passers-by. Many drunken men, the letter continued, left the beerhouse near at hand, especially on Saturday and Sunday !fights, and added to the nuisance. He (Mr. Richardson) was informed that it was in the power of the Board to put a stop to such nuisances, and he would be I glad if they would take steps to do so —Mr. Thomason' said that the police when spoken to about the matter said the matter had been formerly taken out of their hands by the Board, and the Board must look after it. There was no doubt a great nuisance.—Mr. Dewhurst : We have no busi- ness with it.—The Chairman thought it was certainly not the Board's business to go and pick up drunken people from the road.—Mr. Thomason believed that the only reason for sending the complaint to that Board was to get the matter into some channel as the police would not interfare.—The Chairman suggested that they hand it over to the nuisance committee to discuss. (Laughter.)—Mr. Dewhurst : That is very unkind, Mr. Chairman.—Mr. Thomason said that in consequence of what had been complained about it was hardly safe to go to church on a Sunday night. —Mr. Dew- horst : I quite agree with you about that, but I don't think it is the Local Board's duty to do anything. I never thought that we were the guardians of the morals of the people.—Mr. Thomason: The police won't do anything at all, and say it is the Board's duty.—Mr. Deivllurst : The police must be made to do their duty.—The Clerk said that if be bade grievance of the kind be should first write to the superintendent, and if nothing ails done then, to the chief constable, or even to the 11. roe Secretary.—Mr. Thomason: That is what it will come to at last.—After a little further Conversation the matter dropped.—This was all the business of public interest.

THE REPRESENTATION OF WARRINGTON. A meeting specially convened by circular to the mem- bers of the Warrington Libeial Association—the Liberal " 200 "—w a s held in Wycliffe Hall, on Tuesday evening. The object of the meeting was to take into consideration the letter of Mr. McMianies, M.P., which we published in our last issue and which announced his intention to retire from the representation of the borough at the close of the present Parliament. There was an unusually large attend- ance, and the proceedings throughout were of the most har- monious character. Mr. S. Rigby, J.P., President of the Association, occupied the chair. The following were a few of the gentlemen present:—Messrs. S. Rigby, J.P., Z. Armitage, J.P., Councillor John Platt, Councillor James Barker, Alderman Holmes, J.P., Rev. J. Yonge, Rev. T. Ripon, Geo. Blackburst, Walter Cartwright, Councillor F. Monks, J.P., George Plumpton, John Harrison, George Wal- lington, jun., F. A. Roberts, C. S. Burgess, J. Mounfield, jun., John Craik, jen., John Crosfield, J.P., John H. G-or- nail, Noah Legge, J. Dunbobbin Councillor C. Broadbent, J.P., Councillor W. Pierpoint, W. Bibbv, T. P. Taylor, J. Strange, John Podmore, H. Thornton, J. W. Hall, T. Flood. J. Hedgecock, A. Stirrup, Leslie Barker, W. Wright, W. C. Baines, William Stirrup, P. T. Winskill, jun., Councillor F. Dixon, R. Siddall, Dyson Whitham, Alderman Webster, Absolom Taylor, William Grimshave, Charles Simpson, Jae. Haynes, R. Roberts, Thomas Miller, W. Crosskill, George Holford, J. J. Sanderson, S. Jones, J. Davies, Jas. Woods, John Burnes, jun., William Perry, A. Browne, J. T. Fair- dough, A. H. Corney, E. Twins, and William Twiss. The CHAIRMAN having read the circular convening the meeting, next read the letter which he had received from Mr. MclAinnies (previously published) and added that he was sore they were all in deep sympathy with their es- teemed member under the circumstances which had caused , him to say he could not look forward to being their candi- date at the next election. He thought their first business should be to express their thanks to him ,for the great ser- vices he had rendered in the past to the Liberal party in Warrington. (Applause.) Mr. Joao CROSFIRLD then moved the following resolu- tionz—" The members of the General Council of the War- rington Liberal Association desire to express to John Gor- don McMinnies, Eeq , M.P., their hearty appreciation of the invaluable services he has rendered to the Borough of Warrington, and also to the Liberal paiLy, and, while deeply and sincerely regretting that the state of his health has rendered it impossible for him to accept the candidature of the party at the next general election, hope that he may speedily recover his usual 'rigour and be able on many occasions to assist us with his presence and advice." (Applause.) He said he did not I doubt that the first thought which they all bad in hearing of Mr. McMinnies' letter was that they should, if possible, induce him to re-consider his decision ; but he could assure them that there was ho hope of that being done. He was very sorry to say that his friend had come back from Spain where he had been in search of health, in a worse state than be was in when he left home. Mr. McMinnies had rendered valuable services to Warring- ton before he was member, but that was as nothing to the sacrifice be had made since in his determination to do his duty to his constituents. He knew from personal observa- tion that he had attended to his duties in Parliament when ought to have been trying to recruit his energies away from the House of Contmons. He had, in fact, sacrificed himself to a sense of duty, and the least they could do was to pass such a resolution as he had to propose. (Applause.) Mr. H. Weernear seconded, and Mr. S. BARLOW supported the resolution, both gentlemen testifying to their admiration of the conduct of Mr. McMinnies as member for Warring- ton, and expressing their deep regret that they were likely to lose his services in t..e future. The motion, on being put to the meeting, was adopted with cheers.. The CHAIRMAN said it now became their duty to consider what further steps they should take. He feared that meet- leg was too large to go, at that stage, into the question of the selection of a suitable candidate, and would suggest that a committee should be appointed to consider the matter and niport to a further meeting. (Applause.) This suggestion being approved, the following gentlemen, after some little discussion, were constituted a committee with the object stated by the Chairman, who had in the meantime left the meeting, amid cheers, in order to catch a train to his residence in Chester :—S Rigby J.P. (chairman), L Gilooley,W Stirrup, J G McMinnies, M.P.,Councillor John Crosfield, J,P., Councillor John Platt, H Whitham, T Flood, Councillor C Broadbent, J.P., Councillor F Monks, J.P., F A Roberts, and H Roberts (sec.) Mr. CROSFIBLD, who took the chair on Mr. Rigby retir- ing, said the committee would be open to receive suggestions from Liberal electors as to suitable candidates; and Mr. H. ROBERTTS said if any such communications were forwarded to him he would see that they were laid before the com- mittee. He proceeded to explain that they had a favourable register, and if they remained united they were certain of victory at the next election. (Applause.) The proceedings were then brought to a close.
SHOCKING DEATH AT A FORGE.

Mr. Brighouse, coroner, opened an inquiry at the Unicorn Inn, Winwick-road, Warrington, yesterday evening, into the circumstances attending the death of a young man named Frederick William Nurse, aged 17, the son of James Nurse, el barman, who resides at 22, Watkin-street. The deceased met with a shocking death on Wednesday at Bewsey forge, Where he was working in Na. 4 sheet mill. Ile is des- cribed to have been in the act of raising one of the rolls with a hand screw, when his foot slipped and he was caught be- tween what is called the " wabbler " and the coupling box, and fearfully mutilated. He was removed to the lodge at the forge by the foreman under whom he was working, and al- most immediately afterwards expired. The Coroner informed the jury that the works were under the regulations of the Factory Act, and it was his duty to send to the Inspector to inform him of the inquest so that he might attend. lie had communicated with the Inspector at Blackburn, and had received a telegram saying that he must communicate with the Inspector at Manchester, as the &lath occurred in his district. It would therefore be their duty to view the body and the scene of the accident, and then take formal evidence sufficient to adjourn the enquiry until the Factory Inspector could attend. The jury then viewed the body and were conducted to the scene of the accident by the manager of the works, Mr. Morris.

_ On returning, the Coroner explained that it was impos- sible, owing to definite instructions from the Home Office relating to accidents happening in works under the opera- tions of the Factory Act, to avoid a postponement o'. the inquiry, and then proceeded to take formal evidence. James Nurse, father of the deceased, said that his son was a sheet iron roller at the forge, and that on Wednesday he saw him alonh at 5-30 in the morning, and afterwards saw him dead the same day. Henry Beard, 95, Bewsey-road, a sheet roller in the em- ploy of Pearson, Knowles, and Co., Bewsey Forge, deposed that he saw the deceased at work on Wednesday morning. He was turning the screws, which was his own particular work, and witness, turning round, saw him between the " wabbler " and coupling box. Witness did not see the de- ceased fall, and when be did see him part of his chest was going through, and his head followed. Witness thought that the distance between the " wabbler " and coupling box wopid be about four inches. Nothing could be seen but his legs and the lower part of his body protruding from the hole. He (witness) pulled him out, and he was not then quite dead, as he moved slightly and groaned. Witness thought that he died at the lodge at the works. A juryman ob3erved that there must be great precaution

taken at the works to prevent more accidents than now oc• marred. Havins seen the machinery, he felt astonished that there were not far more accidents. The enquiry was then adjourned until 11-15 on Friday morning next.

WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The ordinary monthly meeting of this Authority was held on Friday morning, in the Board-room, at the Workhouse. The members present were—Messrs. W. Derbyshire. E. C. Cooper, Jos. Swinton, R. Kilshall, John Houghton, William Houghton, W. Gibson, Forster, R. Owen, jun., and W. Long (ex-officio), William Owen (surveyor), J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), and George Rawlings (inspector). APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN.— The Assistant Clerk intimated that the first business of the Authority would be to appoint a chairman and vice-chair- man for the ensuing year.—Mr. Cooper moved that Mr. Derbyshire be re-slected as chairman. Mr. Derbyshire, he said, had filled the post with satisfaction to the Authority, and, he was sure; to the ratepayers at large.—Mr. Owen se- conded, and Mr. John Houghton supported this proposal, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. Derbyshire, on taking the chair, said it was a great satisfaction to him to hear that he had given satisfaction to some extent to the members of that Authority in his manner of conducting the business. He was sure it would be his endeavour to carry out the Acts of Parliament which affected them, and also the bye-laws firmly and closely, and at the same time not harshly, to any of the ratepayers or to any member of that Authority. (Hear, hear.) He concluded by moving the re-election of Mr. Cooper as vice-chairman.—Mr. John Houghton having seconded this propoial, it was carried unanimously. TIME OF MEETING.—OR tne motion of Mr. John Houghton, it was agreed that the Authority should con- tinue to meet as hitherto at 10.30 a.m, on the first Friday of each month. PENKETH DRAINAGE DISTRICI.—The Assistant-Clerk stated that there had as yet been no answer received from the Local Government Board with respect to the applica- tion to make Penketh into a separate drainage district. They could therefore do nothing in the matter that day, but would have to convene a special meeting for the purpose of appointintr a Parochial Committee.—The Clerk said that Mr. Forster was present, and would perhaps be in a position to suggest certain names to be appointed as the committee. —Mr. Forster then gave notice that at the next meeting be would move that the following gentlemen constitute the committee, viz: Messrs Pilkington, Kerfoot, R Garnett, Routledge, H Hughes, R Boardman, and James Turner. He thought these gentlemen would form a very representative committee. IsrsrEcrou's REPORT.—Mr. Rawlings, in his monthly rep%rt, said that two samplea of water had been submitted to Mr J Carter Bell for analysis during the month, one from Mr W Shelton's house at Great Sankey, and the other from Mr Thomas Grime's at Tnelwall. Mr Bell said : " I consider both these samples of water are very good for Idomestic purposes. The solid matters in the waters is rather high, which would be inconvenient for boiler purl poses." 1 SURVEYOR'S REPORT.—Mr. Owen reported that on the 24th April he inspected the six cottages at Collins Green and found that the wore required by the Authority had been fulfilled with the exception of the re-building of two stair- case walls in two cottages occupied by Mr. J. Aspinall as house and shop. It appeared that the tenant did not wish the walls interfered with until he leaves, which he intended doing as soon as he had completed the erection of a house for himself. One of the staircase walls was in such a state that he ordered Mr. Aspinall to have it propped and made temporarily secure. Mr. William Bennett submitted plans of two cottages he proposed to form out of a barn and ship- pon adjoining the Cheshire Lines Railway at Padgate. So far as the buildings are concerned the plans were in accord- ance with the bye-laws; but the open space in front of part of the the cottages would not be of the full width required by the bye-laws along the whole frontage.—This plan was, however, adopted. MEDICAL OFFICER AND INSPECTOR.—Mr. Cooper gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the medical officer (Dr. Watkins) and the inspector (Mr. Raw- lings) be re-appointed on the same terms as hitherto.

ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE..—The monthly meeting of this Committee was also held in the Board room at the Work- house on Friday morning. There were present Messrs. John Rylands, William Darbyshire, George Blackburst, E. C. Cooper, John Greening, C. EL Cartwright, W. Balharry, G. Appleton; and W. Long, Ziba Armitage and A. McCorquo- dale (ex-officio) ; Mr. Owen (valuer), Mr. Sutton (clerk), and the assistant overseers of the various townships. APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN AND VICR-CIIMEMLN.—Mr. Z. Armitage moved the re-appointment of Mr. Rylands as chairman.—Mr. Derbyshire seconded. and Mr. Cooper sup- ported this proposal, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. Rylands, on taking the chair, said he was much obliged for the reception he had always received from them. He would not detain them by making any remarks, but he did think they might take credit for one thing, and that was that they had avoided any extremes. (Hear. hear.) They had no £1,0C3 of damages to pay, as a neighbouring Assessment Committee had had to pay recently. He was quite certain that he might safely say that if Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.'s works had been in this district there would have been no appeal. (Hear, hear.) That committee had always endeaveured to do as fairly as possible between the town- ship and the ratepayers, and hitherto they had succeeded. (Hear, hear.) He (the chairman) then moved that Mr. Derbyshire be re-appointed vice-chairrnan.—Mr. Cooper seconded this proposel, which was carried unanimously. THE TIME OF MEETINO.—It was agreed, on the motion ol Mr. Armitage, that the time of meeting should be 11 a.m, on the first Friday in each month, as hitherto. CANAL AND RAILWAY ASSESSMENT.—The Clerk read some correspondence which had taken place between him and Mr. H. Edmonds, with respect to the assessment of Sanke:,, Canal. In his first letter Mr. Sutton stated that with reference to the subject of canal assessments in the War- rington union the Assessment ComMittee had temporarily agreed to reduce the same by one-third, and he had certified the reduction to the respective parishes. The reduction would apply to the unpaid rates, and the whole subject of railway and canal assessments was having the consideration of the sub-committee.—ln an answer to this letter Mr. Edmonds wrote that he was surprised to hear that the Assessment Committee proposed to make so small an altera- tion in the assessment of canals, for after the verification of the figures by Mr. Owen he (Mr. Edmonds) could not con- ceive how they could arrive at any other conclusion than that it should be assessed at some small nominal sum. He hoped, therefore, to hear that the committee bad recon- sidered the matter, and were prepared to reduce the assess- I ment to such sum as the merit of the case fully justified.-- In a further letter sent by the Clerk he repeated that the whole subject of railway and canal rating was being con- sidered. If he (Mr. Edmonds) could not agree to the figures It would be necessary for him to send in a notice of objection. As regarded the unpaid rates he (the. Clerk) was quite sure the committee would not reduce the amount be- yond the extent mentioned in his previous letter..—ln reply to this Mr. Edmonds wrote that he had laid the matter be- fore the directors, and they had instructed him to prosecute an appeal agaiast the. assessments. They were unable to understand how the committee came to the conclusion to make so small a reduction after the facts which have been fnroiahed to their valuer.—After thelreading of a little fur- ther correspondence on the suject, a telegram was received from Mr Edmends,asking that the hearing of the case might be postponed as he had to attend a Parliamentary commit- tee that clay (Friday.)—After a few remarks bad been made by Mr. Cooper, ttari Chairman, and Mr. Appleton, the sub- ject was left over to the next meeting. VALUER'S REPORT.—Mr. Owen (the valuer) reported that, acting under the instruction of the committee, he had made the following valuations and entered them in the Union books:—Mr. Thomas Locker, wire works, Ellesmere- street, Warrington, gross value £42, rateable £3s.—Collins Green Colliery Co., Burtonwood. mine rent and rent for surface plant, gross value 24,669, rateable £4,569; and for the water sold 'to the St, Helens Corporation, gross £5OO,

rateable £425, as fixed by the committee in 1382.—Messrs. Greening and Son wrote him that the addition to their works would not be occupied for two months, and that as soon as the building was nearing completion they would communicate with him—He (the valuer) had gone over the property of Mr. S. Reynolds, Latchford, requiring ft-assess- tnent. Now that it was completed—that was the house, stables, and conservatories, together with the gardens, which had the total area of I acre, 3 roods 19- perches—he was of opinion au assessmen of—gross £2OO, rateable £l7O, would be a fair one to give.—The White Bull, Llorsemarket-street. He had inspected, these premises, and was of opinion the present assessment might be reduced from £lOO gross and 05 rateable to £B5 gross and £72 rateable.—The report was adopted.' THE LONDON AND NORTH•WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY AND ITS RATES—AS the meeting was breaking up Mr. Cooper asked if the London and North .Western Railway Company were again going to escape the next rate. The burden had to be borne by the people least able to bear it, while they were letting the company off in the meantime. He had hoped that the sub-commitee would have been able to report on the subject at that meeting.—The Chairman said he had made arrangements to do the same. He hoped they should deal with it before the next nteeting.—A Mem- ber: It will not be in this rate book.—Mr. Cooper : No, but it would have been if dealt with to-day.—The subject then dropped, and the meeting terminated.

PRESENTATION TO FATHER POZZI. On Tuesday evening the Rev. A. B. Foul, 0.8.13., late chaplain of the Total Abstinence League of the Cross, was presented, in the Total Abstinence League Hall, Warrington, with a token of esteem and appreciation by the members of the society, in the shape of a Missal. The ball was crowded to excess by members and friends. The Rev. Father Sumner, 0.5.8., occupied the ehair, and was accompanied to the platform by Rev. Father Pozzi, the Right Rev. T. A. Bury, 0.5.8., Rev. J. J. Thomas, 0.5.8. (chaplain). Mr. James Minion (president), Mr. L. Gillooly (vice-president), Mr: S. Mullins (secretary), Mr.D. Houghton, Mr. T. Houghten, and others. The CHAIRMAN said it was his pleasing duty to intro--' duce to them their late chaplain, the Rev. Father Pozzi. (Applause.) After an absence ef something like a year be came there to receive a mark of their love and gratitude. It Was about eight or 10 years since he founded and became chaplain of the League of the Cross, and during that time he had laboured week after week in conjunction with many who were then present, to further the end of total abstin- ence; and he (the speaker) knew that many who worked with him were then veterans and gloried in that title, and had continued members ever since its commencement and brought other members to aseist in putting down that great monster—drink. In old times they read of a great monster which used to ravage the whole country, but at last there came a great man named Hercules, who undertook to put this monster down ; it was hard work for him at first, but by his valour and perseverance he did manage to put it down. Well then, that monster may very well represent the great monster drink, which was always in the midst of them bringing people to ruin both in body and soul. He went on to say that Father Pozzi had dcne good work there. and although he had not been a Hercules he bad tried to make the Catholic League of the Cross a Hercules in the torn of Warrington. (Applause.) They coald not say that they had killed the monster yet, but he hoped that the good work would still go on. Reverting to that night's special object, he said that the testimonial which they were about to present to Father Pozzi did not in any way represent his labours in behalf of the League since he had been amongst theFn‘but he was sure Fattier Pozzi would look upon it as representing something more than that, that he would look upon it as representing their love and esteem for all the good be had done for them. (Applause.) In conclusion, he said there was another great friend there that evening; he referred to the Right Rev. Father Bury. (Applause.) The Right Rev. Father BURY said that be was very glad to hays the opportunity of saying a few words on the subject of the presentation to his old friend, Father Pozzi. (Ap- plause.) He was not able to be present at the last presen- tation, but he had determined to be present that night. He had known Father Pozzi a great many years, and be always had one and the sime opinion of him. He remembered in 1870, when he (the speaker) WAS appointed to that mission, one of the first things be did was to ask the Provincial to send him Father Pozzi to help him, and he got his request granted. Father Pozzi came to Warrington in 1871 and remained amongst them 12 years. During those 12 years the mission had prospered very much, and he might say that that lfappy result had been effected in a great measure by the exertions of Father Pozzi. He did not like to say too much about him as he was present ; he could talk a great deal better behind his back. In concluding his re- marks he said that most of the work that had been done was done by Father Pozzi. The Children of Mary had been es- tablished under his superintendence, and 'he need not men- tion the Confraternity, for that he had established 25 years ago. He did not include that in his work of the past 12 years, and although he had left them to work elsewhere, he thought that his heart was amongst them. He was sure the testimonial they were presenting him with would remind him daily of those from whom he had received it, and it would be a source of pleasure for him to reflect that the I offering was the outcome of a grateful spirit. (Applause.) I The Rev. Father Turmas, the present chaplain, said they bad already beard the reason why they were assembled there that night. Whenever they were pleased with any- body they showed their pleasure by words, but if very pleased they proceeded to deeds, and in order to show their appreciation of the good services done by Father Pozzi, they presented him sea proof of their good will with a mis- sal. They knew well enough that that present was not to be measured by what he had done for them. (Applause.) He thought that if one wanted to discover how much a priest was beloved by his people they need not seek it among the higher class, but down the courts and alleys. The ques- tion might be asked whether the priest of the mission was liked there' and since he (the speaker) had been in War- rington he had had frequent opportunities of testifying to the love and esteem in which the name of Father Pozzi was held amongst the poor people. (Applause.) He said it was his duty to present to Father Pozzi the testimonial which was before them, and in presenting the missal to him in his own name and in the names of the members of the League of the Cross, he would like to ask that he would not forget the members of the League of. the Cross in Warrington. The book bore the words—" Ptesented to the Rev. A. B. Pozzi, 0.5.8., by the members of the Warrington League of the Cross as a token of their esteem and respect as spiritual director for eight years." (Loud applause.) The Rev. Father Pozzi, who, on rising was greeted with cheers, said that be felt rather awed at the rapturous wel- come which they had given him. They had totally over-. powered him with the praise they had bestowed upon him ; he really felt that he had not deserved it. He thanked them very much. for that welcome, espe- cially the members of the League of the Cross for the beautiful present they had made him that evening. He could assure them that it had always been A satisfaction to him to labour in their midst- He said he had been two periods in Warrington, and when Father Bury made a request to his superiors for his return to Warrington, be (the speaker) did not know what to say on his part, for be felt a reluctance to leave the mission he was then serving; and on the other band he knew he had many kind friends in Warrington, for when he left previous- ly it was a sad parting on his part, and he felt sure it was on their's.also. (Applause.) He might say that when he undertook the extra labour of establishing the League of the Cross some eight or nine years ago, he did not expect aty remuneration from a material point of view. His sole object was to advance the interests of the noble cause in which they were engaged and the spiritual welfare of his flock. (Applause.) He esteemed that offering most sin- cerely, and looked upon it with feelings of the highest gra- titude: and when he considered that that was the third presentation from a distinct section of the Cathelic Com- munity, it was a source of consolation to him in his forced absence from them, that there did exist in his favour such an amount of sympathy. (Applause.) There had been many difficulties and disappointments to contend with dur- ing his labour amongst them, as many in that room could testify. and a difficult task it was to extend the spirit of advancement to the League of the Cross, but the present state of the League ought to be an encouragement to all of them in spite of their difficulties. He had taken great in- terest in the society and was anxious to know how it was progressing, and he was pleased to find that their numbers had increased, especially the younger portion of the League -,-the juvenile branch. (Applause.) He said he could not really accept all the kind words that had been spoken of him, he did not deserve them. Although he had the merit of sowing the seed, there had been others to whom a great deal of credit was die, and he would not by any means rob them of it. There had been chaplains who had succeeded him, and he had no doubt that they had devoted better talents than he had, and he wished to congratulate them upon having such zealous chaplains at the head of the League of the Cross. (Applause.) He was pleased to find that the League was still doing good in the town, and he remembered some time Father Bury saying to him that he (Father Bury) had witnessed a. great decrease of drunkenness amongst the Catholic body. At one time it was a most rampant monster, and seemed to thwart all their efforts and discourage them in the advancement of virtue and morality, but he, (Father Pozzi,) was glad to sea that temperance and morality were extending on all sides. (Applause.) Father Bury had given him encouragement in everything connected with the League of the Cross, and he applauded his efforts in trying to grapple with the evils of intemperance and in devoting that hall to that great cause. (Applause.) His great alto was to spread the principles of temperance, to eradicate the obnoxious weed of drunkenness, aOC4 to pro- mote that morality which their faith taught. (Applause.) He again expressed to them his gratefulness for The grand testimonial, and he assured them that it would bean induce- ment to him to make a memento fur them in the service of the Mass, and he hoped that God would give them thoee favours which he could not give, and which he hoped would conduce to their etmnal salutaticm. (Loud ap- plause.) A vote of thanks to Ithe chaleman, proposed by Mr. J. Momates, and seconded by Mr. D. HoPouros, was unani- mously passed. An excellent concert was given during the evering, in which Mrs Dagnall, Mr H Brown, Mr P Mather, acid Mr J Mullins took part. Mr T Mather actetl as accompanist.

Mr. Ben Brierley left Manchester by the 10-30 a.m. ex- press on Thursday for Liverpool., en route for New York. A large number of his friends, including al/ the members of the testimordal f%nd ~s.opamittze, aisembled to bid him good- bye.

div.head: FASHIONABLE WEDDING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: FASHIONABLE WEDDING AT WARRINGTON.

_ On Thursday morning the marriage of Mr. Sydney White of London, nephew of the proprietor of the Engineer, and Miss Mary Houghton, only daughter of Mr. W. Houghton, steel wire tnanufacttner,The Beeches, Moore, was solemnised in the Cairo-street Chapel, Warrington. The marriage seems to have excited much interest in the neighbourhood of the bride's residence, and also in Warrington, so that on Thursday morning the Cairo-street Chapel, of which Mr. Houghton is a prominent member, was crowded a consider- able time before eleven o'clock. the time fixed for the cele- bration of the nuptials. The interior of the chapel had been beautifully decorated for the occasion, the porches, pulpit, organ, windows, and in fact almost every possible part of the chapel having been tastefully wreathed with flowers and evergreens from the conservatories of Mr. F. Monks, Mr. William Long, and Mr. Houghton, and by wild and garden flowers. Prior to the arrival of the wedding party the organist played suitable selections on the organ, including a march by Smart and a pastorale by Hopkins, and as the bride, accompanied by her father, and followed by her retinue of bridesmaids, entered he struck no Men- delssohn's "March of the Priests." The anthem "Remem- ber" was then sung by the choir, after which the service was performed by the Rev. R. Pitcher, B.A. On the party leaving the chapel the organist struck up the "Wedding March," and .a number of prettily dressed girls strewed the aisle along which the bride and bridegroom passed, Outside the churchyard and a portion of Cairo-street. con- tiguous to the chapel were crowded with people who seemed to be greatly interested in the proceedings, and it was only with some difficulty that a way was kept clear for the car- riages by Chief Constable Hunt and a staff of policemen. By the time the party left the church, the rain, which had been threatening all morning, began to fall, but notwith- standing this fact, the people still remained in undiminished numbers, and the bride and bridegroom were greeted on the way to their carriage with an abundant shower of rice. The party were conveyed away from the chapel in eight car- riages in the following order :—First carriage, Mr and Mrs White; second, Miss Kenrick, Miss A Houghton, Mr 8 Davis, and Mr M Ashcroft ; third, Miss Booth, Miss Rough- sedge (St. Helens), Mr J Houghton, Mr W White; (mirth, Mr and Mrs W D Houghton, Mr Thorley, and Miss Dean ; fifth, Mr and Mrs W Houghton, Miss Wheatley, and Mr J Houeleton; sixth, Mrs J Heughton, Miss Woods, and the the Rev. R Pilcher 8.A.; seventh, Mr SHoughton,and Mr E Houghton ; eighth, servants. The bride, it may be men- tioned, was attired in a travelling robe, and the dresses of of the bridesmaids were plain but neat and becoming. Mr mid Mrs White, we believe, will spend part of their honey- moon at Colwyn Bay. and the rest on the continent. In the evening a gathering of the teachers, scholars, and friends was held in the Cairo-street school-room, when about 200 children were regaled with a substantial repast provided by Mr. W. D. Houghton, the father of the bride. The room was decorated with the following mottoes, appropriate to the occasion, viz. Welcome come and with good wishes go," "Health and happiness to the bride and bridegroom," "Hope on, hope ever," "Strength and union," and "May groom and bride be long allied." After tea the children indulged in various games, and subsequently the room was cleared for dancing, which was heartily enjoyed by the adult visitors, the children having been dismissed to their homes. The music was supplied by Mr. Ford's band, and refreshments were served on side tables. Amongst those who were present at the tea and subsequent gathering were the Rev. R. Pitcher, 8.A., Mr. Robert Pemberton (superin- tendent), Mr. C. Travers (secretary), Mr. William Rowlands (assistant secretary), Messrs. T. Birchall, J. Chalmers, J. 1 H. Knowles, T. Knowles, J. B. Mellor, W. Mullard, J. Owen, A. Penaberton, W. H. Travers, S. Wellings, Mrs. Chamber- lain, and the Misses Medlicott, Rogers, Wheeler, Worrall, ' Wright, Monks, Houghton, and Bancroft. In all about 270 tickets were issued to the adults and children. Before the latter were dismisa,d the Rev. R. Pilcher, 8.A., gave a short address, remarking alat he did not think that they shouid allow the children to leave without saying a few words on the occasion which had brought them together. They would see in very beautiful letters—more bautifal he had not seen in that school that they were present to say "Welcome come, and with goad wishes go" to the bride and bridegroom, and also to wish them both health and happiness. They all knew that Mr. Honehton had given them that very pleasant entertainment ia honour of the marriage of his daughter, and the children should not depart without having, from the smallest to the biagest, and the your)._ .; to the oldest, an opportunity of expressing how much , [ley had enjoyed Mr. and Mrs. Houghton'e hospitality, and how much obliged thev•were for the kindness they had received. It was not everyone who would remember the little children on an occasion of that sort, but Mr. and Mrs. Houghton had not only done so, but had been most prodigal in their endeavours to give the andchildren l Mrs. . pleasure.H tonHL tivlhr!nitinooßvEeßdT a pvEoltteß zoßf thanksT oti ,p superin- tendent tendent of the Sunday Scho ii. seconded, and bore testimony to the manner in which the children bad enjoyed their treat and informing them that on leaving the room they would each be supplied with some refreshment.—The motion was carried with aoplause.—The following members of the childrenbrid a l partyg a Sunday b san un Houghton, Miss Roughsedge, Miss Booth, Miss Kenrick, Miss Wheatley. and Mrs. Dean, accompanied by Mr. John Hough- ton, Me Frank Houghton, Mr. Ernest Houghton, Mr. Fred Davis, and Mr. A. Ashcroft. Dancing shortly afterwards commenced.
LATEST NEWS.

Toe Prince ef Wales has promised to attend the Royal Agricultural Society's show at Shrewsbury next July. He will be the guest of the Earl of Bradford. In The House of Commons Select Committee, yesterday, the committee decided that the preamble of the Blackpool Hallway Bill had been proved. Yesterday morning a married woman named Mary How- Kin, the wife of a ;stonemason, living at Clayton-le-Moors„ near Accrington, committed suicide by cutting her throat; with a razor.

No tidings have yet been received of the American liner State of Florida, which left New 'York en the 12th ult. for Glasgow, and is now eight days overdue. Twenty-fivet guneas per cent, was paid yesterday to effect reinsurance. Last night's Gazette publishes a despatch from General Graham, dated Suakim, March 30th, reporting, in terms of warm praise, on the conduct of the Naval Bilgade during the recent operations connected with the relief of Tokar.

The case of the Central News v. the Eastern Telegraph Company and the Exchange Company was resumed yester- day before the Lord Chief Justice and a special jury. Several witnesses gave evidence, and the hearing was again adjourned.

THE 'CROYDON TRAGEDY.—Fredrick Night was com- mitted for trial at Croydon yesterday for attempting to murder his child aged two years. The prisoner cut the child's throat with a razor, and afterwards attempted suicide in order to spite his wife, of whom he was jealous. Tint SCOTCH CROFTERS.—Yesterday a deputation of Scotch landlords waited upon the Lord Advocate with the view of refuting the statements that they had evicted tenants for giving evidence before the Crofters'Commission. The Duke of Argyle, in introducing the deputation, said the charges were wholly untrue. Summonses of removal for refusal of rent bad been issued, but it did not follow that they would be enforced. Other members of the deputation having spoken, the Lord Advocate said he was glad to be fully and accurately informed on both sides of the queation, as the Government were anxious to do only what was, just and right.

FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR STOCK- PORT. A shocking accident occurred on Thursday night on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnehirs Railway, near Stoek- port. Two labourers; Wm.Shawcross and George Hadfiel4, of Hyde, had been to Stockport May Fair, and having mis- sed the last train, were walking to Hyde along the railway. when they were met full in the face by the 11-45 train from Woodley to Stockport. Shaweross was completely decapi- tated, his head and hand being cut off. Hadfield was knocked to the ground, one arm was broken and his thigh severely cut. He was at once conveyed to the infirmary; where he lies in a very dangerous condition. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

The Lords Select Committee met again yesterday morning when Mr. Penaber, QC.,. continued for the promoters his cross-examination of Mr. Lyster, engineer to the Mersey Dock Board. The witnessargued that the low water channel would disturb the equilibrium of natural forces which kept open the estuary, and silting up would inevitably follow. He did think with regard to the channel itself that there would be more silting than could be removed by constant dredgings.—Sir Frederick Bramwell, C.E., was next called. He agreed that a reduction of the tidal capacity of the estuary would lessen the quantity of water flowing over the bar. The practical effect of the execution of the proposed works world be the diminution of tidal capacity. Accretion would certainly take place behind the walls, and in time the estuary would be silted up. —Cross-examined: Sir F. Bramwell stated that enormous benefit had undoubtedly accrued to Rouen in consequence of the works in the Seine.—Mr. Michael asked whether the position of Havre, Which was alleged to have been injured by the works, did not correspond to the position of Formby rather than Liverpool.—The witness said that was true to some extent, but the works proposed were analogous in bath the Seine and the Mersey.—The Committee then adjourned.

SCHEME FOR THE RELIEF OF GENERAL GORDON. Cmno, FRIDAY, EVENINCI,--The Egyptian Government has offered an influential Soudanese chief, now here, £5OOO to go to Khartoum and bring back General Gordon. The chief will go under certain conditions which the Govern- ment have under consideration.

The " Daily News " correspondent at Khartoum tele. graphs on April 21st as follows :—We are all safe here. Trade will be carried on, even if Khartoum be taken, for then we shall trade with the Mandi's men. ADMIRAL HEWITT'S MISSION TO ABYSSINIA. CAIRO, BRlDAL—Letters received here announce that Admiral Hewitt, who was expected. to reach Adowa on the 26th ult., has sent back the detachment of 200 Bashi Bazouks escorting him, as King John of Abyssinia would not allow troops to cross the frontier between Egypt and Abyssinia.

div.head: TONQUIN EXPEDITION.
div.p: THE TONQUIN EXPEDITION.
PARIS, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—The Government will ask Parliament for a further Touquin credit of forty-five mil- lion francs.

div.head: LA.ST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LA.ST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met at four o'clock.
Earl DELAWAIIII gave notice to ask the Government, on Monday, whether they would be willing to permit Turkey to send troops for the relief of Gordon.—The House then adjourned.
HOUSE OF conmeNs.

The House met at four o'clock. PROPOSED VOTE OF CENSIIRE.—Si7 M. BEACH said he intended to move the following resolution :—" That this House regrets to find that the course pursued by Her Majesty's Government has not tended to promote the suc- cess of General Gordon's mission; and that if such steps as might be taken to secure his personal safety were still delayed, on Monday, he would ask whether the Govern- ment would give him facility for bringing forward his motion."

TELEGRAPH CLERS.S.—Mr. FAWCETT, replying to Sir H. Maxwell said he could hold out no hope of improving the condition of the telegraph clerks who have not received promotion consequent on the last revision that took place in the department.

THE EGYPTIAN QI,JESTION.—Lord E. FITZMALTRICE, reply- ing to Mr. A. Bartlett, said all telegrams relating to General Gordon bad been produced, with the exception of those the publication of which would be attended with military danger to him. Replying to M. Labouchere, the noble lord had no information- as to the stoppage of a French jour- nalist at Dongola, on his way to the residence of the Mandi. The gentleman had Lis rights as a French subject.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Mr. Fhurhe, said the invitation to the conference on Egyptian affairs would be produced. He could not produce the answers, as all were not yet received.— Mr. &mums said, on going into Supply, he should call at- tention to the subject.—Mr. GTADSTONE, in reply to Sir S. Northcote, said on Mbliday the Army Estimates would be taken; on Tuesday morning, if his motion was agreed to, the Cattle Diseases Bill ;. and on Thursday the Navy Estimates. BustwEss —Mr. Gladstone then moved that until the end of June the House should meet on Tuesdays and Fridays at two, the pressure of public business rendering the motion necessary.

THE SELECTION OF A LIBERAL CANDIDATE. Sir,—As one who was present at the meeting of the General Council of the Warrington Liberal Association last Tuesday night, I wish to enter my protest against the in- accurate and misleading paragraph published in reference thereto by your contemporary, the "Guardian," on Wed- nesday last. The statement that "during the meeting, and subsequently, the merits of several gentlemen for the vacancy were discussed," is totally incorrect, And I have little doubt that the paragraph in question, as ,well as the letter signed "Elector," which appeared in the same issue, are from the same source, and are both animated by an in. tention too obvious to be mistinderstood.—Youss, , _
AN OLD RAD.
THE NEW. WESLEYAN SCHODI.S.
Sir,—Your "neutral contemporary " in its gift of a repe- sentation of the new Wesleyan Schools haa certainly mot told the whole truth.

A novice would imagine that the building:was surrounded by everything of a healthy nature, but I was muell as- tonished on visiting the site to find it surrounded by high walls, two or three stables, and their ammoniacal associa- tions, and a number of privies. . . .

Is this what the Wesleyan body call legislating ft)r the masses ? Surely not ; it is a continuation of a system of overcrowding and detective ventilation which ought not to be tolerated by our health authorities,and it is a.mystery to me how the plans have been sanctioned by the officials of that body. Surely the Borough Surveyor or Medical Officer of Health cannot have been coasulted ?—Yours, &UNITAS:

Prebend- ary Grier, Vicar of Rugeley. Speaking in reference to "local option," the rev. gentleman said:—" He (the vicar) was certain that men who occnpied like positions with his own through the country would not lend their support to parliameatary candidates at Oa next general eleation who refuse to support measures for the moral elevation o. he poor. The Church existed kr the natiomand the secutity .of her position and property would be too dearly bought by the perpetuation of a griming oppression and a disgraceful ;in. It would be disastrous if the clergy were again to be found the political allies of the supporters of a huge national wrong. Better a thousand times that the Church should be dis-stablished and disouclowed, and her ministers turned out of their homes with their families, without a penny of compensation, than that her great influence and prestige should be used as a handle to the perpetuation of an octious vice." Are all the Church parsons in Warrington alike so overawed by brewery influence that they are afraid to raise a single protest against a connection so degrading p—Yours truly, AJAX.
